en: The First Chapter of the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
Oṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa. The Introduction: At the commencement of this work, one who desires the completion of the undertaking without obstacles [offers] to the Goddess of Speech—
By being censured, they bring about the humiliation of the Goddess of Speech herself.
Invocation:
May that Goddess of Speech, whose splendor is as beautiful as the autumnal moon, illuminate for my mind all objects of inquiry, dispelling the continuous darkness.
The fruitfulness of this [work] consists precisely in its fruits of poetry, which are expressed through poetic composition.
He states the fruits of poetry:
"Since the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of human life occurs even for those of dull intellect through poetry alone, its essential nature is therefore defined."

The attainment of the fruit of dharma is indeed well-established through the means of instruction regarding engagement in what ought to be done and avoidance of what ought not to be done— such as "one should act like Rāma and others, and not like Rāvaṇa and others.
And so it has been said:
“Devotion to excellent poetry produces proficiency in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as in the arts; it creates splendor and joy.
Furthermore: “O Blessed One, the attainment of the constituent parts of poetry [arises] from the service of the lotus feet of Lord Nārāyaṇa...”

From Vedic statements such as, "A single word, well-employed and correctly understood, fulfills one's desires in this world and in the heavenly realm," the attainment of the goal is also well-established. In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, [it is said that] the attainment of the meaning is... [the sentence continues].

The attainment of liberation (*mokṣa-prāpti*) is established; it is the attainment of one's own goal, because it is the fruit of the dharmas produced by that [treatise], and because it instills proficiency in the sentences conducive to liberation.
Indeed, the attainment of the four aims of life (*caturvarga-prāpti*) from the Vedic scriptures results only from hardship due to their lack of aesthetic flavor (*nīrasatva*).

It arises from the intellects themselves; because it generates a mass of supreme bliss, even for those of tender intellect, it arises precisely from poetry and nothing else. Now, one might ask: "If that is so, why should those of mature intellect exert effort toward poetry when the Vedas and Śāstras already exist? This objection is not valid.
It must be said: for a disease that is to be pacified by pungent medicine, would it not be more appropriate for a patient to employ white sugar as a remedy?
Furthermore, the worthiness of poetry as something to be pursued is also stated in the Āgneya Purāṇa:
"Human birth is difficult to obtain in this world; therein, knowledge is very rare;
poetic talent is difficult to obtain therein; and therein, fame is very difficult to obtain."
And in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa it is said that poetry is a boat for crossing the three goals of life:
"Whatever poetic discourses there may be, and all songs whatsoever—
these are the limbs of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears the form of sound."
For that reason, the essential nature of that poetry is being defined; by this, its subject matter is also demonstrated.

Now, when we inquire what the essential nature of poetry (*kāvya*) is, someone has proposed this definition: "It consists of word and meaning that are free from defects, endowed with qualities (*guṇa*), and furthermore, sometimes adorned with figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*). This, however, requires reflection. For instance, if it were accepted that only that which is devoid of defects constitutes poetry, then...
“It is a humiliation for me that my enemies are there, and even he is a mere ascetic;
yet he too destroys the race of Rākṣasas right here while Rāvaṇa still lives! (First Chapter)”
"Fie, fie upon Śakrajit! And what was the use of Kumbhakarṇa waking him up?
What is the point of these arms, which were so eager to plunder the wretched village of heaven?"

If [it were argued that] because this world is marred by the defect of indecision (*avimarṣa*), it would not possess the nature of poetry (*kāvyatva*), on the contrary, it would follow that it is the highest form of poetry due to its possession of *dhvani*; therefore, there is the defect of being both under-defined and over-defined. If it is objected: "But surely only a certain portion here is defective, and not the whole?"

In that case, since the presence of a defect in a certain part would be the cause of its being non-poetry, while the presence of *dhvani* in another part would be the cause of its being excellent poetry, there would be nothing— neither poetry nor non-poetry— that could be characterized by both of these simultaneously. Nor can it be argued that those who find fault with only a certain portion of a poem [are not poets].

Are defects such as vulgarity (*duṣṭa*) and so forth [defects] only in certain cases? Rather, they are defects in poetry in every instance. For it is thus: if they cause a diminution of *rasa*, which constitutes the very soul of poetry, their status as defects is not even admitted. Otherwise, there would be no established distinction between permanent (*nitya*) and non-permanent (*anitya*) defects. As stated in the *Dhvanyāloka*: [text follows].
“The defects such as those corrupted by grammar (*śrutiduṣṭa*) and others which have been shown,
are declared to be abandoned when they occur in a poem whose soul is *dhvani*.”

Furthermore, in this way, poetry would have either very few subjects or no subjects at all, because a work entirely free from defects is in every respect impossible. If it is argued that the particle *nañ* is used here in the sense of "slight" (*īṣad*), then [one might say] "poetry consists of word and meaning with slight defects"; however, in that case, the status of being poetry would not apply to those [works] that are entirely free from defects.

If it is argued that when possible, these two are slightly defective, this too must be stated in the definition of poetry, just as the piercing by insects and so forth is excluded in the definition of a gem. For piercing by insects and the like are not capable of subverting the gem-nature of a gem; rather, they [merely affect its] acceptability.
To establish this very gradation, even those [verses] in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* that are defective in terms of *śruti* (phonetics) and so forth are considered here as poetry. And it has been said:
"The status of poetry is held to exist even in defective works, provided that there is a clear emergence of rasa and the like, regardless of whether they consist of mere insects, stones, or jewels."
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, furthermore:

"The qualities (*guṇas*) are not established as having a distinct nature from word and meaning; for, according to the statement beginning with 'Because the qualities have rasa as their sole essence... they are the attributes of the principal element (*aṅgin*), namely rasa, or [they belong] to itself [the word]," and so forth.

Because it has already been established by that very [argument]. If it is argued that it is justified through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) due to its being the cause of the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*), even so, it is incorrect. For instance: does aesthetic flavor exist or not in those two—word and meaning—which are intended to constitute the very nature of poetry? If it does not exist, then even the status of being "poetry" (*kāvya*) is lost.

It does not exist, because the qualities (guṇas) follow the positive and negative concomitance of that [taste]. If it does exist, why is there no qualifying term such as "both possessing taste"? If you argue that this is understood through the necessity of otherwise explaining the words of the teacher, then it would be more appropriate to say simply "possessing flavor" (*sarasau*) rather than "possessing qualities" (*saguṇau*).

For one should not say "regions of the east" when it ought to be said "regions of the east"; why then is it said "regions of the north"? If it is argued that by the statement "word and meaning possess qualities," the intended meaning is that word and meaning which manifest those qualities are to be employed in poetry—no, for [the qualities] do not... [manifest themselves].

Even the power of suggestive words and meanings serves only to enhance poetry; it does not constitute its essential nature. For it has been said: "The word and meaning are the body of poetry, while rasa and the like are the soul; the qualities (guṇas) are like robustness and so forth, and the defects (doṣas) are like lameness and so forth; likewise, the style (rīti) is like..."

“Just as there are specific arrangements of grass, so too are there ornaments such as bracelets, earrings, and the like. By this, the statement that “there is also some [poetry] without ornament” is refuted. Its meaning is: “In this context, even those words which possess ornaments that are clear and manifest are [intended by] the word ‘ornament’ (alaṅkāra).”

[It is called] "poetry" (*kāvyam*). In that regard, even the *alaṅkāra* (ornament) and the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*) contribute only to the excellence of poetry. By this, the statement by the author of the *Vakroktijīvita*, namely that "oblique expression (*vakrokti*) is the life-breath of poetry," is also refuted; for *vakrokti* is of the nature of an *alaṅkāra*. And as for what some [say]...
It is stated in the *Daśarūpaka*:
"He who took away my maidenhood is indeed that same bridegroom; those same mango blossoms are the arrows of the God of Love.
This is the first chapter.
Those mature kadamba breezes, fragrant with the scent of blossoming mālatī flowers,
and I myself am still here; yet, even so, my heart yearns for the practice of love upon the bank of the Revā river at the foot of a vetasī tree.

This is indeed so; for here, there is a clarity of doubt rooted in the figure of speech *vibhāvanā* (causation by something other than the usual cause) combined with *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation). By this [it is said]: "Poetry is that which is free from defects, possesses excellences (*guṇas*), and is adorned with figures of speech (*alaṅkāras*)."
The poet, by composing works imbued with aesthetic flavor (rasa), attains both fame and joy.

By these and other such arguments, the instability of poetry has been refuted. As for what the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* stated—"Dhvani is the soul (*ātman*) of poetry"—does this mean that *dhvani*, consisting of the three forms [of matter, ornament, and rasa], is the soul of poetry, or is it merely the form of rasa and so forth? It cannot be the first.

Because [the definition] would over-extend to things such as a *prahekhikā* (a type of dramatic performance). If you say the second [definition], we reply: "Yes. Now, if *dhvani*—consisting solely of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth—is indeed the soul of poetry, then [consider this verse]:
"O you who are immersed here, look at me for a moment!"

"If you do not serve Rantideva, you will fall into my power"—if one asks how there can be the designation of "poetry" (*kāvyavyavahāra*) in such examples where only the matter (*vastu*) is present, we reply that here too it is because of the presence of a semblance of aesthetic flavor (*rasābhāsa*). Otherwise, [the verse] "Devadatta goes to the village... [would also have to be considered poetry].
If it were so, then even a statement such as "It is thus," which conveys a suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) consisting of following that [truth], would possess the status of poetry (kāvyatva).
If you say, "Let it be so," we reply: No; for only that which possesses aesthetic flavor (rasavat) is accepted as poetry.
For the purpose of poetry is indeed the bestowing of a mass of happiness through the tasting of aesthetic flavor (rasāsvāda), unlike the Vedas and the Śāstras.
The meaning of the Sanskrit: "She is immersing herself here; therefore, I shall create a diversion during the day itself.
Do not, O lady, cause me distress by binding me with your love. Commentary:
*Sāhityadarpaṇa*.

For those of tender intellect, such as princes and other disciples, there is the instruction regarding the engagement in what should be done and the avoidance of what should not be done—namely, that one should behave like Rāma and others, and not like Rāvaṇa and others; for this has been established by the ancients. Thus it is stated in the Agni Purāṇa:

"Even when verbal ingenuity is predominant, it is rasa alone that constitutes the life here. Thus it was stated by the author of the *Vyaktiviveka*: "No one has any notion of the soul of poetry being anything other than the form of rasa and so forth. And the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* has said: "Indeed, for the poet..."

"The attainment of selfhood for those who merely subsist on the three modes of conduct occurs through the *itihāsas* (histories) and so forth"—thus [it is said]. Now, if it is objected that in that case, certain flavorless (*nīrasa*) verses occurring at the end of a composition would not possess the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*), we reply: no. For even within a flavorful work, there may be verses lacking rasa...

For, just as in the case of individual verses (*padya*), their possession of aesthetic flavor (*rasavattā*) is accepted only through the aesthetic flavor of the composition (*prabandha*). As for the conventional usage of the term "poetry" (*kāvyavyavahāra*) even in that which is devoid of flavor (*nīrasa*), it occurs because of the presence of qualities (*guṇa*) that manifest [excellence], the absence of defects (*doṣa*), and the existence of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*); this refers to the composition of poetry possessing flavor and so forth.

It is indeed identical [to the previous definition]. As for what Vāmana stated, namely, "Style (rīti) is the soul of poetry," that is not so, because style is a specific kind of arrangement (saṅghaṭṭanā). And since arrangement consists in the configuration of parts, it is distinct from that [soul]. Furthermore, as the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* has said:
“The meaning (artha) and the sensitive reader (sahṛdaya)—which was intended as the soul of poetry—have both been stated to have two divisions:
the expressed (vācya) and the implied (pratīyamāna).”

In that regard, the claim that the denoted meaning (*vācya*) constitutes the soul of poetry is refuted by the very contradiction of one's own statement, namely, "Suggestion (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry. Therefore, what then is poetry? It is said: (3) Poetry is a sentence whose essence is aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

We shall define the nature of rasa. Rasa alone is the soul [ātman], for it is the essence that sustains the life of this [poetry]; without its brilliance, the status of being poetry is not admitted. Thus ends the first chapter. It "tastes" (rasati).

By virtue of its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti-yoga*), the term *rasa* also includes emotions (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and so forth. Among these, an example of *rasa* is as follows:
"Having looked at the bedchamber, rising slightly and slowly from the bed—"

Having kissed the face of her husband— who had long feigned sleep— with full confidence, the young woman noticed his cheeks bristling with horripilation; then, with her face cast down, she was kissed for a long time by her smiling beloved.

For this is the sentiment (rasa) known as erotic in its aspect of enjoyment (sambhoga-śṛṅgāra). An example of a transitory emotion (bhāva) is found in the work of the Mahāpātra Raghuvānanda Sāndhivigrahika:
"In whose stride the ocean was measured, and upon whose back the circle of the world and the sky [were contained]..."

In his staff is the Earth, in his claws the Lord of the sons of Diti, in his feet Heaven and Earth, in his anger the host of serpents, in his burden the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), in his hands the demon Pralamba; in his meditation is the entire universe—salutation to this one who is the family of the unrighteous! Salutation to him! Salutation! Salutation! *Note: This verse appears to be a riddle (praśnottara) praising Śiva, where the "unrighteous" (adhārmika) family refers ironically to the divine manifestations he bears.*
In this [verse], the aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) is the state of love (*rati*) directed toward the Blessed One. An example of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) is as follows:
“The honey-bee, following its own beloved, drank from the single vessel of the flower;
and the black antelope, vying with her, scratched the deer-mate who had closed her eyes in sport.”
For here, because the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) of enjoyment has animals as its object, it is a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).
The same applies to other cases. Furthermore, what is the nature of defects (*doṣa*) in poetry? It is said:
(4) Defects are those factors which detract from it [the rasa].

Defects of grammar (*śrutiduṣṭa*), lack of full meaning (*apuṣṭārtha*), and improper diction (*vācya*), which— like being one-eyed or lame— are manifested through the medium of the body or the wife [of the speaker], and defects such as the explicit naming of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) or the direct expression of the poet’s own name (*svaśabdavācyatva*),
like stupidity and so forth, directly diminish the *rasa* which is the very soul of poetry; thus they [are defects] of poetry.
In the *Sāhiladarpaṇa*, the "establishers" (*sthāpakas*) are mentioned; we shall likewise state specific examples.
It is now stated what the nature of these "weighty" [qualities] is: (5) "The qualities (*guṇa*), ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), and styles (*rīti*) are declared to be the causes of excellence.
The qualities are like gold and so forth; the ornaments are like bracelets, earrings, and so forth.

The *rītis* possess specific configurations of constituent parts. Just as [the body] through the medium of the physical frame, these [styles], by means of the words and meanings, enhance that very *rasa* which constitutes the soul of poetry; thus, they are called the "enhancers" (*utkarṣaka*) of poetry.
Although here the qualities (*guṇas*) have *rasa* as their substratum, nevertheless, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) in this context refers to the...

The term "suggestive" (*vyañjaka*) is applied metaphorically to both the word and its meaning; therefore, it has already been stated that words which manifest the qualities (*guṇa*) are those which enhance the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). We shall provide specific examples of these as well.

Thus [ends the work] of the illustrious poet Śrī Viśvanātha, who was a bee at the lotus-feet of the venerable Nārāyaṇa, a pilot for the ship of the essence of literature, the supreme establisher of the path of sound (dhvani), a mine of jewels among poets, a king of the land, a lover of the courtesans of the royal court, and a great minister (mahāpātra) in charge of foreign affairs.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Definition of the Nature of Poetry," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa composed by Rājaśekhara.
He states the nature of a sentence:
(6) A sentence is a collection of words endowed with semantic competency, expectancy, and proximity.

Competence (*yogyatā*) is the absence of contradiction regarding the mutual relationship between word-meanings. If this were absent, even a sentence such as "he sprinkles with fire" would be a valid sentence.
Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the lack of completion in the cognition [of the sentence meaning]; it consists in the listener’s desire to know.

[If] a sentence were merely that which possesses form, then even such expressions as "A man is an elephant" would have to be considered sentences, as they possess form. A sentence is a sequence of words that is free from expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Even when there is an interruption in cognition, there is still the perception of a second word.

In a sentence, there would now be a syntactic connection between the word "Devadatta," which has been uttered at this moment, and the word "goes," which is uttered on another day. Here, although expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and compatibility (*yogyatā*) are properties of the meanings of words, they are metaphorically designated as properties of the words themselves.

(7) A collection of sentences is a "great sentence" (*mahāvākya*), provided it is endowed with semantic competency (*yogyatā*), expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and contiguity (*āsatti*). (8) Thus, a sentence is considered to be of two kinds.

Thus, [it is established] by way of both subordinate sentences (*vākya*) and great sentences (*mahāvākya*). And it has been said: "For sentences whose own meanings are complete, a state of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) arises again through their combination, depending upon the relationship between the primary and the auxiliary."

In this regard, an example of a sentence (*vākya*) is: "The dwelling was empty," and so forth. An example of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) is the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, the *Raghuvaṃśa*, and so on. Since it has been stated that "the faults of words [apply] to the sentence," one might ask: what is the definition of a word (*pada*)? To this, he says:
(8) [A compound] is tall; its position is that which conveys a single meaning through connection with the application [of its members].

For example, "a jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*). The term "capable of being used" (*prayogārhāḥ*) excludes nominal stems (*prātipadika*). The term "mutually connected" (*ananvitāḥ*) excludes sentences and great sentences (*vākya-mahāvākya*). The term "single" (*ekāḥ*) excludes groups of multiple words that possess mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*). The term "conveying meaning" (*arthabodhakāḥ*) excludes [individual phonemes] such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*. The plural number (*bahuvacana*) is used because there are many [such words].
The name has not been discussed.
In that regard, it is held that there are three types: the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
He states their respective characteristics:
(11) That which is to be understood in the primary sense is conveyed by denotation (*abhidhā*); that which is indicated is considered to be conveyed by indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
There are three powers of a word: *abhidhā*, *lakṣaṇā*, and *vyañjanā*. These are defined in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*. Among them, the first is *abhidhā*, because it conveys the conventional meaning.

When an elder commands a middle-aged person, "Bring the cow," and perceives that the person has begun to act accordingly, the child first understands the meaning of that sentence to be "the object denoted by this word is that lump of flesh possessing a dewlap. Immediately thereafter, [he hears] "Bind the cow, bring the horse..."

In passages such as “naya,” etc., one determines the established view that the word *go* has the meaning “possessing a dewlap, etc.,” and that the words *grāma* and *vana* have the meanings “bringing” and “forest,” respectively, through the insertion (*āvāpa*) and removal (*udvāpa*) of the syllable *oṃ*. Sometimes this occurs through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with well-known words. For example:

For example, from the instruction of a reliable person (āpta), such as "Here, in the interior of a blossomed lotus, the bee drinks honey," or as in the case of "This is what is denoted by the word 'horse'. And that function of a word which,
making known an object established by convention, is not mediated by any other [function], is denotation (abhidhā).
[The name] ||
(12) You are born from that [source], and [you excel] in qualities, substances, and actions.

Genus (*jāti*) is that which exists in things such as the *gopiñcha* (a type of ox) and is [the universal] such as "ox-ness" (*gotva*). Quality (*guṇa*) is an established property of a real entity (*vastudharma*) that serves as the cause for imparting a distinction; for qualities such as whiteness differentiate a cow and so forth from those of the same class, such as black cows. Substantive words (*dravyaśabda*) denote a single individual.

Hari, Hara, ṛṅ, ittha, ḍavittha, and so forth [are examples of substances]. Actions, such as cooking and the like, are properties of things (*vastudharma*) whose nature is to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*).

For this collection of operations, consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages such as placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, and stirring with a ladle, is what is denoted by words such as "cooking. Indeed, these very [actions] constitute the differentiators (*upādhi*) of the individual (*vyakti*).
Your two [reasons] are not new, because the fault of deviation (vyabhicāra) would apply to them.

Now, indication (*lakṣaṇā*): When the primary meaning is obstructed, that power by which another meaning—either through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*)—is understood as being connected to it, is called indication; this is a transferred capacity.
The Second Chapter:

In expressions such as "Kaliṅga is a brave man," the word *kaliṅga* and others, being impossible in their own primary sense (svārtha) as a particular region and so forth, through the power of the word (*śabdapratyā*), [denote] the people associated with that [region].

He rejects [the following] views: for instance, in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," because the word "Gaṅgā" and others denote a primary meaning consisting of the river itself and so forth, they—being impossible in the context at hand—convey the bank and so forth, which are related to it through a relation such as proximity; that [conveying] is what is designated by the word (śabdavārpitā).
The secondary [meaning] is either based on its own nature or derived from the association with the primary sense; it is called "transient" (praticalā).

In the former case, it is simply conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or established renown (*prasiddhi*). In the latter case, as in the expression "the hamlet is on the bank of the Gaṅgā," it serves the purpose of communicating to the listener an excellence of coolness and purity that does not belong to the literal sense.

[The word] *bana* [is used]. Lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in defining anything whatsoever as related even without a [logical] cause, it was therefore said: "either by convention (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*). Some, however, cite "skilled in action" (*karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*) as an example of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Their intention is as follows: "the word *kuśa*..."

The primary meaning derived from the etymology "khāti" (he cuts), which consists of grasping with the tips of *kuśa* grass, is impossible in the present context; therefore, it conveys the sense of "dexterous," which is connected to the common property of discernment (*vivekatva*).
Others do not think so, even though the meaning consisting of grasping with *kuśa* grass is indeed obtainable through etymology.

Because that which possesses the form [of the etymological derivation] alone is the primary meaning. For the occasion for the linguistic derivation (*vyutpattinimitta*) of words is one thing, while the occasion for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is another. If the occasion for the linguistic derivation were the primary meaning, then even in the case of "the cow sleeps" (*gāḥ śete*), there would be the suffix *śa*; for by the rule "from the root *gam* comes the suffix *ḍe*," the suffix *ḍe* is applied to the verbal root *gam*.
Because the word "cow," having been etymologically derived, is employed even at the time of sleeping.
He states its subdivisions:
(14) When there is a superimposition of another [meaning] upon the primary meaning for the sake of establishing the connection within the sentence-meaning,
this— occurring through the inclusion of even the self— is "indication by inclusion" (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*).

In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the basis for the indication (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) is as in "The white one becomes" (*śveto bhavati*). In the case of a motive (*prayojana*), it is as in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"The spears enter. For in these two cases, by means of the "white" and the "spears," [the underlying referents are indicated].

Since [the agent] cannot obtain a grammatical connection (*anvaya*) as the agent of the two actions—namely, the mere cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the act of entering—due to being devoid of consciousness, the terms *ātman* and so forth are employed to denote the person (*puruṣa*) for the sake of establishing this [agency]. In the former case, the suffix *ṇic* is absent because there is no purpose [for it]; in the latter case, [it is used] in the sense of "belonging to the person," such as in the case of *kuntādi*.

The purpose is the profundity of the intellect (*matigahanatva*). In this context, there is a distinction between these two: the inclusion of the *ātman* itself as the primary referent (*mukhyārtha*), whereas the inclusion of the *sacapakhalapāṣāṇa* (the stone of the wicked) refers exclusively to another.
It is precisely for this reason that it is said, "here [the word] has the sense of 'going' (*itv-arthīya*)."

(15) The surrendering of one’s own [primary] meaning for the sake of establishing the connection of another is *lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā* (indication by indication), because it serves as the cause for secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). When there is indication due to convention (*rūḍhi*) or purpose (*prayojana*), it is as in: “Kaliṅga is a man of violence.”

And as in the case of "the sound of cows" (*gavāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). For in these two instances—the word *puruṣa* (man) and the word *taṭa* (bank)—in order to establish their respective meanings, the words *gaṅgā* (Ganges) and *gāvaḥ* (cows) surrender themselves [to those meanings]. Or, for example:
"Much has been accomplished there; what more need be said? Your goodness is preeminently renowned."
O friend, from that moment on, you have always been seen by me as one who is merely smiling; [may you] grant a hundred blessings.

In this context, words such as "helper" (*upakṛta*) surrender their own literal meanings so that they may be construed within the sentence-meaning with those who do not help and so forth. Since the primary meaning—namely, the presentation of assistance—is sublated with respect to one who does not help, there is a contradiction of the primary sense; the connection consists in the expression of the opposite. The result is indeed [the communication of] harm.
This very [type of indication] is called "jahatsvārthā" (that which abandons its own primary meaning).

(16) Each of those is also twofold, by way of superimposition (*āropa*) and determination (*adhyavasāna*). Those [refer to] the fourfold characteristics previously mentioned. [End of] the Second Chapter.

(17) When the object [of the primary meaning] is not swallowed up [by the secondary], and there is a transfer of identity that produces pleasure, it is *sāropā* (superimpositional); when it is swallowed up, it is considered *sādhyavasānikā* (residual). The *sāropā* based on conventional usage (*ruḍhā*) as an indication by inclusion (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) is, for example: "The white horse..."

"He runs. For here, a horse possessing the quality of whiteness, whose own form is not suppressed, is perceived through its identity with the quality of whiteness inherent in it. As for the purpose (*prayojana*), as in: "These spears enter. Here, by means of the term "spears" (*kuntāḥ*), which is a general term (*sarvanāman*), there is the apprehension of the men carrying the spears.
The [metaphorical] imposition (*āropa*) characterized by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is as follows:
"The Kalinga man fights. Here, there is a relationship of locus and located between the man and the Kalinga. Regarding usage (*prayoga*), it is as follows:
"Clarified butter is life. Here, although clarified butter is merely a cause of life, it is [treated as] the effect.

The connection between the cause and its effect is perceived through identity with the subject; the purpose is that [the practice] produces longevity by means of its non-deviating nature and its accumulation in other locations.
Or, for example: when a king's servant is walking, one says, "The king is walking.

Here, the relationship is characterized by that of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). Or, for example: when a finger, which is a single part, is present, one says, "This person is here. Here, the relationship is characterized by that of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*).
In the *Brāhmaṇa* as well: "That is the Āma. Here, the relationship is characterized by identity (*tātkarya*). Regarding the pillars for Indra: "These are Indras.
"These are Indras. Here, the relationship is characterized by being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*).

The same applies elsewhere as well. Furthermore, *sādhyavasānā* (superimpositional) [metaphor] consists in the cognition of identity with something else regarding an object that has been swallowed up [by another]. Regarding its four varieties, the examples are the same as those previously cited.

Regarding the phrase "of the object" (*viṣayasya*): it means "of the object free from superimposition. If there is a cognition of identity with something else regarding that which is denoted by an employed word, then—by way of the presentation of the word-meaning produced by itself—there occurs a cognition of non-difference (identity) with respect to that which is delimited by a property other than the delimitor of the primary meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). This is what constitutes secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
The meaning is that there may be eighteen [types].
(Commentary): In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, all of those [metaphors] are pure when based on a relationship other than similarity.
However, based on similarity (*sādṛśya*), there are considered to be six secondary (*gauṇī*) types; thus, they are divided into sixteen.

These [six] are the eight varieties of *lakṣaṇā* when complete. Other relations besides similarity include the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth. Here, the examples for the pure (*śuddhā*) types are the same as those previously cited.

In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is metaphorical application (*gauṇī*) based on the apprehension of the primary sense (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*), as in: "These oils are pleasant in winter. Here, the word *taila*, having apprehended its primary sense—the oil produced from sesame—applies to oils such as mustard. As for the case of purpose (*prayojana*): [as in] "The king... [etc.]
As Māras and their like were passing by, [the people said], "These princes are going."

In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the material cause (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) which is "transferred" (*sādhyavasānā*), as in: "Oils are pleasant in winter. In the case of a specific purpose (*prayojana*), as in: "The princes are going."

The conventional figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on superimposition (*āropā*) is secondary (*gauṇī*), as in: “The King, Lord of Gauḍa, clears away the thorns. The purposive figurative indication is as in: “A *gobāhīka* [a cow-like person from Bahīka]. The conventional figurative indication based on identification (*sādhyavasānā*) is secondary, as in: “The King clears away the thorns.”
An example for the sake of purpose (*prayojana*) is: "He is a master of cows" (*gor jaspati*).

Regarding this, some say: "The qualities associated with a cow, such as being born in Gajāmanya and so forth, are indicated; and these serve as the grounds (*nimitta*) for the word 'cow' denoting the meaning of a Vāhīka."

[This] is consistent. For the word "cow" lacks the capacity to denote the meaning of a *vāhīka* (barbarian) when the conventional linguistic agreement (*saṅketa*) has not been grasped; furthermore, it merely causes the cognition of the object that is the referent of the word "cow.
Since the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) has ceased, and once ceased it does not arise again, others [hold that] by means of the word "cow"...

“It is not that the Vāhīka person is directly denoted [by the word ‘cow’], but rather, through the similarity of qualities co-present with its own primary meaning, it is precisely the qualities residing in the object ‘Vāhīka’ that are indicated. This too others do not accept.
For, in this case, is the meaning of the Vāhīka understood from the word ‘cow’ or not? Even in the first case, from the word ‘cow’—
Second Chapter.

[The word] is either from the deity or from a quality that has been indicated. By way of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), it is not the first [case], because it has not been conventionally designated (*asaṃketita*) for the object "Vāhīka. Nor is it the second, because [it would have to be] obtainable through invariable concomitance—

Because it is impossible for the object denoted by the word "cow" to enter into a verbal relation [with the meaning of "barbarian"], a verbal expectancy is fulfilled only by a word; thus, the second alternative is not tenable. For if the meaning "barbarian" were not understood from the word "cow," then its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that barbarian would be inconsistent. Therefore—

In this instance, the word *go* (cow), failing to obtain syntactic connection with the word *vāhīka* (barbarian) through its primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), indicates the meaning of *vāhīka* by virtue of a relationship based on common properties such as ignorance. The purpose [of this indication] is to communicate the excellence of the *vāhīka*'s ignorance and so forth. And this [type of indication] is called "guṇavṛtti" (metaphorical application) because of its connection with a quality (*guṇa*).
It is called *rati* (passion). But the former [type] is pure (*śuddhā*) because it is unmixed with figurative usage (*upacāra*).
For what is called figurative usage is merely the concealment of the perception of difference between two things that are extremely distinct, by means of the power of an excellence of similarity;
as in the case of the fire and the boy, but not so in the case of two white cloths, where there is no absolute difference.
This is the understanding. Therefore, in such cases as these, there is a secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
(18) Because the suggested meaning may be either hidden or unhidden, the figurative indications characterized by the result are of two kinds.

The eight varieties of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) based on purpose (*prayojana*) have been shown; these become sixteen-fold when each is divided into two types—obscure (*gūḍha*) and non-obscure (*agūḍha*)—according to whether the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of the purpose is hidden or manifest. Among these, the obscure is that which can be understood only by those possessing the intellectual capacity matured through contemplation of the meaning of poetry. For example: "upakṛtam... [etc.]
"In that regard, it is manifold. "Unconcealed" (agūḍha) means that which is perceived by all people due to its extreme clarity. For example:
"It is the intoxication of youth itself that teaches amorous gestures to women."
Here, by the term "teaches" (upadiśati), "manifests" (āviṣkaroti) is indicated;
and the excellence of this manifestation is clearly perceived, just like the subject matter itself.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
(20) These [sixteen] varieties are also twofold, according to whether the fruit resides in the substratum (*dharmin*) or in the attribute (*dharma*).
These sixteen types of *lakṣaṇā* mentioned immediately above reside in the substratum of the fruit.
Each of these becomes twofold by way of being the agent (*kāraka*) and the state of the phenomenon (*dharmagatatva*), resulting in thirty-two varieties.
He illustrates this in sequence:

"The sky is smeared with glossy, dark clouds; the forests are filled with the cries of peacocks exulting in the garlands of rain-clouds; the winds are laden with spray; and the peacocks' sweet warbling is joyful."
May my karma be firm and my heart be hard; I am Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, but what will become of Vaidehī? Alas, alas, O Queen, be steadfast!

When the indicated object (*lakṣya*) is a substratum (*dharmin*) whose nature is inherently difficult to tolerate— as in the case of Rāma— the result is the excellence of that very [nature]. In the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," when the banks and so forth are the indicated objects, the result is the excellence of qualities such as coolness and purity.
(21) Thus, these forty varieties of marks are recognized by the wise: eight are established in terms of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and thirty-two in terms of their fruit (*phala*). Furthermore:
(22) Each of these is also twofold, according to whether they reside in a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*).
These are the ones just mentioned. Among them, by way of being based on the word, as for example: "A hamlet on the Ganges."
As occurring within a sentence, for example: "Much has been done by you. Thus, there are eighty varieties of *lakṣaṇā*.
Now, suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is that function by which another meaning is understood when the primary denotative and other functions have ceased; it belongs to the word, its meaning, and so forth.

According to the principle that words, cognitions, and actions lack further operation once they have ceased, there is no determination of meaning beyond denotation (*abhidhā*) and the rest; thus, among the three functions— denotation, indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and suggestion (*vyañjanā*)— each brings about its own respective understanding.

When another meaning is indicated through the proximity [of words], that function of the word regarding its own meaning—whether occurring in a base (prakṛti) or an affix (pratyaya)—is called *vacana*.
It is the domain of such designations as "suggestion" (*vyañjana*), "resonance" (*dhvanana*), "communication" (*gamana*), and "conveyance" (*pratyāyana*). In that regard:

(24) Suggestion (*vyañjanā*) based on the word is twofold: that which has its source in denotation (*abhidhā*) and that which has its source in indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He states [the first], that which has its source in denotation:
(25) When a word with multiple meanings is restricted by [factors] such as association (*saṃyoga*), etc.,...
When there is a cognition of another meaning regarding a single object, that is *vyañjanā* (suggestion), which is based upon *abhidhā* (denotation).
And [the factors include] the word *ca* (and), the word *ādi* (beginning with), usage (*prayoga*), and so forth. For it has been said:

"Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*viprayoga*), similarity (*sāhacarya*), opposition (*virodhitā*), purpose (*artha*), context (*prakaraṇa*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactic uniformity (*śabdasāmarthya*), and proximity (*sannidhi*)."
"Capability, context, place, time, gender, and so forth are the causes of specific cognition when there is no delimitation of the word's meaning."

In the expression “Hari with the conch and discus,” the word *hari* denotes Viṣṇu alone through its association (*saṃyoga*) with the conch and discus. In the expression “Hari without the conch and discus,” it denotes that same [Viṣṇu] through its dissociation (*viyoga*). In “Bhīma and Arjuna,” *arjuna* refers to Pārtha (the son of Pṛthā). In “Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna”...
Thus ends the section on the hundred sons of Karma. “I bow to Khānu”:
here, “Khānu” means “I bow to the pillar” (khāṇu), for Khālu is Śiva. “The god speaks to me”: here, the god is Bhava. “The one whose banner is the sea-monster is angry.”
*Makaradhvaja* refers to Kāma; *purāriḥ* in the phrase *devaḥ purāriḥ* refers to Śiva;

*madhuḥ* in the phrase *madhunā mattaḥ pikaḥ* refers to Spring; *mukham* in the phrase *pātu vo dayitāmukha* refers to being face-to-face (*sāṃmukhyam*); and *candraḥ* in the phrase *vibhāti gagane candraḥ* refers to the moon.

In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, [the verse] "nidhiścitrabhānuḥ" (the treasure is Citrabhānu) refers to fire (*vahni*); "bhāti rajāī" (shines with dust) refers to the chariot-wheel (*rathāṅga*) because it is neuter; and "kharaḍa" is indeed the Veda.

Regarding the point that poetry does not produce a specific cognition (*viśeṣapratīti*), it was illustrated in that context [by the example of the jar]. However, some, being unable to accept this, say: "Even in poetry, pitch (*svara*) in the form of *kāku* (intonation) is indeed a producer of specific cognition;
likewise, even [pitch] in the form of the *udātta* accent and so forth, according to the method of recitation taught by the Sage, [produces specific cognition]. Regarding the jar...

"It is indeed appropriate to cite this as an example for the view that the specific cognition of rasa arises from the door (dvāra) and so forth. To this we reply: whether they be harsh sounds (*khara*), such as the *kāka* (crow-like) intonation, or the acute (*udātta*) accents and so on, these convey only a specific [emotional] state (*vyabhicāribhāva*) as the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya-rūpa*), and not the primary sense (*vācya*) of a word with multiple meanings (*anekārtha*).
This refers to the specific case where there is a desire for expression (*kāryanivākṣā*). Furthermore, if it were to be asserted that in certain instances,

even when multiple word-meanings are unrestricted due to the absence of constraints such as context (*prakaraṇa*), they are restricted to one by the force of a corresponding accent (*svaravaśena*), then in such a "wasteland" (*khale*) of [linguistic] practice, service (*sevā*) would be required.
This is a flight toward acceptance; yet it is not so. For this very reason, Ājya stated:

"In the context of defining *śleṣa* (paronomasia), [the author] says that in the path of poetry (*kāvyamārga*), *śleṣa* does not exist, and thus it is new. Enough with casting even a mere glance at the commentaries of those venerable authorities who rely [on such views]. From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)...

In such examples as "itāvamālanī," the state of the *śaṇa* flowers and others having the shape of lotus buds is conveyed through gestures such as shortening [the limbs] and so forth. Thus, when a single meaning has been restricted by the primary function (*abhidhā*),
that power of the word which causes the cognition of another meaning is *suggestion* (*vyañjanā*) based on the primary function (*abhidhāmūlā*).
As it was said by my father’s feet, the great poet of Vaṅga, the lord of great poets, the minister of peace and war, Śrī Candraśekhara, who delights in fourteen languages:
“Hūgalattivigraho manasiñjaṃ mammījayaṃsejamā...”
Possessing the majesty of a king, surrounded by serpents like the entire universe,
his desires fulfilled by the Lord, and maintaining a profound devotion toward the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva),
he was like a second Indra in heaven.
Having ascended the Name, his body adorned with sovereign power, he shines like the moon accompanied by Umā.

In this context, through the primary function (*abhidhā*) according to the poetic theme (*prakaraṇa*), the meanings of the words *umā* and *vṛṣabha*—namely, the Great Goddess Umā and King Bhoja, who is like a bull—are restricted; thus, by means of suggestion (*vyañjana*) alone, the meanings "jasmine" and "bull" are excluded. The same applies to other cases.
The *cāru* (the beautiful),
*vāmā* (the perverse), and so forth— (29)— that for whose sake [these] exist in the form of words (*sajagopāstra*) is the *prayojana* (purpose).
That by which this purpose is made known would be *vyañjanā* (suggestion), based upon *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

In cases such as "There is a sound in the manāya [river]," since the primary denotation (*abhidhā*) has ceased after conveying the meaning of the river-bank (*taṭa*) and so forth— having already conveyed meanings such as the collection of cows (*goṣa*)— and since the secondary metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇā*) has also ceased after conveying that same meaning of the bank, that which conveys the excellence of qualities such as coolness and purity is the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), which is based on the literal sense (*mukhya*).
Thus, having explained verbal suggestion (*śābdī vyañjanā*), [the author] now describes situational suggestion (*ārthī vyañjanā*):
(27) [Suggestion arises] from the speaker, the person addressed, the sentence, the proximity of others, the context, the place, the time, tone of voice, gestures, and so forth.
That which, due to a specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*), makes another meaning known is "arising from the meaning" (*arthasambhavā*);

this is connected with the term "suggestion" (*vyañjanā*). In that regard, when there is a specific distinction of the speaker, the expressed object, the context, the place, and the time—as in my [verse]:
The season is spring, and this flower-bowed god of love is enraged;
the winds carry the steady breezes that remove the fatigue of passion; and even this cuckoo here is cooing sweetly with its voice.
"My husband is far away; tell me, what should I do now?"
