"The sandalwood paste has completely vanished from your breasts; the redness on your lower lip has been rubbed away; your eyes are deeply smeared with collyrium; and your slender body is covered in horripilation.
O messenger, you liar, you have learned the arrival of my suffering from your own kinsmen!"
"You have gone from here to take the seed, but not again to the presence of that base man"—

this is a statement made with the contrary intention that she has indeed gone to his side. By conveying the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) "in order to sport," it is expressed through the excellence of the female messenger (*dūtī*).
An example of excellence through the presence of another [poetic figure] is as follows:
“O young woman, you shine like a lotus leaf trembling in the water,
resting upon the surface of a sapphire.”

"Because there is no one here and it is free from obstacles, you are confident; therefore, this place is secluded and suitable for a rendezvous"—this statement is addressed to a lover who has been invited. Herein lies the excellence of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), characterized by the solitude of the location and the absence of people.
The instigator.
(28) A broken sound in the throat uttered by the wise is designated as *kāku*.
Thus, the varieties of the *kāka* [bird] of the *u* vowel should be understood from the *śā* vowel and the others.
He instructed him thus:
"Alas, due to dependence on my guru, I must go to a very distant land. Behold, the young female crane shines upon the lotus leaf, motionless as it contemplates its flight."
"Placed upon a vessel made of *nimba* wood," so it is said. *Saṃ*:
"The meaning is that one should look here. *Ṭī*:
"This is the second chapter."
"O cuckoo rooted in the mango tree, O friend, he will not come during this season of fragrant breezes."
It does not go away; rather, it is suggested by the particle *kāku* that it will certainly go.
An example of excellence in gesture (*ceṣṭāvaiśiṹṣṭya*) is as follows:
"When the rogue was distracted by another woman,
the clever girl closed her toy lotus, having directed her intention toward that very spot."

The phrase "the twilight is the time for the secret signal" is indicated by a certain woman through gestures such as the closing of her eyes; in this same way, it should be understood that the distinction applies to the face and other parts, whether taken individually or collectively.

(28) This [suggestion] of meanings is considered to be of four kinds, each being threefold. Because meanings are either expressed (*vācya*), suggested (*vyaṅgya*), or both, all meanings are threefold. Among these, the suggestion of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha-vyañjanā*) is as follows:

"Springtime is honey," and so forth. An example of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is: "The sandalwood paste [is completely worn away]," and so forth. An example of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is: "O lady, move aside," and so forth.
The analysis of the nature of the base and the suffix will be elaborated later.
(30) The meaning is manifested by the word which is cognizable through it, and the word also rests upon another meaning.
If one [factor] is the manifestor, the other must be its auxiliary cause;

for since a word requires something else when it is a manifestor, [it follows that] even with respect to the object, if one is the manifestor, the necessity of another being its auxiliary cause must be admitted.
(31) It is considered to be of three kinds due to its being qualified by the three adjuncts, such as denotation and so forth.
Sound (śabda) is also [threefold]: denotative (vācaka), indicative (lākṣaṇika), and suggestive (vyañjaka). As stated in the Vākyapadīya:
"The denotative [sound] has denotation (abhidhā) as its limiting adjunct; the indicative has indication (lakṣaṇā) as its limiting adjunct."

[Otherwise] it would be a deceptive [position], being devoid of any limiting condition (*upādhi*). Furthermore: (32) Others maintain that there is a function called *tātparya* (intentional import) for the cognition of the syntactic connection of word-meanings;
they hold that the sentence is the indicator of that intentional meaning, which is its own referent.

The view of the Abhihitānvayavādins (proponents of the theory of "expressed connection") is as follows: since words cease from the cognition of individual word-meanings, it is the sentence—whose nature is that of a single unified meaning—that brings about the cognition of those meanings; thus, a sentence is defined as that which expresses the *tātparyārtha* (the intended meaning) or the *tātparyārtha-khodhaka* (that which makes known the intended meaning).
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Nature of the Sentence," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
Now, what is this "rasa"? It is said:

(33) "The permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), such as love (*rati*) and the like, when manifested by the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and likewise the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), becomes *rasa* for those possessed of sensitivity."
The determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth will be explained [later]. Because the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) are of the nature of ensuants (*anubhāva*), they are not mentioned separately.

In this context, rasa is manifested precisely by means of the transformation into another form under the guise of [the determinants] such as joy; it does not exist as a fully established entity, like a jar revealed by a lamp. As it has been said in the *Locana*:
[This is] by means of the causes (*kāraṇaiḥ*). [The objection is: "The usage [of the term 'rasa'] is like saying 'he cooks the rice' when it is actually the grains that are being cooked.

And here, since the state of being a rasa is already established simply by the employment of words such as 'love' (*rati*) and so forth, the further employment of the word 'permanent emotion' (*sthāyin*) is for the purpose of establishing that love and the others are indeed rasas.

The meaning is that for the ancient Naiyāyikas, who maintain that the understanding of the meaning of a sentence arises from the denotation [of the words] themselves— whether through the process of denotation (*abhidhā*) or through the residual trace (*anuvṛtti*)— first, in the case of those such as the Mīmāṃsakas and the Prābhākaras, who maintain that the denotation [of the sentence] is primary, the understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between the action and the agent arises first. Then...

The apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*). However, the recollection of a specific meaning arises from the co-occurrence with a particular word; what else could it be? Thus they say: "The earth is indeed fragrant. End of the third chapter. *Dīpikā*.

For the sake of the feet [of the verse]: consequently, emotions such as fear and anger are merely transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) within the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), heroic (*vīra*), and other rasas. As it has been said: "The supreme emotion, when abiding in the state of rasa, attains the condition of being relished.
The manner of its aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) is now described, containing within it a definition of its essential nature.
(34) Through the excellence of being, it consists of consciousness whose nature is bliss and whose light is unfragmented;
it is devoid of contact with any other object of knowledge and is a sibling to the savor of Brahman.
This aesthetic flavor (rasa), whose very life is the transcendent wonder, is relished by certain subjects as being non-different from their own mental forms.

The mind untouched by *rajas* and *tamas* is here called *sattva*. Thus, according to the manner described, there is a certain internal quality (*dharma*) that brings about aversion toward false objects; that is *bala* (strength), which consists of the predominance of *sattva* and the subjugation of *rajas* and *tamas*. And herein lies the cause—

The cultivation of the meaning of extraordinary poetry is as follows: this [aesthetic experience] is indeed one and indivisible, consisting of the manifestation of *rasa* (such as love) through the *vibhāvas* and other factors, and having the nature of a wondrous charm (*camatkāra*). We shall state the reason for this below;

its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) will also be explained according to the method to be presented. The term "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*) is used in the sense of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Wonder (*navaṭ*) consists of the expansion of thoughts regarding marvels; it is another name for astonishment (*vismaya*).

Therefore, this is the work of the illustrious Nāvacapāda, who was the most eminent among the circle of poets and scholars who were the heart-friends of his great-grandfather, the venerable Cāmavṛddha. Regarding this, Dharmadatta says in his own treatise:
"In the aesthetic flavor (rasa), the excellence of *sāraṇā* is experienced everywhere."
"In the essence of that aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), the flavor (*rasa*) is entirely concealed;
therefore, the wise Nārāyaṇa has declared that the marvelous (*adbhuta*) alone is the flavor."

"Some" refers to those who possess merit (*puṇyavat*). As it is said: "Those possessing merit perceive, like yogis, the complete measure of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Even though, according to the direction of the statement, "The tasting of *rasa* is the manifestation of the essence of self-bliss due to the distinction from objects such as food," [the experience] arises from the savoring of *rasa*.

In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, although [the distinction] is thus [denied], the usage of the object or the agent [as the subject] is accepted by resorting to an imaginary distinction, namely, that "rasa is tasted. As it has been said: "Merely the state of being tasted..."

"Because it is the essence (*bāra*), rasa is indeed not produced from the body of manifestation (*prakāśaśarīra*). Thus, in other similar instances as well, the remaining [cases] are to be understood through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). By this much, the nature of rasa as something produced has been stated; for it is a specific kind of denotation (*vyañjanā-vācyatva*) that constitutes its essence.
Having fallen into [this] desire, he then says:
"A lamp is considered a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of an object because it is the cause of another's cognition through its own knowledge;
otherwise, what distinction would there be between it and a producer (*kāraka*)? Thus he thinks—

If it is argued that, as with a lamp and a jar, there is indeed a distinction between the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), and thus how can there be "manifestation" (*vyaṅgyatā*) [of rasa], this is well said. For this very reason: this function of *rasāsvāda* (the savoring of rasa) is distinct from the operations of production (*kṛti*), attainment (*āpti*), and transformation (*vikṛti*). Indeed, for this reason alone—[it is called] *rasanā*...

Since [terms] such as *sthāyin* (the permanent emotion), *vyabhicārin* (the transitory emotion), and *vibhāva* (the determinant) are designations applicable only to the discerning (*vicaṣaṇa*), it follows that the agency of the discerning is established here; thus, the status of *rasas* such as *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and *vīra* (heroic) as being grasped through the process of aesthetic realization (*prasādhana*) is set forth. Now, one might object: "In that case, since the *rasas* such as *karuṇa* (pathetic) consist of suffering—"
It is argued that because it is a product of mental construction (*mathana*), it cannot possess the nature of rasa.
(35) As for the supreme bliss that arises even in rasas such as compassion (*karuṇa*) and the like,
the experience of those possessed of sensitivity is the sole authority in that regard.

By the word "etcetera," the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), and so forth are included. Nevertheless, another alternative is stated in order to seal the mouths of those who lack aesthetic sensitivity (*asahṛdaya*).
(36) Furthermore, when there is suffering in those [emotions], no one would be inclined toward them.

For no one devoid of consciousness acts for the sake of their own suffering; rather, it is observed that everyone engages with compassion and the like through an active inclination toward them. This concludes the third chapter, which presents another argument against [the opponent's position].
(36) Likewise, works such as the Rāmāyaṇa will become causes of suffering.

Since the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇarasa*) is a cause of suffering, it would follow that literary compositions such as the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which are dominated by the sentiment of compassion, must also be causes of suffering. [The opponent] asks: "But how can pleasure arise from things that are causes of suffering? [The author] replies:
(37) Causality is observed in those things such as sorrow that depend upon the world;
let it be granted that worldly things like sorrow and the rest arise within the world.
Since they have attained the status of extraordinary aesthetic excitants (*vibhāva*) by virtue of being based on poetry,
what harm is there in saying that the "face" [of rasa] arises from all of them?
Indeed, those very things such as Rāma’s dwelling in the forest, which are called "causes of suffering" in the world,

when presented in poetry and drama, abandon the status of being denotable by the term "cause" due to their possession of an extraordinary function of aesthetic manifestation (*vibhāvanā*), and instead become denotable by the term "extraordinary excitant" (*alaukika-vibhāva*).

Thus it is, sirs. And from those [passions], such as love (*surata*) and the bite of a tooth (*dantaghāta*), pleasure alone arises. Therefore, the restriction belongs to the world alone, namely: "from worldly causes such as sorrow and joy, worldly sorrow and joy arise. But in poetry, however—
"There is no fault whatsoever in the rule that 'from all [the factors] such as the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, only pleasure arises.
How then is it explained that from the sight or hearing of the life stories of Haricandra and others, even in poetry or drama,
tears and other such reactions arise?"

(38) Since [phenomena] such as the shedding of tears arise from the state of the mind, one might ask: "In that case, why does such a manifestation of rasa not occur for everyone through poetry? To this, he says:
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
(38) "At that time, no languor arises without the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion (*rati*) and the like."
Now, it is latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) that is the cause for the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
If the first [type of predisposition] did not exist, then even those such as the *naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins* and *mīmāṃsakas* would experience it;
if the second [type of predisposition] did not exist, then even some who possess passion (*rāgin*) would not experience the arousal of aesthetic flavor.
It is observed in the *Tantra* that it should be so; and it has also been stated by Dharmadatta:
"The members of the assembly who remain seated shall experience the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), but those who have departed from the stage are like wooden logs or heaps of earth."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: how can it be said that the arousal of the Rasa of love (*rati*) and the like occurs through Sītā and others—who are the causes for arousing love and so forth in Rāma and others—when they are [in fact] particularized? (40) There exists an operation (*vyāpāra*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and the rest, which consists in their being made universal (*sādhāraṇīkṛti*).
By his splendor, there arose the ocean, the mountains, and so forth.
The cognizer realizes his own self as non-different from that [universal].
But how, one might ask, can an impulse toward crossing the ocean arise in a mere human being? To this it is said:
(42) The confusion regarding Uṣā and others arises from the conceit of commonality.
Even for human beings, there is no fault in such acts as leaping across the ocean;
he states that even emotions such as love (*rati*) and the like are perceived through commonality (*sādhāraṇya*).
(42) "In the same manner, love and the other [emotions] are also perceived through commonality."

For even in the case of love and the like, if they were perceived as belonging to oneself, the audience would experience shame, agitation, and so forth; whereas if they were perceived as belonging to another, there would be a sense of wonder. He states that the excitants (*vibhāva*) and the other factors are also first perceived through universalization (*sādhāraṇya*).
The giver of the three [refuges] is one who thinks neither "this is another's" nor "this is mine," and neither "this belongs to another" nor "this belongs to me. (43)
In that savoring, there is no discernment of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
But even so, it may be asked: how is it that these excitants and the rest are said to be "extraordinary" (*alaukika*)?
It is said in reply:
(44) Having attained a supramundane activity such as the contemplation of negation (*vibhāvanā*), etc.,...

Their transcendence of the mundane world is an ornament, not a defect. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the figures of] *vibhāvanā* (poetic causation) and *anubhāvanā* (manifestation) are included. Among these, *vibhāvanā* is the state of passion (*rati*) and the like being rendered unfit for the sprouting of aesthetic relish (*rasa*) due to some specific [obstructing] factor. *Anubhāvanā*, on the other hand, is the manifestation of such passion and the like.

The cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consists in the very moment of understanding [the excitants and so forth] as having the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like; likewise, the "circulation" (*sañcāraṇa*) is the thorough circulation of that which has become thus.
Regarding the fact that the determinants (*vibhāva*), etc., function respectively as causes, effects, and concomitants, it is asked:
how can all three be said to be the cause for the emergence of aesthetic flavor? [Response: It is stated [as follows].
For even though causes move toward their effects, they do so according to form as perceived in the world.
In the awakening of rasa, the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are considered to be merely causes.
[Objection: If that is so, then how is it said that they appear as one in the relish of rasa? [Reply: When perceived, each one is first designated as a cause.
Then, for those possessed of consciousness, the entire collection of determinants (vibhāva) and so forth,
being relished according to the analogy of the flavor of a refreshing drink, becomes rasa.

Just as a certain incomplete taste arises in the juice of a *prapānaka* (refreshing drink) from the combination of sugar, black pepper, and other ingredients, so too here [in poetry] it occurs through the combination of the *vibhāvas* and so forth; this is the meaning.

Now, if rasa is produced solely by the combination of determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*), then how can it arise even when only one or two of these are present?
Thus it is asked in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
(47) If there should be attachment, the state of being a servant, or the like, toward one [person],
provided that it instantly implies the other, then no fault exists.
In some cases, it is understood through the force of the context and so forth; for example:
"A face with long eyes, possessing the luster of the full moon; arms sloping at the shoulders;
a chest with closely-set, firm breasts; and sides that are slender..."
Her waist is measured by the span of the palms, her hips are broad, and her feet have toes that rise upward;
her form was created by the Creator just as he had intended for a dancing moon.

In this passage, as Agnimitra gazes upon Mālavikā, the suggestion (*ākṣepa*) of the determinants (*vibhāva*), such as her form; the transitory mental states (*sañcāribhāva*), such as longing (*autsukya*); and the consequents (*anubhāva*), such as the expansion of the eyes in joy, occurs precisely through their propriety (*aucitya*). The same should be understood for other types of suggestion as well. "The Lord—"
To one who says, “the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) resides in the object of representation,” he replies:
(48) Because it is limited, mundane, and subject to obstacles,
the arousal of the emotion (*rati*) and so forth belonging to the character being represented would not constitute *rasa*.

For the arousal of passion (rati) in Rāma and others, arising from the sight of Sītā and so forth, is indeed limited, worldly, and subject to interruption due to the viewing of dramas and poems; therefore, how could it attain the nature of rasa? This is because rasa possesses characteristics that are distinct from these three [qualities].
And it dispels the *lañ* suffix [indicating] his being an imitator.
Furthermore,
(58) by the mere practice of phonetics (*śikṣā*) and so forth, the speech of Rāghava attains its true nature.
A dancer who merely displays [the performance] cannot himself be a relisher of the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
(50) Through the contemplation of the meaning of the poetic work (*kāvyārthabhāvanā*), even this [actor] becomes a fit recipient for the status of a refined spectator (*sabhyapadāspada*).
Third Chapter.
Furthermore, if even a fool, through the contemplation of the meaning of the poetic work, assumes for himself the form of Rāma or others—
Then he too would have to go into the midst of the assembly;
for this [self] is not something to be made known, because its own existence is never absent from cognition. (51)
For that which is to be made known, such as a jar and so forth, although it exists, may at times be unknown;
this [non-existence], however, is not like that, because it does not exist apart from cognition.
(52) Since this [rasa] consists of the nature of an object that is the synthesis of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth,
it is therefore not an effect;
for if rasa were an effect, it would have the cognition of the excitants and so forth as its cause.

It would be so; consequently, at the time of the cognition of rasa, the excitants (vibhāvas) and the rest would not be cognized, because the cognition of a cause and the cognition of its effect are never observed to occur simultaneously. Indeed, the cognition of the moon and the cognition of the pleasure produced by it cannot exist at one and the same time. [The same applies to] the rasa and its excitants...

The intention is that, because it is perceived as being of the nature of a collective representation (*samūhālambana*), it does not possess the temporal sequence of the cognitions of the *vibhāva* and other factors.
(53) It is not eternal, as it is devoid of prior cognition.
Even at the time of non-perception, its existence as consciousness persists;

for an eternal entity, there can be neither non-existence nor cessation at the time of non-perception, because it consists of bliss and is self-luminous by nature. It is distinct from effects and objects of cognition.
Even though existing, [he is so] by virtue of his power.
(54) Because it is the object of the reflective awareness of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth by those possessed of sensitivity.
Furthermore, because it is clearly experienced as consisting of supreme bliss,
non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is not accepted as its apprehender, according to the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
Likewise, because it lacks the capacity for association with verbal expression,
it is cognizable by indeterminate perception; for the capacity for the employment of speech belongs to those things cognizable by determinate cognition, and not to this.
Of Rama; likewise;
and not by way of direct perception.

"The manifestation of that [object] is not indirect (*parokṣa*), nor is it direct (*aparokṣa*), because it arises from words. Therefore, tell me: what is its nature? Thus he speaks regarding one for whom the manner of determining what has never before been heard or seen is as follows.
Therefore, this truly supramundane reality is to be known by those possessed of aesthetic sensitivity.
What, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence? To this he says:
(57) "The means of valid cognition here is held by the wise to be nothing other than *carvaṇā* [relishing] regarding that which is non-different from oneself.
*Carvaṇā* is tasting. And that [tasting] is "the self [of the aesthetic experience] arising from the fusion with the meaning of the poem (*kāvyārtha*)."...

[This refers to] the manner stated [in the verse]: “...arising from the dull [mind]. Now, one might ask: if rasa is not an effect, then why did the Great Sage (Maharṣi) formulate the definition: “The production of rasa results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāva)”? To this it is replied:

(58) Although this savoring (*carvaṇa*) has no status as an effect because it is non-different from rasa, nevertheless, since it occurs only occasionally, its status as an effect is metaphorically attributed to it by means of a figurative application (*upacāra*) of "being an effect."

(59) Its "inexpressibility" and so forth [are established] when it is represented as a *kye* suffix; that is, of that *rasa*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "inexpressible" (*avācya*) and other such qualities are included. Now, if [this is so], the third chapter...
He explains how the [emotions] such as *rati* and so forth, though merged into the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), can possess both luminosity and indivisibility:
(60) "Because the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arises precisely through the identity of the emotion (*rati*) and so forth with the subject's consciousness."

Therefore, its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) and its partlessness (*akhaṇḍatva*) are established. If passion (*rati*) and the like were distinct from the body of light (*prakāśaśarīra*), then its self-luminosity would not be established. But that is not the case, because their identity (*tādātmya*) is accepted. As it has been said:

"Even though the self (*ātman*) is not an effect because it is non-different from the *rasa*, nevertheless, by attributing the status of being an effect to it on account of its occasional nature, there is a conventional usage [of the term 'effect'] even with respect to the aesthetic emotions (*bhāva*) such as love (*rati*), which consist of the manifestation of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within that single essence. [And: "In the acceptance of identity (*tādātmya*) with pleasure and so forth..."

"And may you lie upon our bed of established doctrine for a thousand divine years and fall into the sleep of bliss. And: "Though non-different from the cognizer, it is made the object of the identity with passion and so forth brought about by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). [This refers to] the non-acceptance of the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition.

The Vedāntins themselves must inflict punishment upon those who hold such a view; for it is precisely because of their identity that this [rasa] possesses its indivisibility. Indeed, when the erotic and other sentiments are first perceived individually, yet manifest as having become unified, they attain the state of *rasa*. As it has been said:
"The determinants (*vibhāvas*), the consequents (*anubhāvas*), the involuntary states (*sāttvikas*), and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāris*)—
when first perceived as distinct parts, they attain indivisibility."

Thus: "In the ultimate sense, this [Self] is indeed indivisible, and it is to be known as the Brahman-tattva well-known in the Vedānta. Now, in response to the inquiry as to what those excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*) are, he explains the excitants (*vibhāva*).
(1) In the world, as well as in poetry and drama, the excitants (*vibhāvas*) are those factors that awaken passion.
For in the world, it is precisely those factors that awaken the love, laughter, and so forth residing in Rāma and others which constitute the essence of poetry according to the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.

Once they have been established, they are called *vibhāvas* because "by means of these, the aesthetic emotions (*bhāvas*) such as love in the audience are 'vibhāṣita'— that is, they are made fit for the manifestation of the sprout of relish. As it was said by Bhartṛhari:

“One regards Kaṃsa and others— who have had their forms projected by words and who have thus become objects of cognition— as if they were perceptually present, [and considers them] as the means [of accomplishment].”
Thus [it is said]. He states its divisions: (62) Its two divisions, known as the objective (*ālambana*) and the excitant (*uddīpana*), are both considered dead.
This is clear. And that [ālambana] is:

(63) the *ālambana* is the hero (*nāyaka*) and so forth, because rasa arises by depending upon him; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the heroine (*nāyikā*), the rival hero (*pratināyaka*), and others are included. Herein, that which is the *vibhāva* of the rasa...
He will be described in the section on the description of his essential nature. Among those, the hero (nāyaka) is:
generous, accomplished, of noble birth, possessed of great fortune, and endowed with beauty, youth, and vigor.
The leader is one who is capable, beloved by the people, possessed of brilliance, cleverness, and good character;
"capable" means one who acts with speed, and "good character" means virtuous conduct. A leader, or *nāyaka*, is one endowed with such qualities as these. He states the divisions thereof:
(65) The *dhīrodātta*, the *dhīroddhata*, and likewise the *dhīralalita*.
This first fourfold division is called "the wise and tranquil" (*dhīrapraśānta*).
And the "noble and firm" (*dhīrodātta*) is clearly [defined as]:
one who does not boast, who is patient, exceedingly profound, and possessed of great courage (*mahāsattva*). (66)

The *dhīrodātta* (noble-heroic) is described as steadfast, possessing hidden pride, and firm in his vows; he is free from boastfulness and does not proclaim his own faults. He is of great courage (*mahāsattva*), remaining unmoved by joy or sorrow.
This concludes the third chapter.

The state of one who has overcome [others]; one whose pride is concealed and whose arrogance is covered by modesty; one who is firm and has accepted his duty, such as Rāma, Yudhiṣṭhira, and others. Now, the *dhīroddhata* (the bold and haughty):
(67) he is devoted to deceit, fierce, fickle, and abounding in egoism and pride.

One who delights in self-destruction and is devoid of the qualities of a hero is called *dhīra-dhṛṣṭa* (the brave-impudent), such as Bhīmasena and others. Now, the *dhīra-lalita* (the brave-playful): (68) The *dhīra-lalita* is one who is free from anxiety, gentle, and constantly devoted to the arts (*kalā*).
*Kathā* refers to stories such as those concerning dance and so forth; for example, King Udayana and others in the *Ratnāvalī* and other works. Now, regarding the *dhīrapraśānta* (the calm and wise):
(68) one who abounds in common virtues, such as a twice-born (*dvija*) and so forth, would be *dhīrapraśānta*.
As, for example, Mādhava and others in works such as the *Mālatīmādhava*. Regarding these, he states the divisions based on their forms as *bhṛṅgārin*, and so forth:
(70) "By means of these—namely, those appearing in the forms of the *dākṣiṇya* (courteous), *dhṛṣṭa* (bold), *anukūla* (favourable), and *śaṭha* (deceitful)—there are sixteen types."
For each of these— namely the *dhīrodātta* and the others— there are sixteen types of hero (*nāyaka*), distinguished as *dakṣiṇa*, *ṣṭha* (śaṭha), *anukūla*, *jāḍyala* (jaḍa), and *dhṛṣṭa*.
(71) Among these, however, one who possesses equal passion for many women is called *dakṣiṇa*.

In the four types of heroines (*nāyikās*) who are dear to the heart, one who possesses equal passion for all is the *dakṣiṇa* (courteous) type of lover (*māyaka*). For example: "The daughter of the Lord of Kuntala remains at home; it is the turn of the King of Aṅga."
"This row of mango trees has been surpassed by the splendor of the lotus-eyed goddess,"—
having thus understood the report made by the women of the inner apartments regarding the Goddess, the King, his mind bewildered by indecision, remained silent for several *nāḍikās*.

Khālida (72): Even when he has committed an offense, he is not restrained; even when he is censured, he is not noticed. Though his faults are deep-seated, he speaks falsely; such is the ruined leader.
Save me! "I was about to swallow you whole with my mouth wide open; then, having been struck by your foot, I have suddenly released you."
O friend, because she was unable to do anything there, she shed tears;
yet even her anger, O wise one, stirs curiosity in the mind of meditation regarding that fair-limbed woman.
(73) The *anukūla-nāyaka* (the favorable hero) is one who is devoted to a single woman and attached exclusively to that heroine. For example:
"O friend, our garments are not beautiful, nor is our necklace brilliant..."
Her gait is not graceful, she does not laugh, nor is there any pride in her;
yet even the trees in the forest say, "Her beloved is so fortunate that he does not cast his glance elsewhere.
By this much alone, we consider the whole world to be sorrowful.
This person is indeed deceitful, for he displays affection for one while secretly practicing unpleasantness toward another.

Furthermore, the *bhaṇṭa* hero is one who, though his affection is fixed upon only a single heroine, displays his passion for both heroines and secretly performs disagreeable acts toward the other. For example:
When you suddenly heard that the monastery of another woman was adorned with a girdle set with gems, your waistband itself became loosened;
yet this very thing has been held by you as a word sweet as honey and clarified butter.
“Though she is overwhelmed by poison, my friend does not acknowledge even the slightest [suffering].
This is the section on Intensity (*tīvra-pariccheda*).
(75) And because these [intensities] are of three kinds, all [characters] are classified as superior, middling, or inferior.
Thus, forty-eight varieties of heroes have been described.

[This applies] to all sixteen types of the *amukta* [drama]. Now, as an incidental digression, [the author] describes their many attendants: (76) When the plot (*itivṛtta*) is situated at a distance, there should be a *prāsaṅgika* [character]; however, he is slightly inferior in those qualities, and he is indeed his *pīṭhamarda*.
In the narrative connected to the hero’s extensive activities, there is an assistant named Pīṭhamarda, who is slightly inferior to him in general qualities;
for example, Sugrīva and others for Rāmacandra and others. Now, the great waves of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
(77) The attendants of Pūtanārāsa should be parasites, servants, jesters, and the like;
they are devoted, skilled in jesting, capable of dispelling the anger of their wives, and pure.
