a sweet-toned utterance accompanied by the opening of the eyes and a shaking of the shoulders and head is derisive laughter (avahasita).
A loud laugh with tearful eyes and disheveled limbs occurs when one is exceedingly exhausted,
as in my case: having studied the words of the Guru— the Vedānta scriptures— for five days and for three more days.
And having inhaled these arguments of logic, the venerable Kukuṭamitra has arrived;
his full development is to be seen in works such as the *Naṭakamelaka*.
Śrava—
And for one who experiences fear, if that [fear] is not directly bound anywhere at all, [then it is non-existent].
Nevertheless, this [rasa] is perceived through the power of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and the other factors;
the excitants and so forth are apprehended as non-distinct due to their commonality.

Then, this rasa of his is experienced by the members of the assembly. This concludes the second chapter. In the same manner, it should be understood regarding the other rasas as well. Now, the Karuṇa (the Pathetic).
(230) From the loss of what is desired and the attainment of what is undesired, the aesthetic flavor known as compassion arises.
This [rasa], which has Yama as its presiding deity, is called Kapotavarṣa by the wise;
here, sorrow (śoka) is the permanent mood (sthāyibhāva), and that which is to be lamented is considered the objective basis (ālambana).
Furthermore, his state of being a fisherman and so forth constitutes the excitant (uddīpana),
while the consequents (anubhāvas) are the reviling of fate, the king, weeping, and so on.
Changes in complexion, perspiration, sighing, suppression of breath, and incoherent speech;
as well as despondency, delusion, epilepsy, disease, exhaustion, and loss of memory.
In the thicket of sorrow, the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as intoxication, anxiety, and others arise.
The object of pity (*śocyam*) consists of those whose kinsmen have perished and so forth. As in my *Rāghavavilāsa*:
"In the forest, what is this binding of matted locks for you, and what is this charming body?"
"Clearly, by the method of joining these two, one should fashion a Śirīṣa flower with one's own hand."

Now, this is the lamentation against fate by Daśaratha, afflicted by the grief born of Rāma’s exile to the forest; examples may likewise be cited for the loss of kinsmen, separation from loved ones, the destruction of wealth, and so forth. Its full development, however, is to be seen in the Strīparvan of the Mahābhārata. This [type of pathos] differs from *karuṇa-vipralambha* (pathos of separation).
Māra:
(239) This rasa, such as *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), is distinct because its dominant transitory emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is sorrow.
In *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is passion (*rati*), which is further caused by the desire for union (*sambhoga*).
Now, the Furious (*raudra*):
the Furious has anger as its stable emotion; it is red in color and has Rudra as its presiding deity.
In that context, the object is the excitant (*ālambana-vibhāva*), and that which excites it is the enhancer (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).
For example:
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"By means of the fist, movement, falling, distortion, cutting, and tearing..."
Its intense excitation arises from the agitation of battle and similar causes;
it manifests as the knitting of eyebrows, the biting of lips, the clenching of fists, and the striking of the ground.
The narration of one's own heroic exploits, the hurling of weapons,
as well as supernatural powers such as the display of the power of flight and so forth.
Fierceness, impetuosity, horripilation, perspiration, trembling, intoxication,
delusion, shamelessness, and the like are the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas).
"By those men who have committed, experienced, or witnessed this grave sin, you have been abandoned without regard for the ocean; may they,
together with the enemy of Naraka (Kṛṣṇa), along with Bhīma and Arjuna..."
"I have created a great mass; with marrow, fat, and flesh, I offer this oblation to the directions."
He states the distinction of this [deity] from the Buddha-vīra: (233) "In this case, the redness and the dark eyes are the distinguishing features from the Buddha-vīra. Now, the Vīra..."
The heroic sentiment of the highest character has energy as its dominant emotion.
This [region] is declared to have Mahendra as its presiding deity and to be characterized by rains of gold;
the excitants (ālambana-vibhāvas) are considered to be those who are to be conquered and so forth.
The objects to be conquered and so forth, as well as gestures and the like, constitute its excitants (uddīpana);
the consequents (anubhāvas) in that context would be the searching for allies, self-restraint, and so on.
The third chapter on the transitory emotions (*sañcāribhāva*):

These are fortitude, intelligence, pride, memory, reasoning, horripilation, agitation, munificence, righteousness, and anger; he (the hero) may be endowed with these along with compassion, thus being fourfold.

Furthermore, the hero (*vīra*) is of four kinds: the hero of generosity (*dānavīra*), the hero of righteousness (*dharmavīra*), the hero of compassion (*dayāvīra*), and the hero of battle (*yuddhavīra*). Among these, the hero of generosity is exemplified by Paraśurāma: "Generosity has as its limit the unfeigned giving away of the earth sealed by the seven oceans. In this instance, [the heroism] belongs to Paraśurāma.

The state of enthusiasm for renunciation is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). It is manifested by the excitants (*vibhāva*) consisting of the recipients—the Brāhmaṇas—and the objective excitants such as truth, resolve, and so forth; it is indicated by the consequents (*anubhāva*) such as the renunciation of all one's possessions;
and it is brought to full development by the transitory emotions (*sañcārībhāva*) such as joy and fortitude.
He practices the heroism of generosity, like the Dharma-hero Yudhiṣṭhira:
“The kingdom, wealth, body, wife, and sons—
whatever in this world belongs to me, that I am always ready to give to him.”
The hero of war is exemplified by Śrī Rāmacandra:
"O Lord of Laṅkā, let Janakajā be given; Rāma himself requests her.
What is this delusion of your mind? Remember the code of conduct; nothing has yet been done [by us]."
"If it were not so, this arrow— drawn to the bowstring by my hand, its feathers stained crimson like the bandhūka flower— would not have spared the necks of Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and Triśiras.
An example of the hero of compassion (*dayāvīra*) is Jīmūtavāhana.
“Blood still flows from the openings of your veins; my own flesh remains even now.
Yet I do not see that you are satisfied; why then, O Garuḍa, have you ceased from devouring?
Such states as these are to be understood as in the previous examples.
Now, the Frightful (bhayānaka). In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*: (275) The Frightful [sentiment] has fear as its determinants (vibhāva), Kāla as its presiding deity, and...
Kṛṣṇa, who is skilled in the knowledge of reality, is considered to have assumed the form of a woman.
When fear arises from that [object], it is considered a "connected" (sambandha) [fear];
moreover, the teacher of something even more terrible would then become its "excitant" (uddīpana).
The external manifestation (*anubhāva*) here consists of changes in complexion, faltering speech,
fainting, perspiration, horripilation, trembling, looking toward the directions, and so forth.
Longing, agitation, delusion, terror, languor, dejection,
apprehension, epilepsy, confusion, death, and so forth are the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas).
For example:

"The dwarfish man, having been cast aside by the eunuchs because of the absence of any human reckoning, enters the interior of the water, thinking himself to be a mere servant of the inner chamber. And so forth.

Now, the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome): (236) The *bībhatsa* rasa is said to have disgust as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*); it is declared to be blue-colored and to have Mahākāla as its presiding deity.
The foul-smelling flesh, fat, and marrow are considered the objective basis (ālambana);
therein, the falling of worms and so forth is cited as the excitant (uddīpana).
Spitting, gaping of the mouth, contraction of the eyes, and so forth are considered the consequent emotions (anubhāvas) therein; likewise, there may be transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas).
Delusion, epilepsy, agitation, disease, death, and so forth [are examples]. For instance:
“Having first cut off the skin again and again, and then the flesh, which was abundant with large swellings...”
Having devoured the easily accessible entrails along with the buttocks and thighs,
the actor among ghosts— with eyes rolled back and teeth bared— [performs] the intense section [of the drama]. His senses...
"In this wilderness, even the flesh within the hollow of a corpse, though its bones are scattered, remains undisturbed nearby."
The Marvelous (adbhuta): (237) The Marvelous has wonder as its stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), and the Gandharvas are its presiding deities.
The yellow rain is considered the object (ālambana) that transcends the world;
furthermore, the greatness of its qualities serves as the excitant (uddīpana).
Then there are paralysis, exhaustion, horripilation, faltering voice, and confusion.
Likewise, the consequents (anubhāvas), such as the expansion of the eyes and so forth, have been proclaimed.
The transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) include agitation due to the force of reflection, bewilderment, joy, and so forth.
For example:
"With his arms [hearing] the moon-crested Lord..."
O Noble One, how is it that this sound of the aged—a drum heralding the commencement of the deeds of a child—still does not cease?
Its fierce intensity is concentrated as it whirls within the belly of the vessel of the universe, where the two halves of the cosmic egg have suddenly met together.
Ah, how is it that it still persists? How can it find rest even now?
The Quietistic (śānta): The Quietistic has tranquility as its dominant emotion (sthāyibhāva) and belongs to those of superior character.
Possessing the luster of jasmine, snow, and the moon, with Śrī Nārāyaṇa as his tutelary deity,
he [perceives] that which is the worthlessness of all things through their impermanence and other such qualities.
Alternatively, its object of focus (ālambana) is held to be the nature of the Supreme Self,
or holy hermitages, sacred fords, delightful forests, and so forth.
The association with great men and so forth are its excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).
As stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*: [text follows]
The involuntary manifestations (anubhāvas), such as horripilation and the like, as well as the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas), should likewise be [represented].
"Filled with world-weariness, having reached the forest of the rainy season, and possessing compassion for all beings,
he was looked upon by the citizens with fear, curiosity, and pity— by those travelers who saw him clad in worn-out rags like an aged maiden, and by those at the end of their journey."
"When shall the crow, without hesitation, peck at the handful of nectar from the essence of consciousness— which has been rendered free of duality— while I am sleeping?"
The detailed exposition, however, is to be found in the Mahābhārata and other such works.
(238) In the *nirvyājaka* (uncontrived) form, there is no [conflict] in the *dhīravīra* (heroic) and other rasas;
for in the *dayāvīra* (compassionate heroic), as in the case of Jīmūtavāhana and others, there is the presentation of passion (*anurāga*) for Malayavatī in the middle,
and at the end, the attainment of the status of a Vidyādhara emperor.

Peace (*śama*) is not observed here; however, since the *śānta* (the peaceful) is of a single nature consisting of the destruction of all doors of duality in every respect, it cannot be included therein. Consequently, the predominance of the *śānta* rasa in the *Nāgānanda* has been refuted.
Homage!

"That state wherein there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither anxiety nor hatred or passion, nor any desire whatsoever— that is the Peace described by the Lords of Sages, the supreme authority among all states of being."

Since such a state of tranquility arises precisely in the state of *mūla* (the root), characterized by the attainment of one's own essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*), and since there is an absence of the *sañcārin* (transitory emotions) and other factors therein, how can it be said to possess the nature of *rasa* (aesthetic flavor)?
This is what is being asked.
Since that very tranquility which is observed in one who is joined with or separated from objects is what leads to liberation, therefore,
the movement of the mind and so forth within this state is not contradictory.
This is the intense discernment.
Furthermore, as for the absence of happiness mentioned in this context, there is no contradiction, because that refers specifically to sensual pleasure. For it has been said:
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is in heaven—
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
If they were to attain a state free from all forms of egoism,
then those who are heroic in compassion and the like would also be included herein.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [are included] the heroism of Dharma, the heroism of Giving, passion for the domain of the deities, and so on.
Among these, passion for the domain of the deities is, for example:
"When shall I dwell here in Vārāṇasī upon the bank of the celestial river..."
Wearing only a loincloth and placing my joined palms upon my head,
crying out, "O Lord of Gaurī, O Śambhu, destroyer of Tripura, O Three-eyed One, have mercy!"— thus shall I pass my days as if they were but a single moment.
Now, [the hero] esteemed by the lords of sages is affectionate (*vatsala*).
(241) They know the *vatsala* rasa to be clearly characterized by wonder (*camatkāra*);
its permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is considered to be the relationship with one's children and so forth.
The excitants (uddīpanas) are his actions, learning, heroism, pride, and so forth;
as well as embracing, contact with the limbs, pressing the head, and gazing.
Thrills, bliss, tears, and so forth are proclaimed as the consequent emotions (anubhāvas);
while apprehension of the undesirable, envy, pride, and so forth are considered the transitory emotions (sañcāribhāvas).
The deity is Padmagarbha-Kubera and the World-Mothers (*loka-mātaraḥ*). As stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*: "That first word which was spoken by the nurse..."
Supporting himself on his father's arm, the boy went along; and by prostrating himself on the ground in salutation, that child spread joy for his father.
Thus he states the mutual incompatibility of the sentiments (rasas): "The first [sentiment] is incompatible with the pathetic, the loathsome, the furious, the heroic, and the terrifying."
His [the hero's] connection with the Furious and the Pathetic sentiments involves opposition;
likewise, the Pathetic sentiment is similarly opposed by the Erotic and the Heroic sentiments.
The Furious [sentiment] is also [composed] of the sentiments of Astonishment, Laughter, and Terror;
likewise, the Heroic sentiment is known to be [composed] of the Terrible and the Quietistic.
The *vīra* (heroic), *śṛṅgāra* (erotic), and *raudra* (furious) rasas are [produced] by means of the *śānta* (tranquil) and *śasya* (praiseworthy);
the *bhayānaka* (terrifying) is produced by the *śānta*, while the *śānta* is produced by the *vīra*, *śṛṅgāra*, *raudra*, *dāsya* (servile), and *bhayānaka*.
The opposition between the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*vībhatsa*) has been explained;
the first [of these] is the erotic. The modes of their coexistence will be discussed hereafter.
Even though it may attain stability somewhere due to some cause, (243) [it remains unstable elsewhere].
Mental derangement (*unmāda*) and the like are not permanent (*sthāyin*), because they do not attain stability through the character (*pātra*).
For example, the mental derangement of Purūravas in the fourth act of the *Vikramorvaśīya*.
(244) Rasa and bhāva, their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and the subsidence and emergence of a bhāva [are the types of emotion].
Junction (*sandhi*) and variegation (*śabalatā*)—all these are limbs of rasa.
This is the third chapter.
Because they possess the attributes of rasa, even the *aṅgas* (limbs) and so forth are designated as "rasa" by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Thus it is said.
Generally, the transitory states (*bhāva*) and so forth are discussed.
(245) Transitory states are predominant; [likewise is] love directed toward deities and the like.
"The stable emotion (*sthāyin*) as soon as it is manifested is called a transitory emotion (*bhāva*).
'There is no rasa devoid of bhāva, nor is there a bhāva devoid of rasa;
the establishment of these two, rasa and bhāva, is through their mutual dependence.'"

According to the direction thus stated, although [these emotions] exist together with *rasa*— the supreme state of rest— through higher reflection, they are like servants who engage in marriage following the lead of their king;
therefore, where the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as those directed toward gods, sages, gurus, and kings are predominantly manifested—

The stable emotions (*sthāyibhāvas*)—which are the delight directed toward divine objects, awakened by innate disposition but not yet brought to the state of *rasa* because they have not been fully nourished by the determinants (*vibhāva*), etc.—are denoted by the term "emotions" (*bhāva*). Among these, the transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) is illustrated as follows: "While the divine sage was speaking thus... and so forth. [This refers to] the power...
Attachment directed toward the gods is *rati*. As in the *Kundamālā*:
"O Destroyer of Death, let my dwelling be as I desire—whether in heaven, on earth, or even in hell."
"Even in death, I shall think only of your feet, which have surpassed the autumnal lotus."
An example of delight directed toward a sage is as follows:
"O Sage, by this very glance of yours,
I have been made successful in my purpose and have attained liberation."
Nevertheless, I am eager to hear the words of my elders; for who would not rejoice in that which is most beneficial?
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*,
there is my own verse concerning passion directed toward a king:
“[The dust raised by the hooves of your horses, which has become slippery with the mud of the battlefield...]”
Do not carry Gaṅgā upon your head like Hara, who was burdened by her immense weight.
The same applies to others.
An example of a state that has just begun to emerge is as follows:
"But Hara, his composure slightly obscured, was like the ocean at the onset of the rising moon."
He fixed his eyes upon Umā’s face, where the lower lip was like the bimba fruit.

In this context, the Lord’s aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) has Pārvatī as its object. As Manu says: "Rasa is the single manifestation of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, like water in a fountain. In that case, since the transitory emotions (*sañcārī-bhāva*) lack separate existence, how can they be manifested as predominant? To this it is replied:
Just as when pieces of mirage-water and other such things are combined in a cooling drink.
The predominance (*udreka*) of any one [of the transitory states] over another occurs in some cases within a rasa that is currently manifesting.
Now, regarding the semblances of rasa and bhāva (*rasābhāsa* and *bhāvābhāsa*): when they proceed through impropriety (*anaucitya*), there is a semblance of rasa and bhāva. (247)
Furthermore, in this context, the "inappropriateness" (*anaucitya*) of the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*)— as defined by Bharata and others—

is to be understood as referring to a metaphorical application of the term when they possess only a partial connection rather than the full complement of their constituent factors (*sāmagrī*). This [inappropriateness] is set forth in part for the sake of instructing beginners.
(248) In the case of a woman who belongs to a paramour, one who has gone to the wife of a sage or a guru,
in sexual pleasure directed toward many lovers, and likewise in that which is established in neither [of these roles], [the *śṛṅgāra* is considered "inferior"].

In the case of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment), there is impropriety (*anaucitya*) when it resides in a secondary hero, or in a low character, or in animals and the like; in the case of *raudra* (the furious sentiment), there is impropriety when the anger resides in a teacher or similar superior.
The Third Chapter: When the moon is in its waning phase,
when it is situated in the houses of Jupiter and others,
when it is in conjunction with Jupiter, and likewise when it is in its exaltation or in its own sign, it is auspicious for a wise man.
This should be understood as applying elsewhere as well, such as when [the sentiment] is present in a superior recipient (*uttamapātra*) or in the *bhayānaka* (fearful) [sentiment].
Regarding its presence in the *ramya* (delightful), *adbhuta* (marvelous), and *śānta* (quiescent) [sentiments], it is as in my own verse:
“The master is most innocent; the group is dense; I am but a young girl, all alone.”
"A continuous mass of darkness, as dark as a *tāla* tree, is obscuring the path;
therefore, O handsome one, O Kṛṣṇa, leave me at once! Hearing these words of the cowherd girl, Hari, who is skilled in the arts of love, embraced her—may he protect you!
An example of being the youngest among brothers (*paṇḍanāyakaniṣṭhatva*) is as follows:
"I believe that for the sake of these very [sons], this cheek of Pāṇḍu has become pale, even though he was the beloved of the three worlds."
Regarding the case where [the sentiment] culminates in both [the hero and the heroine], as in Mādhava’s *māyā* in the *Mālatīmādhava*:
"Even though it culminates in both later, it possesses the character of a semblance (*ābhāsa*) because it first culminates in one alone," so say the venerable authors of the *Mocana*.
Just as the moon, the devourer of darkness, [reveals] the state of the jewels, so too did Vatsarāja’s passion for Sāgarikā arise before their mutual sight.

An example of its presence in a secondary antagonist (*pratināyaka*) is found in the *Hayagrīvavadha* [of Māgha], in the forest where Hayagrīva was sporting in the water. An example of its presence in a low-ranking character (*adhamapātra*) is as follows:
A certain mountain-dwelling woman, whose form was as swift as lightning and who was adorned with flowers,
having sat down before the mountain in front of her husband, began to loosen her disheveled hair.
As for its presence in the *śiṣya* (the subordinate) category, it is as stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"Seeking her husband in the forests and among the thickets of creepers, [she wanders]..."
That bee embraces the music produced by the humming of the fivefold unevolved elements as they vibrate.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), ascetics and others are included. An example of the semblance of the Furious (*raudra*) sentiment is as follows:
"With eyes wide, rolling, and blossoming with joy; with trembling arms raised;
having cast aside his bow and lute out of fearlessness; [he stood] at the side of Hari."
"Therefore, repeatedly proclaim your own prowess with harsh words;
that Arjuna, skilled in the art of wrestling, has entered [the arena] to slay Yudhiṣṭhira."
An example of the appearance of the Terrible (bhayānaka):
“Unable to endure the sight of him, as if from the onset of a thousand suns,
the owl of unsteady gaze entered the interior of a cave-dwelling in the Golden Mountain and spent his days in terror.”
For this fear, whose nature is that of a rasa, has women and low-caste persons as its object; so it is elsewhere.
(248) However, the semblance of a transitory emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) may occur when [fear] directed toward objects such as prostitutes arises in relation to things like modesty.
This is clear.

(248) When there is the subsiding of one emotion (*bhāva*), the arising of another, or their mixture, there is respectively the subsiding, the arising, the junction (*sandhi*), and the variegation (*śabalatā*) of emotion. These are considered [the varieties of *rasa*].
For example, in sequence:
"O fair-limbed one, abandon your anger; look at me prostrate at your feet.
Never before has your anger been of such a kind."
Thus the Lord spoke; with her eyes half-closed in a sidelong glance,
she said nothing at all— neither "yes" nor "no"— in that moment of liberation from the bonds of worldly existence,
which was the manifestation of the transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*) known as bashfulness (*nētrī*).
The Fourth Chapter:
"When he turned away from favor because she had rejected his falling at her feet, and when he was addressed with the harsh words 'You are a gambler' in a fit of rage— "
As her lover departed, she sighed deeply; with her hand resting upon her breast, she cast her gaze—veiled by the lashes of her eyes—upon her friends.
Here, there arises despondency:
"Victory to this face of the one with uneven eyes, which is difficult to attain even by the mind's activity;
yet this form of the intoxicating-eyed one gladdens my heart and pains it as well."
Here is the junction between joy and despair:
"Where is the body marked by the deer [of the moon], and where is my lineage? Might she be seen again?
Alas, my learning was for the sake of quelling my faults; even in anger, her face is lovely."
"What will those of evil disposition say? She is difficult to obtain even in a dream;
O heart, regain your composure! What young man indeed would dare to drink from her lip?"
In this [verse], there is the production of reflection, anxiety, intelligence, fear, despondency, fortitude, and anxiety.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Definition of Rasas, Bhāvas, and Others," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
Now he states the divisions of poetry:
(250) Poetry is considered to be of two kinds: *dhvani* (suggestion) and that in which the suggested meaning is subordinated (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*). Among these:
(251) When the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) surpasses the expressed meaning (*vācya*), that is *dhvani*; it is the highest form of poetry (*kāvya*).

By the etymological derivation "that in which something is sounded forth" (*dhvanyate'smin*), *dhvani* is the name for the highest poetry, [referring] to the suggested meaning which possesses a greater aesthetic charm than the expressed meaning.
Regarding the *sāhibadarbha* [the master of words]:
(252) Even within meditation (*dhyāna*), two types are proclaimed by the Sage: that rooted in denotation (*abhidhāmūla*) and that known as *sahacara*.
Among these, the one where the literal meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) is further divided into *anyokti* and *anyaparavākya*.

That which is called "the sublation of the unintended meaning" (*avivakṣitavācyo nāmātyantatiraskṛtavācyaḥ*) is a type of suggestion (*dhvani*). Because it is a sublation of the expressed meaning, the expressed meaning is not intended; rather, it takes the form of that which is sublated. It is the source of denotation for something other than the intended meaning. For this very reason, the expressed meaning here is not intended, as it is directed toward something else.

It is centered on the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyaniṣṭha*). For here, the meaning of speech is that which manifests the intended object through its own form; just as a lamp situated within a jar [illuminates it], so too is the manifestation of the meaning. Thus, after the explanation of the various objects of denotation (*abhidhā*), the classification of cases where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) is stated.
(252) When a meaning is utterly disregarded even though it is not intended to be expressed,
it nevertheless becomes a type of suggestion (*dhvani*) known as *arthāntarasaṃkramita*.

The type of *dhvani* known as "that whose expressed meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*) is of two kinds: that in which the expressed meaning is merged with another meaning (*saṃsṛṣṭavācya*), and that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*). In the former case, where the primary meaning, being itself useless, transforms into another meaning that constitutes its own particularity, there [the primary meaning]—of its own particularity—...
Because it is measured alongside other objects of comparison, there is a state of being expressed as something measured by others. For example:
“O banana tree, you are a banana tree; an elephant calf is an elephant calf; and the trunk of the king of elephants is the trunk of the king of elephants.
Yet, even throughout the three worlds, this pair of thighs of the woman with eyes like a deer’s does not share a likeness with them on the scale.”

In this context, words such as *hitoktṛ*, *kaṭa*, and *khādi*, being precluded from their primary meanings—such as "one who speaks what is beneficial," "a mat," and "a wooden vessel"—due to the fear of tautology, convey meanings such as "wife" (*jāyā*) and so forth;
furthermore, the excellence of the wife and so on is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). In that case, however, [the word] retains its own meaning...

When one abandons all [other] meanings and resorts to another meaning there, because the primary meaning is set aside, it is called "completely set aside" (*atyantatiraskṛta*). For example: "The moon does not shine, as if blinded by its own breath."
The Fourth Chapter.

In the word "blind" (*andha*), the primary meaning being sublated conveys the sense of having the nature of non-luminosity; and because luminosity is the opposite of that, it is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). Thus, there is a relationship of general and particular between blindness and the state of non-luminosity.

The state of being expressed through association with existence, non-existence, or neither: for example, "O friend, wander confidently; that wicked man has been killed by him who dwells in the marshes of Mokhābaī, he whose brilliance is difficult to endure."

In this case, because the injunction to wander—expressed as "O bold one, wander"—is not applicable to the context at hand, it results in a prohibition against wandering; thus, there is no contradiction. However, where both an injunction and a prohibition arise simultaneously, they function as a prohibition and an injunction respectively.

And that [negation] is indeed the meaning of the word *partha*. Furthermore, when through the context and other means the negation of a prohibition and the affirmation of a prescription are understood, there too it is precisely the nature of *dhvani* (suggestion). As it has been said:
"Due to the predominance of the sense here, there may be some sublation of the literal meaning;
in the former case there is a remainder, but in the latter case there is indeed direct denotation."
In the first case, there is a transition or entry into another meaning of the primary sense, but not its disappearance;

for this very reason, it is here *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning) indication. In the second case, however, because its own meaning is set aside, it is *tirohitājahatsvārthā* (obscured non-abandoning of its own meaning).

(254) Even that variety where the expressed meaning is intended is considered first; therein, the suggested meaning may be either of imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*) or of perceptible sequence (*lakṣyakrama*).

Even *dhvani* whose expressed meaning is intended to be subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*) is of two kinds: that in which the suggested meaning is sequential (*kramavyaṅgya*) and that in which it is non-sequential (*akramavyaṅgya*).
Regarding the example "Bhama dhammia" (Go away, O pious man): "Go away, O pious man; that [woman] has been carried off by another."
This was composed by Itasiṃha, a resident of Kunnava, out of pure joy. Thus ends the Saṅgrahī.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
(255) Therein, the first [type] consists of rasa, bhāva, and so forth, which are counted as only one;
for even a single variety is infinite, such that its limit cannot be reached.

The nature of *rasa* consists of *rasa*, *bhāva*, and so forth; it is suggested through a process that involves sequence. Here, because the manifestation [of *rasa*] has the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and other factors as its cause, a sequence necessarily exists; however, due to the extreme rapidity—like the piercing of a lotus petal by an arrow—it is not perceived. And among these, *rasa* and the rest, there is one...
Furthermore, because the varieties [of the erotic sentiment] are infinite and impossible to enumerate, and because they cannot be perceived through sequential order,
this poetry is said to possess only one variety. For instance, even within a single vessel of wine,
the single variety consisting of sexual union includes mutual embracing, drinking from the lips, and kissing.
Due to their different divisions and because each possesses a variety of factors such as the *vibhāvas* and so forth, they are impossible to enumerate; what need is there to mention all of them?
(256) Arising from the cognition of either the word, the meaning, or both, and appearing as if following [them],
*dhvani* with a perceptible sequence (*lakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*) is described by the wise as being of various kinds.

Because it is by its very nature successive, that which is suggested in the form of a resonance (anuraṇana) is threefold: that which arises from the power of the word (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*), that which arises from the power of the meaning (*arthasaktyudbhava*), and that which arises from the combined power of both word and meaning (*śabdārthaśaktyudbhava*). Due to this threefold division of the suggested sense whose manifestation is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), poetry (*dhvani*) is also threefold. Among these:

(257) Because it takes the form of both a matter (*vastu*) and an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), that which arises from the power of words is twofold. Since the word "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) is mentioned separately, the term "matter" (*vastu*) here refers to that which is not an ornament. Among these, an example of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) arising from the power of words in the form of a matter is as follows:
"O merchant, there is neither truth nor falsehood here in this village on the surface of stone;
however, if you wish to dwell here after seeing the removal of high and low, then dwell."

"Panthica" means "O traveler. [The commentary says: "O traveler, having seen a slightly elevated cloud over a village situated on a rocky plateau, if you still wish to stay, then so be it. Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Saṃketa-ṭīkā.
Here, by the power of words such as *satvara* (quick), the fact that "if you are capable of enjoying [this], then come quickly" is suggested.
An example of the form of an *alaṅkāra* (figure of speech) is: "With a body emaciated by difficulties," and so forth.

Here, lest the description of the non-contextual Śiva— the beloved of Pārvatī— should cause offense to the contextual King Bhānudēva, the beloved of the Great Goddess Umā, there exists a relationship of *upamāna* (standard of comparison) and *upameya* (object of comparison) between the two lords, Īśvara and Bhānudēva.
It is stated: therein, the suggested poetic figure (*vyaṅgya*) is the simile (*upamālaṅkāra*), namely, "like Umāvallabha" (the beloved of Umā).
Or, for example:
"O Lord, you are immeasurable (*amita*) because of the excellence attained through your measured (*samita*) efforts;
you are the scorner of those who are harmful (*ahita*), yet you are united (*sahita*) with the virtuous and with glories that have spread throughout the sky."
In the verse beginning with "catrāmita," because there is an absence of the word "api" (even), the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Although it is not established as being directly expressed, it is figuratively designated as such according to the maxim of the "Brahmin who is also a mendicant" (*brāhmaṇa-śramaṇa-nyāya*).

(258) The subject matter (*vastu*) or the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is pervasive; the meaning is twofold: possible by itself (*svataḥ-sambhavī*), or established by the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti-siddha*) of the poet, or of both. Thus there are six [types].
When manifested by these [twelve] types of words,
the suggested meaning— consisting of both matter (vastu) and figure (alaṅkāra)— attains twelve varieties through the metaphorical form (rūpaka).

That which is possible in itself (*svataḥ-sambhavī*) is conceivable even outside of poetic propriety (*aucitya*); that which is established through bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) is not [conceivable] by means of propriety. Of these, examples in order are as follows:
"O neighbor, will you cast even a moment's glance upon our house? For likely the father of this girl will drink the bitter water of the well.
Therefore, though alone, I shall go quickly from here to the stream shaded by tamāla trees."
"Let them draw the outline of the corpse with lines of fire from the flames of a sharp-edged saw."
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:

by means of this matter (*vastu*) which is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*), there is suggested (*vyañjyate*) another mere matter (*vastumātra*) consisting of the concealment of her own agitation caused by the enjoyment of another man and so forth, as expressed by this [statement].
"Even the heat of the sun falters in the southern quarter;
yet in that very direction, the subjects of Raghu did not suffer from his majesty."
By means of this object which exists inherently, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast) is suggested, namely that the majesty of Raghu is superior to the brilliance of the sun.
"Having rendered his prowess useless from afar,
Balarāma gazed at him as he was falling, like a lion looking upon an elephant."

Here, by means of a suggested meaning (*vyañjakārtha*) that is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*) and takes the form of the poetic figure simile (*upamālaṅkāra*), the fact (*vastu*) that Baladeva will bring about the destruction of Veṇudārin in an instant is suggested.
He who, out of anger, bit his own lower lip in battle, thereby releasing the enemy's wives from the peril of the pain caused by the deep bites of their beloveds' teeth—

here, the figure of speech is *svataḥ-sambhavi-virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction based on what is naturally possible), as the lower lip was bitten while simultaneously saving them from being bitten.
And thus, the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
"O Goddess, this month of Hima (Māgha) is auspicious for you; it is the very essence of the welfare of your devotees.
It is the thousand-rayed mouth of the sun, the source of the birth of the umbrella [of sovereignty], and the arrow against misfortune."*

"Spring is the arrow-maker, Love is the bow, young women are the bowstring, and flowers are the arrows"— this object, established through the bold poetic assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, by its manifestation, suggests another object in the form of the blossoming of passion.

"O friend! [Thus he says. "The month of Madhu (Spring) makes fragrant, yet it does not bring under its control the young women who are difficult to subdue; for it has released arrows from the mouths of fresh mango blossoms, like those of a new archer. Thus [says] Saṃketa. [This is] the Commentary (Ṭīkā).
The Fourth Chapter: "O Hero, the continuous stream of your fame, illuminated by the network of rays from the spotless moon during the nights, constantly whitens the entire circle of the world."

Here, by means of the object (vastu) expressed through the bold poetic fancy (prauḍhokti) of the poet, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction/superiority) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), namely that the lineage of his fame possesses the quality of illuminating for a longer duration than the rays of the moon.
“From the crowns of the Ten-faced one,
the royal splendors instantly fell upon the earth in the guise of gems as teardrops.
Here, by means of the poet’s bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*), the future royal splendor— which serves as the cause for the metaphor— is established.
The entity whose nature is destruction is manifested.
“O ornament of the land of Cedi, by the mass of your fame, though it is but one, there has arisen a collection of nine jewels: a white lotus upon your head, a necklace at the region of your throat,
a thick application of sandalwood paste upon the pair of your breasts, and [the rest] upon your body.”
"In battle, she was the ornament of pride for the left arm of the inhabitants of Indra’s city."

Here, by means of the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor), established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, the figure of speech *vibhāvanā* (the production of an effect despite the absence of its cause) is suggested, namely: "Even though you remain on earth, you bestow favor upon those dwelling in heaven."
“O lady with the crest-like hair, where indeed, for how long, and what kind of penance did this wretched young parrot perform,
O fair-faced one, by which he now bites at your bimba-fruit lip that is as red as a fresh leaf?”

Here, by means of this *vastu* (fact) established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a certain amorous poet, another *vastu* is perceived: that "your lower lip is obtainable only with great effort.
"O fortunate one, having approached the peak of Mount Sāla with the arrows of Love..."
"In spring, the fivefold state was abandoned; that fivefold state belongs to the yogins."

In this context, according to the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, the "fivefold state" (*pañcatā*) of the arrows of Kāma— which have reached their peak through the bold assertions (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet— is established by the fact that all those separated from their lovers die.
By releasing arrows that traverse the sky, the poetic figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), based on the [imagined] support [of the sky], is manifested.
"In the bud of the lotus, it shines while emitting its honey-drops, as if filling the conch-shell of the five-headed serpent at the time of its departure."

In this instance, by means of a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a character created by the poet, the fact (*vastu*) is expressed: "O proud woman, how is it that you do not abandon your resentment now that this time, which is favorable for love, has arrived?"
“O Snow, though you are filled with thousands of women, you blow gently;
day after day, you cause my limbs to tremble.”

In the phrase "they do not rest here," by means of the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause) established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) attributed to the poet, the figure *viśeṣokti* (peculiar statement)— that even though darkness has been thinned, it does not abide in your heart—
is suggested. Indeed, [this] is not merely the passion of the poet, as if he were a character created by the poet.

Furthermore, there is the state of being most intensely absorbed (*yāviṣṭatā*). Therefore, the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) fashioned by the poet—being more striking to the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) than even the poet’s own bold assertion—is treated as a distinct category. And among these three types of figures, in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), the primacy belongs solely to the act of imagining (*utprekṣaṇa*), the exclusion (*vyatirecana*), and so forth.
Since it is perceivable by the day but not by silver and the like, its primacy belongs to those [days] alone.
(258) When a single suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) arises from both [the word and the sense] through the power of the word’s meaning, there is one variety of *dhvani*. For example:
“[The lake], beautiful with the moon freed from frost and possessing lotuses...”
Intoxicating the twice-born and having aroused the banner of love:
"O fortunate one, in this heart filled with thousands of women, she,
with her mind fixed on no other, day by day makes even your slender body thinner."
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Saṃkṣipta-ṭīkā;
there occurred a great festival that gladdened the gods.
That Mādhava [remained] for a long time with the young women.
Here, the poetic figure of simile (upamā), wherein Kṛṣṇa Mādhava is compared to the spring season Mādhava, is suggested (vyaṅgya).
And thus, the distinction between poetic works (kāvyas) arises solely from the distinction between their suggested meanings (vyaṅgya).
That *dhvani* is of eighteen kinds:

that in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), that in which the expressed meaning is subordinated to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*), and that in which the expressed meaning is entirely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).

Suggestion (*dhvani*) is of two kinds. First, that in which the suggested meaning is intended but not directly expressed (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*), which is one type when it possesses a suggestible meaning with a perceptible sequence (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*). Second, by virtue of having a suggestible meaning with a perceptible sequence, it is fifteenfold—being rooted in the power of word, meaning, or both.
Thus, *dhvani* has eighteen varieties. And among these:
In a sentence, there is the cognition of the word and its meaning; other than that, [these cognitions] belong to words and sentences.
Among these, an example of suggestion where the expressed meaning is comparable to something else and resides in a word is as follows:
“Blessed indeed is that very tree, which possesses both fear and shame,
before whom this art of enchanting young men appears so fair.”
In this context, the second instance of the word *ayana* refers to an *ayana* characterized by qualities such as being fortunate (*bhāgyavattā*) and so forth.
An example occurring within a sentence is as follows:
“I speak to you: O Unborn One, the assembly of the wise stands here. Having adopted your own perspective, do not establish your abode elsewhere.”

In this context, since the object to be established is already understood from the very fact that it is directed toward me, the repeated statement "you" (*tvam*) indicates the referent "you" as qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*). Likewise, since the agent is already understood from the word "I" (*aham*) alone, the repeated statement "this" (*idam*) indicates the referent "this" as qualified by the exclusion of others.
It arranges itself for my sake. Likewise, in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, in the section on "The Assembly of the Learned" (*viduṣāṃ samudāya*) and so forth, it is not at all [the case that]...
"In the forests of the wise, amidst the trees, she who was seeking her beloved..."
"Which bee accepts the music produced by the five-fold combination of the five elements?"
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [suffering, hunger, and so forth] are meant. An example of the semblance of the Furious (*raudra*) is as follows:
"With eyes wide, rolling, and blossoming with joy; with arms trembling slightly and abandoned by fear;
and having cast off his upper garment—[this is the state] of Hari at the fifth watch."
"O Asoka, at dawn proclaim with harsh words the prowess of Sahadeva; Arjuna, skilled in clapping his arms, has entered [the field] to slay Yudhishthira."
An example of the appearance of the terrifying (*bhayānakābhāsa*) is as follows:
“Unable to endure the sight of him, who was like a great chariot, the owl, his eyes unsteady with fear,
entered the interior of a cave-dwelling on the Golden Mountain and led [the enemy] away, trembling with terror.”
For fear, which has its nature as a rasa, has the courtesan and the like as its object; so it is elsewhere.

However, the manifestation of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) may occur when [passion] is directed toward objects such as prostitutes and the like, rather than [appropriate objects] such as a wife and the like. (248)
This is clear.

(248) When there is the subsiding of one emotion (*bhāva*), the arising of another, or their mixture, there is a transition (*sandhi*) between them respectively; [furthermore], the subsiding, the arising, the transition, and the variegation (*śabalatā*) of emotions are recognized as such.
For example, in sequence:
"O fair-limbed one, abandon your anger; look at me prostrate at your feet;
surely never before has your anger been such as this."
Thus the Lord spoke; with her eyes half-closed sidelong, she neither released nor restrained anything from the gaze born of her eyes—
herein lies the praise for the transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*) of bashfulness (*mepīsya*) in this *Kaṣpamocana*.
The Fourth Chapter: When [the king] was turned away from his favor because she refused to fall at his feet, she said, "O you who act like a deceitful gambler," and spoke harshly in anger.
As her lover departed, she sighed deeply; with her hand resting upon her breast, she cast her gaze, veiled by tears, toward her friends.
Here, there arises dejection:
"This form of Madirā, which is a delight for the pair of eyes and difficult to obtain even through the practice of self-restraint,
intoxicates my heart and yet causes it pain."
Herein lies the juncture (*sandhi*) of joy and sorrow.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of Rasas, Bhāvas, and so forth," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
What business has the moon with my task, and where is her noble lineage? Might she not be seen again?
Even when her great anger is heard, my beloved face remains dear to me. What will those of pure heart and firm resolve say [of me], if she—so difficult to attain—is lost even in a dream?
"Whom indeed, a fortunate youth, shall this lip of yours reach, bringing peace to his heart?"
Here, [there is] the expansion of desire, reflection, joy, fortitude, and thought of people...
[End of fragment]. Now, he states the divisions of poetry (*kāvya*).
(250) Poetry is considered to be of two kinds: *dhvani* and that in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
Among these, (251) when the suggested meaning surpasses the expressed meaning, it is *dhvani*; that is the highest form of poetry.

In this [work], because the suggested meaning possesses a charm greater than the expressed meaning, it is called *dhvani* (suggestion) according to the etymology "that in which something is sounded (*dhvanyate*)"; thus, *dhvani* is considered the highest form of poetry.
— from the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
(252) Even for *dhvani*, two varieties have been declared by [the author] as being rooted in *lakṣaṇā* and *abhidhā*.
One is that in which the literal meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), and the other is that in which it is intended but something else is suggested (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).

That which is called *dhvani* based on indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*) is one in which the literal meaning (*vācya*) is not intended to be expressed. Precisely because it is based on indication, the literal meaning—which takes the form of being sublated—is indeed sublated. That which has another as its primary purpose (*anyapara*) is based on denotation (*abhidhāmūla*). For this very reason, in this [latter case], the literal meaning is intended to be expressed, as it is directed toward something else.

In this context, the meaning of speech resides in the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*); its own nature is such that, while manifesting itself, it manifests the suggested meaning, just as a lamp, while illuminating itself, illuminates a jar. Since the basis of denotation (*abhidhāmūla*) has many objects, no specific enumeration is provided. He now states the divisions of that in which the expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*).

(249) When the distinction between the two is merged and the literal meaning is completely set aside, even though the expressed meaning has been investigated, there is a recollection of the twofold nature of *dhvani*.

The type of suggestion known as *abhivacitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is not intended) is threefold: that in which the expressed meaning is merged with another meaning (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*), and that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*). In the first case, where the primary meaning, being itself unsuitable [for the context], transforms into another meaning that is a specific form of itself, there the primary meaning—its own specific...
The state of being expressed as something else occurs because the object is not cognized as its own form, but rather as another thing; for example:
“The plantain is a plantain, the elephant’s trunk is an elephant’s trunk, the king of elephants’ trunk is the king of elephants’ trunk.”
"Even at the summit of the world-mountain, this pair of breasts does not equal the measure of the eyes of a woman with tremulous glances."

In this context, words such as "second wife" (*dvitīyakadā*) and others—being barred from their primary meanings, such as the general category of "wife" and so forth, for fear of tautology—convey a meaning characterized by qualities such as being a wife who is [particularly] devoted to her husband;
furthermore, the excellence of the wife is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). In that case, however, regarding its own literal sense...

In every respect, when [the primary meaning] is set aside and transforms into another meaning, there is "Extreme Exclusion" (*atyantatiraskṛta*) because the primary meaning is completely discarded. For example: "The moon in the mirror is as if blinded by its own breath; it does not shine."
The Fourth Chapter. Here, the word "blind" (*andha*), its primary meaning being sublated, conveys the sense of having the nature of non-luminosity (*aprakāśarūpa*);
and the excellence of this non-luminosity is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). There is a relationship of general and particular between blindness and non-luminosity.

The *cala* (moving) [type of *śleṣa*] is that which is joined with the intervals between the forms of existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*). For example: "O friend, wander! That wicked one has been killed by me; he who was the terror of the inhabitants of the Gośāla marshland. *Note: The Sanskrit provided in the source text appears to be a Prakrit verse. A possible reconstruction for clarity is:* *bhrama dharmaja viśrabdhaḥ sa śvāpadah praṇato mayā | gośālaka-kaccha-kuñja-vāsināṃ darpa-śoṣaṇaḥ ||* (Translation of the reconstructed verse): "Wander confidently, O son of Dharma; that beast of prey has been subdued by me, the one who dwells in the thickets of the Gośālaka marsh, the dryer of the pride of those [who dwell there]."*

In this case, from the statement "O bold one, wander about," the injunction to wander—being irrelevant to the context—is reduced to a prohibition against wandering; thus, it is a *viparītalakṣaṇā* (contrary indication). Indeed, in such instances, the injunction and the prohibition arise simultaneously, with the prohibition being the primary intended sense.

The occasion for that [suggestion] exists precisely where it is present; however, where injunctions and prohibitions are understood as prohibitions and injunctions through the consideration of context and other factors, there it is indeed *dhvani* (suggestive poetry). As it has been said:
“In some cases there is a persistence through the primary sense, while in others there is a sublation of it;
in the former case there would be indication (*lakṣaṇā*), but in the latter case there is indeed denotation (*abhidhā*) itself.
Here, in the first [case], there is a transition or entry of the primary meaning into another meaning, but not its disappearance.

Therefore, in this case, there is a non-abandoning indication (*ajahatvārthalakṣaṇā*); but in the second case, it is an indication that completely abandons its own primary meaning (*atyantatiraskṛtasvārthā*).
(254) Even that variety where the expressed meaning is intended is considered first;
therein [is found] that in which the suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence, as well as that in which the sequence is perceptible.

Even the *dhvani* (suggested sense) whose expressed meaning is intended to be subordinate (*anyapara-vācya*) is of two kinds: that which is manifested through a sequence (*krama-vyaṅgya*) and that which is manifested without a sequence (*akrama-vyaṅgya*). For example:
"Bhama dhammia... ("Go away, O pious man..."). [The full verse: "Go away, O pious man! That woman who killed him has been seen by me."
"The Godāvarī river, the Kuśa grass, the moon, and the haughty bull"— thus ends the section on *saṃgata* in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
(255) Among these, in the first type, only a single rasa, bhāva, or the like is counted here.
Since even a single variety is infinite, it cannot indeed be numbered.

That which has been described as having the nature of rasa, bhāva, and so forth, is that in which the sequence [of the process] is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*). Here, because the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyapratīti*) has the cognition of the excitants (*vibhāva*), etc., as its cause, a sequence necessarily exists; however, due to the extreme rapidity—like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals—it is not perceived. And among these, in the case of *rasa* and the others, there is one...
Furthermore, because the varieties [of suggestion] are infinite and thus impossible to enumerate, this poetry— defined as having its sequence imperceptible (asamlakṣyakrama)—
is stated to have only one variety. For instance, there is only one variety of the single [type of] hero.

Even a single variety of the *sambhoga* [rasa], such as mutual embracing, drinking from the lower lip, kissing, and so forth, is impossible to enumerate individually due to the diversity of the *vibhāvas* and other factors; what then need be said of all of them?
(256) Regarding the suggestiveness arising from the power of both word and meaning, which resembles an echo,
