The components of the arts (*śilpāṅga*) are as follows, which will be explained: for example, the *Devīmahādevya*. Now, regarding poetry (*kāvya*), there are six chapters (*pariccheda*).
(546) This poetic work is devoid of the Ārabhaṭī style, consists of a single act, and is crowded with female servants;
it is composed in the Khaṇḍamātrā and Dvipadikā meters and adorned with broken rhythms.
The *kaḍulikā* meter consists of a single *varṣa* [syllabic instant]; it is spoken with erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
The hero and the heroine here are both noble (*udātta*); likewise, the first two and the final *sandhi* [are so].
And likewise the *ādhavadāya*. Now, the *preṅkhaṇa*:
(547) A *preṅkhaṇa* is composed with the *garbha* and *avamarsa* junctures, features a dejected hero, consists of a single act (*ekāṅka*), and lacks both *aviṣkambha* and *praveśaka*.
Accompanied by wrestling and combat, and based upon all modes of dramatic action,
the *nāndī* is sung in the *nepathya*, as is the *prarocanā*.

For example, the *Bālibadha*. Now, as for the *rāsaka*: (548) A *rāsaka* consists of five acts (*aṅka*), is endowed with the *mukha*, *nirvahaṇa*, and other [junctures], abounds in *bhāṣā* and *vibhāṣā* dialects, and is characterized by the *bhāratī* and *kaiśikī* styles.
It shall have one act, all the limbs of a drama, and be endowed with artistic refinement; it should contain a clever prologue (*nāndī*), a heroine, and a foolish hero.
Some also declare that the *pratimukha* juncture here consists of a succession of increasingly elevated emotional states (*bhāva*).
As in the *Menakārita*. Next is the *Saṃlāpaka* (or *Saṃsāpaka*). In the *Saṃlāpaka*, there are four or three characters, including the hero;
the heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*) should be present there, and the sentiment (*rasa*) should be either the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) or the pathetic (*karuṇa*), but not otherwise.
There may be obstructions, blockages, dryness, and exhaustion;
in that state, neither the Vṛtti nor the Kaiśikī style of speech prevails.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*: [The *Prakaraṇa*] is like the *Mālatīmādhava*, but with a *Kāpālika* as the hero. Now, the *Śrīmaditaka*:
(550) It has a well-known plot, consists of one act, and features a noble hero.
It has a well-known protagonist and is devoid of both the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures.
Abounding in the *bhāratī* style of delivery and endowed with the word "śrī," this work named *Śrīgadita*, proclaimed by Śrī, is a dramatic composition (*rūpaka*) of the *vīthi* type.
"The *Bālacarita* is a drama concerning the childhood sports [of Kṛṣṇa].
Some say that in the *Śrīrañjī*, one may recite even a little of the *Śrīgadita*; it consists of a single act and is mostly in the *Bhāratī* style."
An example of *ācam* follows. Now, regarding *śilpaka*:
(551) In *śilpaka*, there should be four *akās*, as well as four meters (*vṛttis*). The sentiments (*rasas*) are those other than the peaceful (*śānta*), and the hero is considered to be a Brahmin.
The Upānāyaka (the secondary hero) may be a cemetery attendant or one of similar status;
its twenty-seven constituent parts (aṅgas) are as follows.
Hopes, conjectures, doubts, distress, agitation, and attachments;
efforts, compositions, yearnings, and failures to comprehend.
Amorous playfulness, indolence, and perversity; excellence, fickleness, and dullness;
the means, the pursuit, the attainment, the sighs, and likewise astonishment.
Gain, forgetfulness, agitation, fearlessness, awakening,
wonder, and the absence of mentation— because these are clearly manifest, they are called "eating."

The section on the Vaḍha [drama]. Since the definitions of the *saṃpheṭa* (collision) and *grathana* (intertwining) have already been established previously, their characteristics are proven. As in the *Kanakāvatīmādhava*. Now, the *vilāsikā* (sportive woman).
(552) It consists of the *paṭākā*, *ārava*, *vaṭa*, *lāṭa*, and *ekāṅkā* [sentiments], and is endowed with the ten aspects of the *lāsya*.
It is adorned by the *vidūṣaka* and the *viṭa*, as well as the *pīṭhamarda*.
It possesses the *mārgī* [style] along with the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures (*sandhi*), and features a dejected hero (*dīnanāyaka*).
She was of natural grace, elegantly attired, and renowned as a woman of refined charm.
Some read "lāsikā" instead of "vidyāsikā" in that context; others maintain that its inclusion is within "dutikā. Now, regarding *dutikā*: (553) *dutikā* is fourfold: *kaiśikī* and likewise *bhāratī*.
The city of Nāgārā is shallow and adorned by an inferior leader.
On this [occasion], the first day shall consist of the amorous play of the courtesans,
while the second day shall be filled with the dalliance of the Vidūṣaka.
The third is the *ghacālika*, who is full of the playful charm of a *pīṭhamarda*;
the fourth is the *daśanāli*, the hero who delights in amorous play (*krīḍita-nāyaka*).
*Bacā* is *Bindumatī*. Now, the *Prakaraṇikā*:
(554) A *Prakaraṇikā* is essentially a *Nāṭikā*, wherein the hero is a merchant (*sārthavāha*) or similar figure, and the heroine belongs to the same lineage as the leader.
An example must be sought. Now, the Sośa:

(555) The Illośa consists of a single act, lasts for seven or ten days, features ten women, has a high-pitched voice, involves a single male character, and is characterized by the Kaiśikī style and suffering.

Likewise, the two joints at the end of the *mukha* (introduction) have a duration established by many *tāla*s and *laya*s; this is the *vālidatha*. For example, the *Keśirai-vaitaka*. Now, the *bhāṣikā*:
(556) A *bhāṇikā* consists of twelve types of costume, is provided with an introduction (*mukha*) and an interlude (*nirvahaṇa*),
employs the *kaiśikī* and *bhāratī* styles (*vṛtti*), and is composed by a single author.
Udāttanāmikā, Mandapuruṣa, Ajāisaptaka,
Upanyāsa, Vinyāsa, Vibodha, and likewise Sādhvasa.

Entrustment (*samarpaṇa*), cessation (*nivṛtti*), and collection (*saṃdāra*) constitute the seventh [type]. An *upanyāsa* is the mention of a matter by way of a contextual connection (*prasaṅga*). A *vinyāsa* is the mastery of words expressing world-weariness (*nirveda*); that is considered the eighth.
The destruction of delusion is awakening; false proclamation is trepidation; speech accompanied by reproach is the affliction of anger;
surrender is the presentation of an illustration; and cessation is so described.
And "transition" (saṃcāra) refers to the completion of what is to be performed by the noble ones.

The examples are clear, such as Kāmadattā. Thus, even though the nature of the drama is the same for all, there is propriety (*aucitya*) and attainment (*lābha*), as well as the specific adoption of particular dramatic elements (*nāṭakauśaviśeṣaparigraha*). And where there is a re-introduction of what has already been mentioned in the drama...

And its existence constitutes the restrictive rule. Now, regarding *śravya-kāvya* (poetry intended for hearing): (557) *Śravya* means that which is merely to be heard; it is of two kinds, consisting of verse (*padya*) and prose (*gadya*).
Among these, he describes those consisting of verse:
558) Verse (padya) consists of words bound by meter; by one such [verse] it is called "isolated" (muktaka);
by two, "couplet" (yugmaka); and by three, it is intended as "sandānitaka."
A *kalāpaka* is considered to consist of four [verses], and a *kulaka* of five. This concludes the chapter on meters (*dhaṇḍaparicheda*).
An example of the *mujhaka* meter is as follows, by me:
Even those who are masters of speech strive in vain to describe that supreme reality— which is blissful, infinite, imperishable, unborn, and beyond all plurality—
while the young women of Mathurā city, out of curiosity, gaze upon it directly with their own eyes.
They embrace, converse, pull [them] by the hair a hundred times, and kiss them.”
The *ghummaka* meter, as in my example:
"What are you doing? At this moment when passion has risen and she is inclined toward love, why do you release your anger in private against this friend of [her] cheek?"
Thus, while we were still searching for the source of the sound,
there arose from the mango tree a sweet humming of bees.

The same applies elsewhere as well. (558) A composition consisting of cantos is a *mahākāvya* (great poem); in it, there is a single hero who is either a god or a kṣatriya of equal status, endowed with the qualities of a *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) character.
Whether there be many kings born of a single lineage or many born of various lineages,
it is held that only one rasa— be it the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the heroic (*vīra*), or the peaceful (*śānta*)— should be the predominant sentiment.
All the constituent elements, all the sentiments, and all the junctures of the drama;
the plot derived from history or otherwise, provided it rests upon virtuous characters.
Its sections should be four, and there should be a single fruit within them;
at the beginning, it should consist of an act of homage, a virtuous practice, or a presentation of the subject matter.
It may consist of the censure of the wicked and others, as well as the celebration of the virtues of the virtuous;
it is composed in a single meter throughout the verses, with a change of meter at the conclusion.
In the Sāhityadarpaṇa:
A canto (sarga) is neither too short nor too long;
it consists of various meters, and sometimes a particular canto is seen to contain only one meter.
At the conclusion [of a section], there should be an indication of the narrative of what is to follow.
[The topics include: twilight rites, the moon, night, the onset of darkness, the end of night, and day;
morning, midday, hunting, mountains, the earth, and the ocean.
And [the topics] include union and separation, sages, heaven, cities, and sacrifices.
In this [work], these topics— such as the departure for battle, marriage, the reception of mantras, and the birth of a son—
are to be described according to their relevance, along with their primary and secondary components (aṅga-upāṅgas),
either by the name of the poet's composition or by that of the hero or another character.
Its name, however, is "Sarga" (Creation), because it tells of that which is to be undertaken for the sake of creation.

The *sandhyābhāṣa* (twilight language) should be employed according to the intended meaning. At the end, the plural number in the phrase "by other meters" (*anyavṛttakaiḥ*) is not intended to be significant. Regarding the term "with its limbs and sub-limbs" (*sāṅgopāṅga*), this refers to the *jalakeli*, *madhu*, and *pāmāratha*. Examples include the *Raghuvaṃśa*, the *Tripuravadha*, the *Naiṣadha*, and so forth; or likewise, [other works].
My [work] is the *Rāghavapāṇḍavīya*.

(560) Furthermore, in this work composed by a seer (*ārṣa*), there are cantos (*sarga*) designated as "births" (*bhava*), "states" (*avasthāna*), and "assemblages" (*saṃjñaka*). In this great poem (*mahākāvya*), it is just like the *Mahābhārata*.
(561) In that drama composed by commoners (*prākṛta*),
there is a lack of confidence; it is written in the *āskandaka* meter, and in some places even in *galitaka* meters,
as in the *Setubandha*, or as in my own *Kuvalayāśvacarita*.
(592) In this work composed in Apabhraṃśa, the cantos are designated as *kaḍavakas*. Likewise, there are various meters suitable for Apabhraṃśa. Chapter Six.
Just as in the *Karṇaparākrama*:
(563) Due to the restriction of speech and its variants (*bhāṣā-vibhāṣā*), this poem abandons the formal divisions of cantos (*sarga*);
it consists of verses directed toward a single purpose and is devoid of the regularity of formal junctures (*sandhi*).
For example, *Bhikṣāṭana* and *Trāyavilāsa*.
(564) A *khaṇḍakāvya* (minor poem) follows a single portion of a [larger] poetic work;
for example, the *Meghadūta* and others.
(565) A *kośa* is a collection of worldly subjects that are independent of one another; yet when arranged according to the sequence of topics (*vrajyākrama*), it becomes exceedingly beautiful.

The arrangement of similar elements in one place is *vrajyā*, as in the *Muktāvatī* and other such works. Now, regarding prose compositions (*gadyakāvya*): therein, prose (*gadya*) is of two kinds—*muktaka* (unconnected) and *vṛttagandhi* (resembling verse)—being devoid of metrical composition (*vṛttabandha*).
There are four types [of prose]: that which consists mostly of *utkalikā*, and *cūrṇaka*.
The first is composed of compounds and endowed with metrical sections;
the next is rich in long compounds; the fourth is characterized by few compounds.

An example of the *muktaka* (detached verse) is: "The teacher in speech, Pṛthu in generosity," and so forth. An example of the *vṛttagandhi* (verse-like prose) is my own: "He whose bow was encircled by his staff-like arms, thickened by the itching of battle, and who awakened the cities of his enemies with the twang of his bowstring. Here, [the phrase] *kuṇḍalīkṛtakodaṇḍa-*...

The foot of the *anuṣṭubh* meter consists of eight syllables. Furthermore, the same foot, when deprived of its first two syllables, is called *samarakaṇḍūna*. An example of the *utkalikāprāya* meter is as follows, from my own work:
“*aṇisa visvamara ṇisidadarasara visara vidalitasamaraparigadapavaraparaba-*” (O you who, with the discharge of arrows from your drawn bow, have shattered the pride of the enemy host in battle...)

In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, it says "letyādi" (and so forth). An example of the *cūrṇaka* [verse] is my own: "O ocean of the jewels of virtues, sole abode of the earth, O Madana to women, O creator of the world," and so forth.
(567) A *kathā* is a composition of a juicy subject matter fashioned entirely in verse.
In some instances herein it may be in *āryā* meter, and in others in *akkāpaka*. At the beginning, there is a salutation in verse, followed by a description of the conduct of villains and the like.
As in the *Kādambarī* and similar works.
(568) An *ākhyāyikā* should be like a *kathā*, [but] it should contain a description of the poet’s lineage and so forth.
In this work, as well as in those of other poets, prose and verse appear here and there; the division of the sections of the narrative is composed in the form known as *ākhyāyikā*.
In the form of consolation at the beginning of a discourse, there is the statement of future events by noble speakers using any meter whatsoever under the guise of another subject.

As in the *Harṣacarita* and other such works. However, according to the statement of Daṇḍin Ācārya, "But no fixed rule is seen there either, because it is proclaimed by others as well," some maintain that the *ākhyāyikā* is composed by the hero alone.

“It should be composed,” they say; thus [the *ākhyāyikā*] is included. Furthermore, because it is subsumed within the categories of *ākhyāna*, *kathā*, and *ākhyāyikā*, it is not mentioned separately. As Daṇḍin himself stated: “The remaining types of *ākhyāna* will be included herein.”
An example of these is the *Pañcatantra* and similar works. Now, regarding those consisting of prose and verse: (568) Poetry composed of both prose and verse is called *campū*.
*Aṇiśam iti*: "Forget incessantly [the world], O you who have shattered all [obstacles] by the spreading forth of your exceedingly sharp..."
*Parigata-prabala-parabala-ityādi*. Commentary (*ṭī.*): This is the section on the *Vala* (the *Vilāsa* or *Vala-pariccheda*). For example, as in the *Deśarājacarita*.
(570) A panegyric of a king composed in both prose and verse is called a *viruda*,
such as the *Virudamaṇimālā*. (571) A *karambhaka*, however, is composed in various languages.

Just as my *Praśastiratnāvalī* consists of sixteen languages, so too other varieties have not been separately described here, because they are well known by mere mention and because they do not follow the sequence of the varieties already stated.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Visible and Audible Poetic Compositions," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*,

the sequence for the presentation of defects (*doṣa*), merits (*guṇa*), styles (*rīti*), and figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) in poetry has first been shown here. Now, in response to the inquiry as to what these are, [the author proceeds with] the defects, which follow according to the order of their enumeration.
He states its nature: (572) "Defects are those which detract from the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
The meaning of this has already been clarified previously. He now states its specific characteristics.
Furthermore, these are considered to be fivefold,
as they occur in the word, its constituent part, the meaning of a sentence, and even in aesthetic flavor (rasa).

(574) It is difficult to hear [if it contains] the three types of harshness (*ajīla*), the improper application of meaning, or the lack of connection; it is vulgar, or if it is obscure, doubtful, of secondary meaning, or has its meaning suppressed.
Inexpressiveness, obscurity, the production of a contrary cognition, and the non-distinction of the element to be predicated— these defects pertain to words and sentences.
Certain defects occur in these [words], even within a single word;
namely, meaninglessness, lack of semantic competency, and corruption of grammatical formation.
Harshness (*paruṣatva*) consists in being painful to the ear and difficult to hear, as for example:
"When will that slender-limbed woman go to the Kātya-tirtha, becoming subject to the power of the bodiless god [Kāma]?
Obscenity (*aślīlatva*) is threefold, according to whether it suggests shame (*vrīḍā*), disgust (*jugupsā*), or inauspiciousness (*amaṅgala*). In order:
An example:
"O King, in the conquest of your arrogant enemies, your means were very great;
O slender one, at that time they advanced slowly toward their destruction."
The Seventh Chapter. Here, the words *sādhana*, *vāyu*, *vināśa*, and *śabda* are used in their secondary (lākṣaṇika) senses:
"In the sacrifice of battle, those who have become cattle attain the state of immortality."

The word *papada* (a vulgar term for the anus) manifests cowardice; thus, it constitutes the fault of *anucitārthatva* (inappropriateness of meaning). Similarly, even if a word is well-known [for a certain meaning], its lack of respectability among poets constitutes the fault of *grāmyatva* (vulgarity). For example: "A lotus (*padmaḥ*) shines in the lake. Here, the word *padma* is used in the masculine gender. An example of vulgarity is: "At the waist... (*kaṭisse*).

"An angry mind. Here, the word *kaṭi* is vulgar (*grāmya*). Obscurity (*apratītatvam*) is the state of being known only in a limited portion [of usage]. For example: "One whose heart (*āśaya*) has been shattered by yoga. Here, the word *āśaya*, meaning "latent impression" (*vāsanā*), is used only within the Yoga treatises.
“O Āśī, having drawn [the bow] upon the venerable lineage, show mercy!

Here, regarding the word *vandyām*, there is a doubt: does it mean "one who has become a captive" (*vandībhūtāyām*) or "one worthy of worship" (*vandanīyāyām*)? Since there is neither conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) nor a specific purpose (*prayojana*), this is an instance of "forced interpretation" (*neyārthatvam*), where the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is produced by constraint.
Manifestation (*prakāśana*). For example:
"O fair-faced one, your face dealt a kick to the lotus.
Here, by means of the "kick of the foot," the state of being defeated is indicated (*lakṣya*). This is [an instance of] "the subordination of the literal meaning" (*mihatārthatva*) in both cases.

The use of a word in a sense not established for it; for example: “Yamunā spread out the *śambara* in the sky. The word *śambara* is well-known in the sense of a Daitya, but here it has a non-literal meaning, namely water. [In the phrase] “*karṇamādaḥ* in songs,” the former [word *karṇa*] is non-expressive (*avācaka*) in the sense of giving (*dādhāna*).
Or, for example:

"Day [has come] for me when you have arrived; even the night is darkness. Here, the word *dinam* (day) is non-expressive (*avācaka*) in the sense of "that which consists of light," because the meaning is understood only through effort (*kliṣṭa*).
The state of being separated by a word (*vrvyavahitatvam*): "The waters, the birthplace of the lotus, which is the abode of Lakṣmī born from the Ocean of Milk, are clear.
Here, *corodajā* refers to Lakṣmī; her abode is the lotus, and its birthplace is the waters. [This is] for the sake of prosperity in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
"May you be the son of Bhavānī!"— here, the term *Bhavānīśa* (Lord of Bhavānī) conveys a contradiction, as it implies having another wife besides Bhavānī.

"What is the use of these arms, which are merely fit for tearing down the small villages of creation?"— here, the word *grāmaṭikā* (small village) conveys a contradiction by implying that they are only capable of destroying insignificant things.

In this case, *tṛpālam* (sufficient) is what ought to be predicated; however, because it is subordinated within a compound, it fails to produce the intended understanding. Or, for example: "My younger brother Rāma is capable of slaying even the demons before [my very eyes]. Here, "Rāma’s" (*rāmasya*) should have been stated. Or, for example: "The ocean-bed... [and so forth].

Regarding [the term] *śānām*: it should be stated as *prajāsamudram*. Or, for example: "O fair-browed one, this side-glance of yours falls upon me like a sixth arrow of the Five-Arrowed One. Here, one should employ the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that it is "as if a sixth [arrow]. Or, for example:

"O Lord, by you, that [city] was formerly [ruled] even for a moment"—in this instance, *pracāmukā*, the negative particle (*nañ*) possesses the sense of a "partial negation" (*prasavyapratiṣedha*); thus, it is appropriate that it enjoins the very act [of ruling]. As they say:
"When there is a lack of prominence for the injunction and prominence for the negation,
this is a 'direct negation' (prasajya-pratiṣedha), provided that it does not occur here [in the following example] along with a verb:
'This is a fresh rain-cloud adorned with lightning, not a swift-moving night-stalker.'"

In this example, within a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the fact that the negation is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is not understood. As they say: "Where there is affirmation, there is primacy; where there is negation, there is non-primacy."
That should be understood as a paryudāsa (presuppositional negation) where the subsequent word is not *nañ*.
"Who here, afflicted by thirst, has resorted to the self as his own well?
By him... [End of] the Seventh Chapter.
Then Aṭabhu took it up and experienced the happiness of one who has attained his goal.

In this case, since the state of being unafraid is restated and the act of self-concealment (*ātmagopanā*) is what is to be enjoined, it is appropriate that the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), thereby assuming a subordinate status. One might object: "Just as in examples such as 'a Brāhmaṇa who does not eat at a funeral feast' (*aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ*) or 'the king's wives who do not look at the sun' (*sūryyampaśyā rājadārāḥ*), should there not also be a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) in the phrase 'not liberated' (*amukte*)?"

If it is argued that [the negative particle] does not [apply], we say no. Even here, if the connection of the negative particle were with the aspect of the action consisting of eating and so forth, only then could it be said to be a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). But it is not so;
for the connection of the negative particle is only with the object of consumption (*tadbhojya*), which is the primary element as the substantive.
As it is said: "Since the agent is understood from the habit of eating at a *śrāddha*,
it is not merely the act of eating that is enjoined for the agent."

However, since the pearl is connected only with the action (*kriyā*), it is indeed a fault. Furthermore, these faults such as *śliṣṭatva* (ambiguity) and so forth are word-faults occurring only within compounds. An example of harshness (*duḥśravatvam*) in a sentence is as follows:
"O enemy of Mura, when shall I, blinded by longing, attain my goal in separation from you?"
One who has engaged in the practice [of poetry] appropriately joins the suffix *kavin* with its etymological meaning.
In this instance, there is the quality of *jugupsāvyañjakatā* (suggestiveness of disgust):
"The body is adorned with curved [objects] having the redness of a blooming lotus. Here, "the redness of a lotus" refers to rubies (*padmarāga*), and "curved" means "crooked" (*vāmābhiḥ*).

“Whose mind, having beheld the beauty of Dhamila—who possesses the nature of a deer—does not become intensely impassioned? For his mind has never before experienced such a bond. Here, the syntactical connection is: “Whose mind becomes impassioned upon beholding the beauty of the weapon of Dhamila?”

[The fault is] *kliṣṭa* (obscured). In the verse, "This very thing is my humiliation (*nyakkāraḥ*)—that [he should have been killed]," the intended meaning is that this very thing constitutes the humiliation;

thus, the status of being the predicate (*vidheyatva*) belongs to "humiliation. This, however, is due to a reversal in the arrangement of words (*śabdaracanāviparyāsa*), as stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
By that [reason], it becomes subordinate. Furthermore, because the arrangement of the two words is reversed, this constitutes a syntactical fault (*vākya-doṣa*).

In examples such as, "O fair-browed one, he who has arrived gladdens your limbs," and so forth, according to the rule that "there is an obligatory connection between *yat* and *tat*," the [expectation] initiated—

In order to establish the lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) of the word *yat*, the words *idam*, *etad*, and *adas*— which are presented as having the same meaning as the word *tat*— ought to be understood as being precisely the things to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

However, in this case, because they stand in close proximity to the word *yat*, they produce the cognition of being the subject of reference (*anuvādya*), and thus the word *tat* [is likewise affected].
When situated near the word *yat*, it serves merely to refer back to what is already well-known. For example:
"O fair-browed one, he who brings delight to your eyes has arrived.
However, when situated with an intervening *yat* word, they convey a state of being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*).

In some cases, when a word-meaning is to be expressed, there is the statement of a sentence, such as: “The light arising from the eye of Atri. In other cases, when a sentence-meaning is to be expressed, there is the expression of a single word, such as: “O bestower of excellent rain,” [used] when the meaning of the sentence—“a woman whose limbs are delicate despite the heat of summer, the cold of winter, and the warmth of the season”—is intended to be conveyed. In some instances...

"Expansion (*vyāsa*) consists in the expression of a single sentence-meaning through multiple sentences by means of introducing some particular qualification; contraction (*samāsa*), on the other hand, consists in the expression of what is conveyed by multiple sentences through a single sentence. Such definitions and others of this kind [are not considered] *guṇas* by others.
However, there is a variety of specific applications;
therefore, the qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇas*) are not separate [from those of sound]. In that manner, the qualities of meaning—namely *ojas*, *prasāda*, and so forth—have been explained.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Qualities," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
In the *Vākyapadīya*,
[the author] now states the *rīti* (diction), which has been introduced as a distinct category (*bhedatvena*) following the examination of its varieties (*ākhyāvirūpaṇa*).
(24) *Rīti* is the arrangement of words, like a particular configuration of the limbs; it serves as an auxiliary to the *rasas* and so forth—
meaning to those *rasas* and other elements which constitute the soul of poetry, whose body consists of word and meaning.
Furthermore, that [rīti] is fourfold:
Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī, and likewise Lāṭikā.
That is *rīti*. Among them,
(626) the Vaidarbha style is held to be that which consists of grace, characterized by syllables that manifest sweetness (*mādhurya*),
and which is either without compound or possesses short compounds.

For example: "The source of auspiciousness for the inauspicious," and so forth. Rudraṭa said: "The Vaidarbhī style is characterized by the absence of compounds, the use of single compounds, and is endowed with the ten poetic qualities;
it abounds in the second class of consonants (the dentals), has its life-breath in short syllables, and is easy to compose."
In this regard, those ten qualities have been explained, beginning with *ojaḥ*. Furthermore, a composition that is ostentatious, characterized by words that manifest *ojaḥ*,
and abounding in compounds is the Gauḍī style.

As in the passage beginning with "cañcamuje" and so forth. Puruṣottama Svāmin says: "The Gauḍīya style is characterized by an abundance of compounds, very long-syllabled words, and is dependent upon the majesty of alliteration, while its sentences are free from *stobha* (filler syllables)."

Furthermore, when composed with the remaining syllables of two [lines],

"With a sweet voice, which was intensified by the abundance of honey from the *mādhavī* vines awakened by spring, and which repeatedly bore the intoxicated humming of female bees, the nightingale sang softly."

(30) However, in some cases, there are different arrangements and so forth in certain bodies;
[this refers to] the *Sāhibadaba*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "speech and so forth," the *Ākhyāyikā* and *Prabandha* are included. By the word "and so forth" in "arrangements and so forth," [other literary forms are meant].
Regarding propriety (*aucitya*): therein, [propriety] by way of the expressed (*vācya*) is as follows: "The caravan leader Manyāya," and so forth.

Here, although the expressed meaning is anger, the composition and other elements are elevated by virtue of being attributed to Bhīmasena. An example of propriety by way of the expressed is as cited: "When the head was being shaken..."

...and so forth. Furthermore, due to the propriety of the literary form (*prabandha*), as in the case of drama (*nāṭaka*) and similar works, long compounds and the like are not employed in the Furious Sentiment (*raudra-rasa*) because they are incompatible with its representation through performance (*abhinaya*). Similarly, in the Erotic Sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), even in prose narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), there are no excessively soft or flowery expressions. In a narrative tale (*kathā*), even when the Furious Sentiment is present, the style should not be overly bombastic.
In this way, other [cases] should also be understood.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of Styles" (Rītiviveka), in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.

Just as the limbs and so forth, by surpassing the beauty of the body, [contribute to] the embodied being—

Likewise, those figures such as *anuprāsa* (alliteration), *upamā* (simile), and so forth—which enhance the beauty of word and meaning by assisting with rasa and the like—are called *alaṅkāras* (ornaments) because they are unstable; thus, unlike the *guṇas* (excellences), there is no fixed rule for their application. This is because, between word and meaning, the word first becomes an object of cognition.

Since it must be discussed among the figures of sound (*śabdālaṅkāra*), and because the ancient masters have classified even the figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) known as "semblance of tautology" (*punaruktavadābhāsa*) within the category of figures of sound, he first explains that very one:
(632) "The semblance of tautology is the appearance of a meaning's repetition upon its initial presentation."
That which appears like a tautology consists of words that possess different forms.

Now, the occasion having arrived, the ornaments are described: Those attributes of word and meaning which are non-essential, yet produce an excellence of beauty and assist the aesthetic sentiments (rasa) and so forth, are called ornaments (alaṅkāra), like armlets and other such jewelry.
May Śiva— the one who wears serpents as earrings, whose cool rays are manifest like those of the bright moon,
and who captivates the mind— protect the world forever from calamity.

Here, at first glance, words such as *bhujaṅgakuṇḍalī* appear to be tautological because they seem to mean "one who has serpents [as earrings]"; however, in their ultimate sense, they mean "one in whom there exists an earring (*kuṇḍala*) that has the form of a serpent (*bhujaṅga*)," and so forth. In the expressions *pāyāt* ("may he protect") and *avyāt* ("may he preserve"), this is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) residing in the verb.

Because the word "pāda" [is used] from the beginning up to the end of "āditya," the first of the two words "bhujaṅgakuṇḍalī" and "iti-jña" is accompanied by direct perception (*paridṛṣṭi*). In the pair "haraḥ" and "śivaḥ," it is the second alone;
in "śiśu-bhrāṃśu," it is both. [As for the verse: "He shines always, never abandoning... [this is the example].

Even when employing synonymous terms, there is utility for the subject at hand; this is stated in the *Vāhaladarpaṇa*. By means of the abundance and lack thereof in the recurrence of words such as "thief" (*cora*), there arises the figure of speech known as *Ayobhava*.

(33) Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is a similarity of sounds even when there is a difference in vowel; however, it is not counted [as a distinct figure] when there is a lack of strikingness even in the mere vowels. It is called *anuprāsa* because it is a pervasive excellence (*prakarṣaṇa-vyāpa*) due to its being repeatedly applied (*anu-gata*).

(34) The similarity of a group of consonants [occurring] multiple times is *che kānuprāsa* (clever alliteration). "Multiple times" means in terms of both its intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) and its sequence (*krama*). For instance, because of the difference in sequence—as in *rasaḥ*, *saraḥ*, and so forth—repetition more than twice is not the province of this figure of speech. Example:
"The abduction of my father’s feet!
Here comes the purifying breeze from the waters of the Kāverī, slowly and gently, making the bees blind with joy at every step by carrying the fragrance of the *vakula* flowers."
In this example, in "gandhānandho" there is the repetition of two conjunct consonants; in "kāverīvārī" there is the repetition of non-conjunct consonants;

and in "pāvanaḥ pavanaḥ" there is the single repetition of many consonants. "Cheka" means a clever person; because it is employed by such a person, this is called *chekānuprāsa* (clever alliteration).
When a single [word] occurs once with similarity, or repeatedly in many ways,
or when a single [word] occurs even once in multiple ways, this is declared to be *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration).
In one way, solely by its own nature and not even by succession; in many ways, both by its own nature and by succession.
By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even that," it is implied that it is also non-sentient (*amaja*). Illustrate:
"The mango sprouts shaken by swarms of bees greedy for the fragrance of emerging honey..."

"O Lord of the Mountain, how— how indeed— can these days pass for travelers whose very lives have been sustained only by the intense longing for reunion with their beloveds, which they find through the focused application of their meditation upon the sweet, warbling notes of the sporting cuckoos?"

Here, O messenger, these [qualities] are equal to Rati’s splendors all at once, and not even in that same sequence. In the second quarter, however, there is repetition of two syllables, and they follow that very same sequence.

In the first [type], there is a single occurrence of the letter *ta* and multiple occurrences of the letter *dha*. An arrangement of syllables that functions upon the objects of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), by being excellently placed through its conformity to that [flavor] and its repeated invocation, is called *anuprāsa* (alliteration).
(636) When the same consonant is pronounced once at one place, such as the palate or the teeth,
and again in a similar manner, it is called *śrutyanuprāsa* (alliteration based on sound).
An example:
"The eyes of the Three-eyed One, which burnt the Mind-born [God of Love], seem to revive him; for the beautiful-eyed women have been brought under his sway."
In this context, regarding the words "jīvayanti," "bā," and "jamini," because the palatal [sounds] are pronounced in place of the single [consonant] cluster *jya* (ja + ya),
the examples of the dentals and gutturals should also be cited. And this is extremely pleasing to the ears of connoisseurs.
Because it brings ease, it is auditory alliteration (*śrutyanuprāsa*).
Thus,
(637) if the consonant, remaining as it is, [repeats] with the same vowel— whether initial or otherwise— [it constitutes this type].
Because it is to be joined with the final [word], it is repeated; thus, that is indeed "final alliteration" (antyānuprāsa).

“*Yathāvaskham* (according to its place)” means as it occurs, joined with anusvāra, visarga, vowels, and consonants. This [the *yati*] is generally to be employed at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*) or a word (*pada*). An example occurring at the end of a quarter-verse is from my own work:
The field is the blossoming cluster of *kāśa* grass; the body displays the graceful movements of an elephant's trunk;
the eyes are like burnt cowries; yet the mind does not abandon its longing for love.
An example of [the *śṛṅgāra* rasa] occurring at the end of a word is found in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"Smiling softly, bearing horripilation," and so forth.
(638) When there is repetition of both word and meaning despite a difference [in form], consisting merely of a difference in intended sense (*tātparya*),
it is called *lāṭānuprāsa* (the alliteration of Lāṭa).
An example follows.
"O lotus-eyed one, why are your eyes closed?
Behold your beloved, who has conquered Kandarpa yet remains under the sway of Kandarpa."

In this case, although the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not redundant, because the primary referent— the substratum (*dharmin*) expressed by the three nominal stems— is identical in meaning, it is indeed *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration). In the example,
"his very face and his eyes," the second occurrence of the word "eyes" refers to [the eyes] as qualified by attributes such as good fortune.
The meaning is different merely by virtue of the difference in form (rūpa), as for example: "Whoever has his beloved near him, for him the sun is a forest fire;
whoever has his beloved near him, for him the moon is a forest fire."
Here, there is the repetition of multiple words; this is the *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration) favored by the people of Lāṭa, O Prāleya. Alliteration is thus fivefold.

This is clear. (640) When there is a single meaning [for the whole], the repetition in that very same order of a sequence of vowels and consonants that possess distinct meanings is declared to be *yamaka* (chiasmus).
In both cases of these two words, sometimes there is meaningfulness and sometimes there is meaninglessness;
sometimes one is meaningful while the other is meaningless. Therefore, it is said that "it possesses meaning. This is the tenth chapter.

By the phrase "in that very same sequence," it is indicated that [the repetition] has an undifferentiated scope in cases such as *dama moda*. Furthermore, because this occurs across words, quarters (*pāda*), and half-verses (*ardhaloka*), and because the repetition of quarters and half-verses is of a single type, it possesses a vast number of varieties. A mere illustration is provided here.
Before him, he beheld a forest of fresh palāśa leaves and lotuses covered with manifest pollen,
where the ends of tender creepers swayed gently.
[He saw] the *masūraka* [tree], fragrant with its abundance of *sumana* flowers.

In this regard, there is repetition of words (*padāvṛtti*) in *palāśa palāśa* and *palāśe*. In *surabhiṃ surabhim*, both [instances] possess meaning. In *latāntalatānta*, the first [instance] is meaningless; in *parāgaparāga*, it is the second. Thus, other examples should also be cited accordingly.

According to the stated principle, "The *yamaka* and so forth may occur even once [in a verse], as well as at the beginning, middle, end, or both," there is no loss of the *yamaka* in the verse: "The women of the enemy host [attained] dullness of limb."
(649) If one should interpret a sentence intended for one meaning in another way—
either through punning (*śleṣa*) or by intonation (*kāku*)— that is *vakrokti* (indirect speech), and it is thus twofold.

The *didheti* (the "thus-he-shines" type) involves a remainder (*śeṣa*) of crooked speech (*vakrokti*), while the *kākuvakrokti* (crookedness through intonation) is as follows; the examples in their respective order are:
"Who are you? "We are indeed travelers. "What is the specific object of your inquiry? "He who speaks is the Lord of Serpents, or else Hari is asleep."
"O fair ones, what kind of god of love is this, who takes such delight in great mockery that he makes our minds devoid of discernment, so that we, though men, behave like women? — *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.

Here, because the word *viśeṣa* possesses two meanings—*vi* meaning "bird" and *śeṣa* meaning "serpent"—it is a *sabhanga-śleṣa* (a pun with a break). In other instances, however, it is *abhaṅga* (without a break):
"At a time when the cuckoos are vocal and the mango trees are enchanting..."
"He is not pained by the abandonment of one who has committed an offense, for he is free from the desire for retaliation."

In this case, although one friend enjoins [the lover] with a prohibition, another expresses it through irony (*kāku*) as if it were an injunction; thus, even within a single type of word, there are various forms across different languages. (642) Even in diverse languages, by means of words of a single kind alone—
Where there is such a sentence, this is intended to be called "equal to the language" (bhāṣāsama).
As in my own verse:
"O sweet-voiced cuckoo, why are you so despondent on the shore of this lake of pleasure, where the anklets of beautiful jewels jingle,
and where the fragrant breeze from the *sārasa* lotuses blows so gently?"
This verse [states]: "In Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Māgadhī, Śaurasenī, Prācyā, Āvantī, Māgadhī, and Apabhraṃśa, it is of one and the same kind.
However, in [verses] such as "saramaṃ karaṇa kavvaṃ... and so forth...
Even when both Sanskrit and Prākṛit are present, if they do not occur within the same sentence,
this is not considered a figure of speech due to the absence of aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*).
(645) For this [figure] is intended only when multiple meanings are expressed by means of words that are identical in form.
This also applies to the two verbal roots *varṣ* and *pratyay*, as well as to the two words [ending in those roots].
And that [poetry] is eightfold according to the [qualities of] *śleṣa* (punning), *bhakti* (devotion), *vacana* (number), and *bhāṣā* (language).
"The poet's poetry is full of flavor (*sarasa*)"—thus says the Sanskrit commentary.

"The rays, the horse-tail [whisk], and the southern wind..."

Here, in the phrase “sudhākira,” there is the suffix *cip*. Furthermore, because the plural and singular forms here share the same phonetic shape (*ekarūpya*), there is also the absence of case endings (*vacanaceṣa*). “The blossoming of the night-lotuses, and likewise their closing.”

In this context, there is also hatred toward words, namely hatred for neuter and feminine genders:

The term *vahivacāḥ* means "one who speaks outside," according to the capacity [of the suffixes] *kvan* and *kvanip* applied to the roots *śas* and *kṛ*.
[Examples include] "a broad vessel of Kārttakharapātra," and so forth.

In this case, due to the difference between the case-ending and the compound within the word-break (*padabhaṅga*), it is a fault of the *pada* (word), but not a fault of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). And thus: "Of those who have been brought to a state of confusion by the arrows of the God of Love..."
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"On its bank, there is a likeness to lotuses grown in the forest."

In this case, although words such as *sudhā* (nectar), *śilīmukha* (arrow), and others possess three genders, there is no change of gender because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) remains the same; thus, it is an instance of the retention of the original form (*prakṛtiśeṣa*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of retaining the original word-form in all cases.
"Seize the entire wealth of everyone; may you be intent upon the destruction of all."
"O you who approach with the primary intent of providing guidance, [and] whose conduct is subtle"—here, in the sense of "Hara," it is a vocative case ending (*sup*) addressing Śiva;
and in the other sense, it is a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) from the root *hṛ*. Likewise in "Bhava" and so forth, this distinction belongs to the suffix.

Even though the meaning is already conveyed by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), it is mentioned separately because it relies on a specific distinction (*vichitti-viśeṣa*) based on its occurrence within different suffixes, *subanta* (nominal) forms, or *tiṅanta* (verbal) forms.
"O Great One, bring about that very union which is a mass of nectar, a source of arrival [of bliss]..."
O Hara, O Ume, take refuge in that many-fold refuge; destroy the delusion of the mind together with its obstacles.
In this regard, between the Sanskrit and the Prakrit:
(644) furthermore, it is threefold—namely, with a break (*sabhaṅga*), without a break (*abhaṅga*), and consisting of both.
And these three varieties should be understood as occurring, as applicable, within the eight varieties already mentioned. For example:
"By whom, when he was yet unmanifest, the body of the conqueror of Bala was assumed in ancient times;
by whom the serpent-garland and bracelets were taken away; and who bore the Gaṅgā."

May that Hara, whose moon-bright head bears the name "Hara" praised by the immortals, and who himself is the destroyer of Andhaka, protect you— he who is Śiva, the consort of Umā, and the Lord of all.
In this context, the verse beginning with "yena dhvasta... is *sabhanga* (with word-splitting), while the verse beginning with "andhaka...

is *abhaṅga* (without word-splitting). Since these two can occur in a single instance, they constitute a *sabhanga-abhaṅga* type; however, for fear of increasing the bulk of the work, it has been cited separately. On this point, some maintain that only *sabhanga* [śabdaśleṣa]...

The Tenth Chapter: The Subject of *Śeṣa* (Pun). Where two words, though distinct because they are pronounced with different efforts due to differences in accent such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth, form a *śleṣa* (pun) according to the analogy of lac and wood; however, when there is no such phonetic split (*abhaṅga*), it is indeed a case of *arthaśleṣa* (semantic pun).

Where, due to the non-difference of the harshness (of sound) and the non-difference of the effort required for pronunciation, there is a non-difference of the words, the identity of the two figures follows the maxim of "the fruit residing on one branch. For that which depends upon something else is indeed an ornament of that very thing; this relationship between the object to be adorned and the ornament is established through the relation of the substratum and the dependent, just as in the world.

Others, however, maintain that here there is a fixed rule regarding the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the figures of speech—such as *dhvani*, *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*, *doṣa*, *guṇa*, and *alaṅkāra*—based on whether they reside in the word or the meaning. Nor is it the case that in examples such as "the multitude of Andhakas... [the rule fails], because of the words...

There is a distinction, because of the principle that "there is a difference in words based on a difference in meaning. Furthermore, since in this case the word itself is primarily grasped by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*) as the means for conveying variety, it is indeed a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*). And in the composition of two dissimilar words, such a variety [is produced].

Because of the absence of a fixed status, if poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*) were defined solely by their dependence on the meaning (*artha-mukha-prekṣitā*), then even alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like would result in being considered figures of meaning, since they too depend on the sentiment (*rasa*) and other factors through their dependence on the meaning. Furthermore, if a figure were considered a figure of meaning simply because it is dependent on the word (*śabda*), then there would be no distinction between them.

"In the case of [the verse] beginning with ‘When fate has turned adverse,’ even though there is a difference in the words, the status of being a figure of sense (arthālaṅkāra) would follow for you as well; therefore, in both cases, it is indeed a figure of word (śabdālaṅkāra). However, that is not so where the figure remains intact even when the words are substituted."
"In one moment he attains high status, and in a moment he falls to a low state;
oh, how similar is the conduct of a scale-beam and that of a wicked man!"

In such cases, there is *śleṣa* (punning) of meaning. Regarding this, some maintain: "Since it is impossible for this [śleṣa] to have a scope distinct from other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), even when other figures are present, it functions as an exception (*apavāda*) that supersedes them, thereby serving as the cause for the manifestation of their semblance. This is what is investigated here.

In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, in cases such as *samāsokti* (metaphorical expression) and *prastutapraśaṃsā* (eulogy of the relevant), because the second meaning is not directly denoted, there is not even a scent of [the figure] *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Even in the *rūpaka* (metaphor) "O swan of the minds of the wise," within the *sevagarbha* variety, the term *mānasa*— [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary discussing the distinction between *śleṣa* and other figures of speech (*alaṃkāras*) based on whether a secondary meaning is directly expressed or implied.]

Even though the word has both meanings—of mind and of enemy—the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is set aside by the *rūpaka* (metaphor), because the meaning consisting solely of the form of the body (*barorūpa*) serves as the primary locus of repose.
In *śleṣa*, there is a sense of wonder regarding both meanings, as in: "She who possesses the splendor of the sun, yet has the darkness of a nearby girl... and so forth.

Even in the absence of actual contradiction, there is no aversion [to the verse], because the contradictory meaning merely appears as a mental impression (*pratibhāsa*) without taking root. The same applies to cases that appear to be redundant (*punaruktavadābhāsa*). Therefore, in verses such as "yena dhvasta...
and "prākāśikayoḥ," there is a single cognition regarding things that are not topical (*aprākaraṇika*), such as "not being manifest" (*anuttāna*) and so forth.
In the case of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), due to the connection [of the two meanings], [the verse reads]:
"Though its object has arisen by mere whim, it does not go to say 'give'; rather, it gives pain through the very act of begging."
"Out of delusion, this lord of feeble intellect, though distinguished by his learning, miserably casts away his life in the midst of its prime.
Here, there is a *dīpaka* (illuminator) due to the connection of a single attribute between the contextual and the non-contextual.

"Even though a simile exists in such cases as 'this entire city has now become the orb of the moon,' that [simile] is set aside because of the presence of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the remainder [of the expression].
And since these [other figures] also persist even when the scope of *śleṣa* is excluded, *śleṣa* occupies this domain."

Since there is a perception of wonder through its predominance, it is proper that it be designated by that [predominant] quality alone; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the designation [of *śleṣa*] being entirely non-existent. To this it is replied: first of all, in an ultimate sense, *śleṣa* does not have as its object a domain that is indistinguishable from other figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*). For...
Because [the word] has as its object something distinct [from the literal meaning], there is no *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) here;
for in that case, there would be no restriction to both meanings being equally applicable. Indeed, in this instance, Mādhava is the tenth descendant of Mādhava.

If it were a rule that one [quality] must be expressed (*vācya*) while another is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), then there would be a contradiction. Furthermore, in cases of equal association, in one instance a single attribute is perceived as being connected to multiple attributes, whereas here [in the verse beginning with] "sakalakale," multiple subjects are perceived as being connected to their respective attributes individually. [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a portion of a commentary on the verse beginning with *sakalakala*, likely from the *Kāvyaprakāśa* or a related work on poetics.]

The remaining [type of] *mopamā* is the cause for the non-arising of the semblance (*pratibhā*). This is because the previous *upamā* would otherwise fall into the error of having no object of comparison. If it is argued that there is indeed an object of comparison in such instances as "this face is charming like a lotus," we reply: if, in examples such as "all... and so forth, it is merely a *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal pun), then it is not *mopamā*.

In that case, what offense has been committed? In examples such as "manojñam" (pleasing), it is clear from the remaining sense (*arthaśeṣa*) that these two are indeed the figures of speech *upamā* (simile) and *samuccaya* (conjunction); however, according to the direction of Rudraṭa’s teaching—that "even here, based solely on the word, they are possible through a commonality"—they may also exist by means of a word [denoting] similarity of quality or action.

Because the similarity between a bamboo and a flute is the cause of the simile. Now, it may be argued that it is only the equality of qualities or actions that is properly the cause of a simile, since in those cases the common property (*sādharmya*) is real; however, this is not so for the similarity of words, because in that case the common property is unreal. Therefore, [the definition] would otherwise fail to apply to the *pūrvopamā* (prior simile).

If it is argued that, because the equality of qualities and actions is impossible [in the case of words], the scope of *upamā* (simile) must be restricted to the equality of meaning (*artha-sāmya*) alone—since the scope of the definition of simile as "similarity is *upamā*" is thus limited—and not to the equality of words (*śabda-sāmya*) as in the example "sakalakala" and so forth, we reply:
No; for the general definition of simile, "similarity is *upamā*," remains unrestricted even with respect to the equality of words.
Or rather, [it is] non-existence. And if, due to the lack of reality, similarity based merely on verbal identity does not serve as the basis for a simile (*upamā*),

then how can it be that in examples such as "O wise one, [you are] like a lake," the superimposition of a lake and so forth upon the mind— which serves as the substratum— is the basis for the metaphor (*rūpaka*) consisting of the superimposition of a king and so forth?

Furthermore, if a simile (upamā) were to be accepted only when there is actual identity (*vāstava-sāmya*), then how is it that you yourself accept a "simile consisting of the object of comparison" (*adhyabhūtopamā*) in such cases as "sakalakaletyādi"? Moreover, in this instance, it is the *śeṣa* (the remaining poetic figure) that serves to sustain the similarity, and not the similarity that sustains the *śeṣa*, because of the composition of the *śeṣa*.

First, because equality is impossible [between the two], it is more appropriate to designate the simile itself as the *aṅgin* (the principal element), according to the principle stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"Designations are made by means of the principal. Now, regarding verbal... [text fragment]

If it is argued that in the domain of *dvāra* (the "door" or secondary figure), the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is not accepted, then how can there be such a relationship of principal and subordinate here in the case of *śeṣopamā* (the "remaining simile")? [We reply: No, because such a relationship is not accepted in the case of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like when they are devoid of a connection with the meaning. This should be understood to apply similarly to *dīpaka* and other such figures as well.
“Virtuous kings, sweet-voiced, adorning the quarters of the horizon and intoxicated with pride,
fall upon the surface of the earth under the power of time.”
In this context, because the words *dhārtarāṣṭra* and so forth are restricted to denoting swans and the like by the section on autumnal lotuses (*śaradabjana*),
the meaning in the form of Duryodhana and others constitutes a "word-suggestion" (*śabdaśaktimūladhvani*).
And here, there is the suggestion of the secondary meaning (*vyañjanā*) of the intended subject matter of the present composition, which is [the nature of] the moon.

In the same way, because it is not intended to be expressed, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is not intended; thus, this *śeṣa* [compound] is not a case of simile (*upamā*). Everything is now clear.
(645) When the descriptions serve as the cause for the appearance of a lotus and so forth, it is called *citram* (the marvelous).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [figures such as] the sword, the drum, the discus, and the cow's urine pattern (*gomūtrikā*) are included.
And by virtue of such specific triple arrangements (*triveśa*) within the three directions, there are also verses that produce a sense of wonder.

Thus, due to the influence of a particular conjunction with the auditory faculty and space (*ākāśa*), which produces a sense of wonder, and because of the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of it as non-different from the manifesting sounds,
it possesses the status of a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*). Among these, an example of the *padmabandha* (lotus-arrangement) is as follows, by me:
May that beautiful Ramā— who is the most excellent among the wives of Māra due to her lovely luster, who is the foremost among the daughters of Māra,
and whose abode is free from the thickest darkness of deceit— be ever dear to me.

This is the "Eighteen-Swans" lotus-band; in the petals of the cardinal directions, it consists of three *triṣṭubh* verses through both exit and entry, but in the petals of the intermediate directions, the *kartarī* verses are arranged differently. The rest is exactly as before.
In this same manner, the "Sword-band" (*khaḍgabandha*) and others should also be understood.
The Tenth Chapter. (646) That which is experienced as part of poetry is not elaborated here; because it acts as an obstacle to rasa, the *prahelikā* is not considered an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

That [type of *prahelikā*] consisting merely of verbal ambiguity includes the *cyutākṣara*, the *dattākṣara*, and so forth—the *cyutākṣara* (where a syllable is deleted), the *dattākṣara* (where a syllable is added), and the *cyutadattākṣara* (where a syllable is both deleted and added). An example:
"The cuckoos warble on the *sāla* tree; the lotus has blossomed in its youth."
"What can the doe do, her face pressed against his?"

In this context, where one should have said “*rasākha*,” it is composed as “*sāla*,” with the *r* displaced; where one should have said “*vaje*,” it has become “*yovana*”; and where one should have said “*vadanena*,” it is “*madanena*,” with the *d* displaced. By the word “etcetera,” [one includes] the concealment of action, agent, and so forth. Among these:
By way of illustrating this: "Duryodhana approached the Pāṇḍavas in the midst of their assembly hall;
to him [he gave] cows, gold, and all kinds of ornaments."

Here, in the phrase "duryodhana," [the analysis] is "tra-duryo'dhana," where the verbal root *ad* (to eat) is concealed by the prefix *adu-*; so it is in other cases as well. Now, since the types of concealment of meaning (*arthagupti*) that have reached their proper occasion are to be illustrated—beginning with those based on similarity (*sādṛśya*) due to their predominance—and because they serve as the basis for others, first...

Now, regarding the figure of speech *pamā* (simile): (647) Simile (*upamā*) and the like consist in a similarity (*sāmya*) between two things that is expressed (*vācya*), not merely implied, and which lacks dissimilarity (*avaidharmya*).
In figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor), the similarity is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), and in *vyatireka* (contrast), there is also the mention of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, it is stated that the distinction between *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) and *ananvaya* (self-comparison) lies in the fact that the former involves two sentences, whereas the latter involves the expression of similarity for a single object alone.

(648) If that [subject] were complete with a common property (*sāmānyadharma*), a word expressing comparison (*aupamyavācin*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and if there were a *dāp* suffix, that would be a full simile (*upamā*).
The common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) consists of qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*) which are the cause of similarity (*sādṛśyahetu*) between the two.

The qualities such as being pleasing (*manojñatva*), the words expressing comparison such as *iva*, the object of comparison (*upameya*) such as the face, and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) such as the moon—
this, moreover, is [the basis of the simile].
The *śrautī* [metaphor] occurs when there is a word such as "like" (*iva*), provided that the *vanir* (the object of comparison) possesses the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*).

Words such as *ārtha*, *tulya*, *samāna*, and so forth, or where the suffix *-vat* is used in the sense of "equal to," as well as words like *yathā*, *iva*, and *vā*— even though these are common to other meanings when employed in comparison—
indicate, by their mere hearing, the relationship characterized by similarity existing between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*).

They cause awakening; thus, when they exist, there is a simile for the hearer. Likewise, in that context, by the phrase "of that very [thing]," there is the employment of the suffix *vati* prescribed for the sense of comparison. However, words such as *tulya* (equal) occur only in the object of comparison (*upameya*), as in "the face is equal to a lotus" (*kamalena tulyaṃ mukham*). But in cases such as "that which is equal to the face is a lotus" (*yat tulyaṃ mukhasya tat kamalam*), [they occur in the standard].

It is indeed *māna* (pride). In cases such as "The lotus and the face are equal," since [the cognition] rests upon both [terms], it conveys the similarity only through the mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of the meanings; therefore, when that [synthesis] exists, it is *ārthī* (implied).
Likewise, it is so when the suffix *vati*, prescribed in the sense of equality by the rule "tena tulyam" and so forth, is employed.
(648) [The suffix] *taddhita* occurs in a compound or in a sentence; for example, *he tīrtha*. An illustration:
"O you whose face is like a cluster of lotuses, whose breasts are full like two jars..."
"O young girl, your face gladdens the heart just like the autumn moon."
The Tenth Chapter.
Herein, various sentiments (*rasas*) appear in succession:
"The lower lip is sweet like nectar; the hand is exceedingly delicate, like a lotus."
Her eyes, tremulous and fickle, were like those of a startled doe.
In this regard, there are three types of ellipsis (*luptā*) occurring in sequence:
the complete (*pūrṇā*), which consists of exactly six [types];
and the elliptical (*luptā*), which occurs when there is an omission of either one or two of the common attributes (*sāmānyadharma*).
Or, when there is no grasping of the three, that [negation] is both verbal and implied, as before.
That [type of ellipsis] is omitted. He states its divisions:
"Clearly, when there is the elision of a property (*dharma*), it is like the full [simile], except for the *śrautī* [simile] and the derivative (*taddhita*) [simile]. (652)

That is *luptopamā* (elliptical simile), which—like the *pūrṇā* (complete simile)—is of six types according to the aforementioned method when there is the elision of the common quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or form (*rūpa*). However, in this case, because the suffix (*taddhita*) is not heard [in the sense of "resembling"], it is of five types. An example:
"O beloved, your face is like the moon, your hand is equal to a young sprout,
your speech is like nectar, your lip is comparable to the bimba fruit, and your mind has become [like] the earth."

(653) The base (*ādhāra*), the object (*karman*), and the procedure (*vidhi*) are of two kinds, namely *kyac* and *kyaṅ*; furthermore, there are five types including the agent (*kartṛ*) and the suffix *ṇamul*. In the case of the elision of a property (*dharmalopa*), the term *supta* is supplied [from the previous rule]. According to the Kalāpa school, *kyac*, *kyaṅ*, and *ṇamul* [are treated as such].
Bāyiṇama: Examples in order:
"You dwell within the inner apartments; you are well-versed in battles; the city-dwellers always delight in you; and Fortune is ever fond of you."
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"O Lord of the Earth, you are seen by your beloveds as the moon, and here upon this earth you move about like Indra."

In the example “atrāntaḥpurīyasī,” there is an elision of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—namely, “being weary of dwelling in pleasure”—in the word *antaḥpurīyasī*. In the example “sutīyasī,” there is an elision of the common attribute—namely, “abundance of loveliness”—in the word *sutīyasī*. It is the same elsewhere. And here, since the beginning [of the comparison] is absent, there is no consideration of specific types such as the *śrauti* (verbal) and so forth.

It does not exist. Furthermore, some take pleasure in the suffix *vate* as an indicator of comparison (*aupamya*), but that is incorrect; for even *kyaṅ* and so forth are indicators of comparison because they are prescribed for that very purpose.
Now, one might object: "In the case of *kyaṅ* and the others, there is no correct perception of comparison, since they are suffixes (*pratyaya*)."

One should not say that [the suffix *kyaṅ*] does not apply because of a lack of independence or because of the absence of the use of words such as *iva*; for if that were so, the same consequence would follow for the *kalpa*-suffixes and others. Furthermore, while the *kalpa*-suffixes and others are expressive of similarity (*aupamya*) through their own independence, the *iva*-suffixes and others are not; rather, it is the *kyaṅ*-suffixes and others that possess the capacity to express the state of being a stream (*srotas*). Nor is it the case that the *iva*-suffixes and others are not expressive.

Because there is no absence [of meaning] at the time [of usage]. Or, if they possess denotative power, then the word as a whole is the denoter; and since both views maintain that "the base and the suffix convey their respective meanings," the status of the *vati* suffix and the *kā* suffix is indeed identical. As for what some say: "The *vati* suffixes and so forth do not denote substances..."

As for the statement that "the suffixes *kyaṅ* and so forth are taught in the sense of behavior (*ācāra*)," that too is incorrect; for *kyaṅ* and the others do not have the mere sense of behavior as their meaning, but rather the sense of behavior characterized by similarity (*sādṛśya*).
Thus, in this way, there are ten types of elided [suffixes] when a grammatical element (*dharma*) is dropped.
(654) When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not explicitly mentioned, there are two types: in the case of a sentence and in the case of a compound.
An example is:
"There is nothing as beautiful as her face, nor is there anything equal to her eyes."

In this context, there is an elision [of the standard of comparison] (*upamānalopa*), because the face and eyes are suitable as other standards of measure (*māna*) by way of being representatives. And in this very case, regarding the phrase "similar to the face," one might say "the face is like this."

In the reading “*nayanatulām ityādi*” and “*dṛg iveti*,” *śruti* (verbal similarity) is also possible; thus, although there is a possibility of four types based on the distinction between *śruti* and *artha* for each of these two [types of *śleṣa*], we have stated that there are only two types according to the method of the ancients.
(655) When a word expressing a comparison is elided, there are two types of compounds: those ending in *k* and those ending in *pi*. The examples follow in order:
"The face of the deer-eyed one is as enchanting as the moon."
"Roaring in front of the great-souled ones, he made Śakra tremble with words harsh to the ear."

In this instance, in the word *gaībhatītyana*, there is the elision of the suffix *kvip* which expresses the sense of comparison (*upamā*). However, here there is no elision of the object of comparison (*upameya*) either, because of the very mention [of the form] as *nimadan*. (656) In a compound, when both the common property (*dharma*) and the object of comparison (*upamāna*) are elided, it is called *dharmopamānalopa* (elision of both).
In the passage beginning with "by her mouth," where the reading "loke" (in the world) replaces "ramyam" (delightful), there is an example of *anugra* (favor).
(657) Is [the figure] contained within a compound two-fold: either in the attribute (*dharma*) or in the elision of the subject (*vādi*)?

An example: "vidhavati mukhāmbujam asyāḥ" (Her lotus-face acts like a widow). Here, there is the elision (*lopa*) of both the root *dhav* (to move/shine) and the suffix *kvip* (expressing the sense of "acting like"). Some maintain that even here there is the elision of the suffix; and "mukhāmbujam" is an instance of [the figure] occurring within a compound (*samāsagā*).
(58) But when the object of comparison (*upameya*) is omitted, there may be one [type] where the suffix (*pratyaya*) remains, as in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"Rātivikrama, Akhaṇḍala, Vikasvaratrilocana, Kṛpālu, Ugradordṛṣṭi— he suddenly becomes wise.
Here, in the sentence "he behaves as if he were Sahasrāyudha himself," there is a simile (*upamā*).

There is the elision of the suffix *bāman*. Nor is there an elision of the word expressing the object of comparison here, because it is understood from the context itself. Regarding this, some say: [the term] *sahalāyudhavat* is derived from the sentence "he exists together with Sahalāyudha" (*sahalāyudhena saha varttate*), or "he behaves like him" (*sa iva ācarati*).

The claim that there is an elision of the *upamāna* (the object of comparison) here because the word expressing the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished in its base form (*padasiddha*) cannot withstand scrutiny; for this does not contradict the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) governing the formation of the denominative suffix *kyac* when it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*).
(659) Another [type of simile] occurs when both the object of comparison (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) are omitted,
as for example:
"When your fame spreads, all the oceans become white with foam."

In this case, because they act as if they were the ocean itself, it is a simile (*upamā*) where both the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) and the agent (*śakata*) are elided; and when the attribute is elided,
it is a simile contained within a compound (*samāsagā*).
For example: "The one with deer-eyes shines.

Here, in the compound *mṛgalocanā*, there is an elision of the word expressing the comparison (*upamā*), the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharmma*), and the object of comparison (*upamāna*), [the analysis being] "she whose eyes are as tremulous as the eyes of a deer."

(661) Thus, there may be twenty-seven varieties of simile. The complete [simile] is of four kinds, the defective is of one kind, and the [simile] with a single common attribute is of twenty-one kinds; thus, when combined, there are twenty-seven types of simile. Among these varieties of simile, those in which the common attribute is not omitted—
The specific distinctions among the varieties are now set forth. Chapter Ten.
(662) A common quality may be uniform in some cases, yet distinct in others.
Either there is a difference in the nature of the reflection of consciousness, or there is a difference in the sound itself.
Among these, the case of a single form (*ekarūpa*) is as illustrated: "The lower lip is sweet like nectar," and so forth. The case of the reflected image (*bimba-pratibimba*) is as follows:
"By their heads, which were severed by the sword and dripping with blood..."
And he spread it out as if with honeycombs filled with bees.

In this context, the phrase "of the enemy's [palace]" (*śatruberityasya*) is a reflection by way of an illustration, as in the phrase "pervaded by bees" (*saraghāvyāptairiti*). This occurs when there is a difference merely in words, as for example: "Having fashioned Meru like a blue lotus in full bloom, she dwelt upon it... (*meruṃ vidhāya navanaṃ vikasitamiva nīlotpalaṃ sa viṣādaḥ*).
The slender-limbed woman related the entirety of her inner thoughts and intentions.
Now, some [hold that] the *prativastūpamā* is indicated by a difference in words within what is otherwise blossomed by gentleness (*soratva*).
Or, it is understood as a *ekadeśavivartinī upamā*.
Where there is a comparison of similarity,
there may be [the following]: “As if with blue lotuses for eyes, as if with lotuses for the beauty of the lakes’ faces.”
At every step it shines with ruddy geese, as if with peaks of Mount Meru."

In this context, the similarity of the eyes and other features to lotuses and so forth is what is to be expressed; the lake is to be understood as the beauty of the Pāñcālī style, extending from the nose to the arms.
For example:
What is the simile based on inversion?
It occurs when the object of comparison (the upameya) is placed above [in the compound], while the standard of comparison (the upamāna) follows.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"The moon acts like the moon even with but a single ray;
the swan acts like a swan by its graceful gait; and the beloved acts like the god of love."
The water, possessing its beloved [clarity], shone with all-encompassing beauty through its purity within the ocean.
(665) A string of similes (*mālopamā*) occurs when many points of comparison are seen for a single [subject]. For example:
“A lake as with a lotus, a night as with the moon.”
Like a woman with youth, Fortune is captivating through propriety.
In some cases, both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison are observed to be contextual (prakṛta).
The swan shines like the moon, and his fame is like the sky;
the stars are as stainless as white water-lilies at the arrival of autumn.
The splendors brought by kings shine at the festival of King Trasa,
like those produced by the wish-fulfilling cow in the palace of Indra.

In this case, since the glories that serve as the subjects of comparison (*upameya*)— namely, "as if they were the glories of Kāla"— will be the glories that serve as the standards of comparison (*upamāna*), this is a *vākyopamā* (sentence simile). Furthermore, because there is a re-statement (*pratinirdeśa*) of the word "great" (*mahat*) by means of the word "in the abode" (*bhavane*), this is a *pratinirdeśyopamā* (simile of re-statement).

And [the examples beginning with] "tyādi" have not been collected, because such a variety is seen to occur spontaneously. (666) Ananvaya is the state of being both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison for one and the same thing.
Now, as occurring in a single sentence, for example:
“As a lotus is to a lotus, as water is to water, as the moon is to the moon— so have you arisen, O Autumn, independent of any other.”
The Tenth Chapter.

Here, for the purpose of establishing that the lotus and so forth possess no other beauty [than that of the face], the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is expressed figuratively (*vācika*). And its [meaning] is as follows: "The lotus is like the face."
The scope [of this rule] includes alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like. However, because it is more appropriate, the use of a single word alone is preferable. As it has been said:
"In the case of non-connection (*amanvaya*), the repetition of words occurs as a secondary consequence due to propriety (*aucitya*)."
"In this case of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration), however, [the repetition] is the direct cause.
(667) By means of alternation, these two are considered "mutual comparison" (*upameyopamā*).
This refers to the state of being both the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), occurring through the sense in two separate sentences. For example:

Her intellect was like a lotus, and her lotus-like wealth was like her intellect; her radiance was like her body, and her body was like her radiance; her fortitude was like the earth, and the earth was like her fortitude.
Ah, that which belongs to you shines forth eternally!
The intention here is that for this king, there exists nothing else comparable to Śrīḍahya and the like.
(668) Recollection (*smaraṇa*) is said to be the mental activity arising from a similar experience;
for example:
"Beholding this lotus, charming with the movement of bees,
I remember her face with its tremulous eyes that seemed to gather it."

And in the verse beginning with "mayi sakapaṭam," [the figure] is not *smaraṇālaṅkāra* (recollection as an ornament), because it has been brought forth without the experience of a dream. However, Rāghavānanda Mahāpātra maintains that even in the absence of a dream, there is *smaraṇālaṅkāra*. An example of this according to them is as follows:
Mebha Bacā | *Sāhityadarpaṇa*: "The Śirīṣa flower blossomed upon the mountains..."
Whenever Sītā spoke of her sorrows,
at those very moments Rāma’s heart was pierced by the arrows of love as he contemplated enduring them.
(668) Metaphor (*rūpaka*) consists in the superimposition of the metaphorical object (*rūpita*) upon that which is not its locus (*aviṣaya*), provided there is no denial (*nirapahnava*).

The term "metaphorical object" (*rūpita*) serves to exclude the figure of identification (*pariṇāma*); this we shall examine in the section on identification. The phrase "provided there is no denial" is for the purpose of excluding the figure of concealment (*apahnuti*).
