(670) That [type of] metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) is of two kinds: *paramparita* (successive) and that which is either with parts (*sāṅga*) or without parts (*niraṅga*). Regarding these:
(679) When the superimposition of one thing is the cause for the superimposition of another, [it is called *paramparita*].
That is indirect (paramparita), based on words that are either desired or undesired.
It is of four kinds: each [type] taken individually, the simple (kevala), and the garland-form (mālārūpa).
Among these, an example of the simple transposed (kevalaparamparita) based on the word *siṃha* (lion) is as follows:
"In the battle against the world-conquering king, in the slaughter of the enemy..."
"O illustrious King Nṛsiṃha, may the pillar be for your arm!

Here, the superimposition (*āropa*) of the circle of kings—the assembly of monarchs—upon the lunar orb serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for the superimposition of the king's arm upon the moon. An example of the "garland" form (*mālārūpa*) is as follows:
"O Lord, you alone on this earth are the sovereign sun causing the lotuses to bloom, the wind of constant motion,
and the thunderbolt that shatters the range of mountains."
In this context, the very rising of Padmā (Lakṣmī) is the rising of lotuses; the arrival of the virtuous is the "tenth chapter";
and the mountains are merely kings—such is the superimposition (āropa) upon the king.
The reason for employing the word *sūryalācā* (the sun’s vine) is as follows: it is based solely on the sound [of the syllables], just as in the example:
"May the eight arms of Hari protect you—those which are the pillars for the pavilion of the three worlds, and which bear the scars from the striking of the string of the Śārṅga bow."
In this case, the attribution of the status of a ceremonial pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) to the three worlds is for the purpose of establishing [the king] as the vehicle of Hari.
An example of the form of *mākhā* is as follows:
"The white parasol of King Manojā..."
The moon’s orb, shining with the luster of a mass of camphor, appears like a lotus in the lake of the sky, its green body variegated with streaks of sandalwood paste.

In this case, the superimposition of qualities such as being a king upon the mind-born [Kāma] and others serves as the cause for the superimposition of the white parasol upon the lunar disc. And among these, the superimposition of the nature of a king upon the arms of the king and so forth serves as the cause for the superimposition of the nature of the lunar orb upon the circle of kings and so forth.
Some [say]:
(672) If the metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of that which possesses its parts (*sāṅga*) is by means of the possessor of those parts (*aṅgin*), then it is indeed "with parts" (*sāṅga*);
and it is of two kinds: having all things as its object (*samastavastuviṣaya*) and having a single part as its scope (*ekadeśavivarti*).
In that regard:
the first opinion holds that all [cognitions] are verbal (śābda) once [the object] has been superimposed;
the first [type of this] has all things as its object, for example:
"Thinking, 'He is exhausted by the drought of the cries [of the enemy],' that dark cloud [Kṛṣṇa], having rained upon the crop of the wind-god [Arjuna] through his word-weapon, vanished."
[This is] *sāhibadatha*.

Here, while the superimposition of "cloud" upon Kṛṣṇa is present, the superimposition of "nectar" and so forth upon his speech and other qualities is [only] partial (*ekadeśavivartin*). That [superimposition] is considered figurative (*ārtha*) when it pertains to a single part [of the subject]. (674)
Of something being compared, as for example:
"Whom would her blossoming face, filled with the honey of its loveliness,
not be drunk by the bees that are the glances of the world?"

In this instance, in the verse beginning with "lāvaṇya," the superimposition of honey is verbal (*śābda*), while the superimposition of lotus-ness upon the face is figurative (*ārtha*). Nor is this a case of "partial metaphorical transformation" (*ekadaṃśavivartinī upamā*), because the property of "blooming" resides primarily in the lotus which is being superimposed, whereas it applies to the face only in a secondary or figurative sense.
(675) The description of the simple alone is "niraṅga" (without parts), and that too is of two kinds. Because it consists of a single form, it is a "mālā" (garland-like);
therein, an example of the "niraṅga" form of the garland-like is as follows:
"She is the mastery of emanation, the moonlight for the elements, and the eye of the worlds;
she is this lotus-eyed one, the pleasure-palace of the Bodiless God."
Simply as follows:
"O beautiful one, it is only proper for masters to strike a servant with their foot when he has committed an offense; therefore, I do not grieve."
With high, harsh bristling hairs and making a painful sound,
if my soft foot is pierced, may there be no pain for me.
[The *senā-rūpaka* contains these piercing sounds.]

The word "by the ancients" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. In some cases, there is also a metaphorical transference (*paramparita*) that occurs by way of a part [representing the whole],
as in the tenth chapter.
"The sky was the arena where the gods of the ten directions triumphed over the Indra among men.
Here, the superimposition of the status of a queen upon the earth is the cause for the superimposition of the status of a sword upon the sky.
An example of this variety [of *samāsokti*] in the form of a "garland" (*mālā*) should likewise be sought, as in the previous case.
(677) In some cases, even in a *rūpaka* that includes its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), the superimposed objects may be seen as being based on wordplay (*śliṣṭa*).
Among these, an example of wordplay where only one part of the meaning is manifested (*ekadeśavivartin*) is as follows, from my own work:
"Upon the breast-peak of the mountain of sunrise..."
"Whose face is this that,
having dispelled the veil of darkness, now kisses the face of the eastern quarter with its blossoming lilies, like the moon, the lord of the immortals?"

An example concerning all objects is as follows: in this very [verse], in the reading “*cucumbe haridbalāmukham indunāyakena*” (the moon-lord kissed the face of the western quarter), there is no *śleṣa* (punning) based on another meaning. For in that case, in [the phrase] “*bhūbhṛdāvalidambholiḥ*” (the thunderbolt against the row of mountains) and so forth, [the word refers to] the king and others.

Without the metaphorical representation of [the king] as a mountain and so forth, the representation of the subject of description— such as a king— as a thunderbolt and so forth is entirely untenable,

because of the total impossibility of similarity. If that is so, how is it that in examples such as "the sun for the day-lotus of his fame," there is a *paramparita* (metaphor based on a chain), given that the similarity between the king and the sun [is not direct]?

It should not be argued that [this is] because it is possible for there to be a cause such as brilliance (*tejasvitā*) and so forth; for while in the case of a king and others, a clearly manifest similarity based on causes such as brilliance is intended,
in the present context that is not what is intended, since the rising of the lotus and so forth alone are intended as the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) of the two.

In this case, however, the similarity between the mountain and the breast, by virtue of their being full and high, is quite evident; thus, it is not a "successive metaphor" (*paramparitarūpaka*). Furthermore, a metaphor is sometimes recognized even in the absence of a compound. For example:
In the *Śālistamba*:
"O Sage, you have said that the world is without beginning.
Even the ritualist (*vidhikara*) says: [so it is].
“Here, the Creator fashioned her eyebrows as a brush for painting the honey-drinking [face].
An example where it occurs even in a non-poetic context:
“He is a wall for the painting of good conduct, possessing the beauty of noble character and virtuous deeds.”

Those who, even while possessing the splendor of the fourteenth day of the waxing moon, served the lineage of kings in this Kali age with such wicked intent— that their devotion to the Lord, which is easily attained through mere faith, was displayed only in their sword-blades— what skillful service was that?

"This is mine. Here, although certain metaphors (*rūpaka*) are rooted in an aversion to [literal] words, they are included among the ornaments of sound because they are specific types of metaphor. This same principle should be understood for the ornaments to be discussed hereafter.

(878) That very same metaphor (*rūpaka*) which possesses the excellence of being superimposed (*adhikārūḍhavaiśiṣṭya*) is itself that [superimposed metaphor]. That same [metaphor] possessing the excellence of being superimposed is the "internal metaphor" (*antarūpaka*). As it is said by me: "This is indeed a battle devoid of swords and the like, a bearer of wisdom..."
Her lower lip is like a lotus long-sprinkled by streams of nectar;
these two eyes possess a beauty exceeding that of day and night;
and her body is a sea for those wishing to bathe in loveliness.
There is a further distinction [of *pariṇāma*] by virtue of its being free from the defects of *kaṇa* (the "speck") and so forth.

(678) When that which is superimposed takes on the nature of the object, it serves the purpose of the subject matter at hand; thus, *pariṇāma* may occur in two ways: with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) or with a different substratum (*atulyādhikaraṇa*).
The tenth is *marīccheda*.
*Parikṣāma* is so called because it is characterized by the complete identification of the object being superimposed with the nature of the locus of superimposition. For example:
"A smile was offered as a greeting by her when I arrived from afar;
and at the game of dice, she made a wager, pressing her breasts against me like a garland."

Elsewhere, the *upāyana* (gift) and the *paṇa* (stake) are employed by way of being speech and ornaments; here, however, they exist in the form of a smile and the remainder [of the face] during the hero’s estimation and the game of dice. Here, in the first case, there is an employment with grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); in the second, there is coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is a metaphor (*rūpaka*).

In expressions such as "I see the moon," the superimposed moon and so forth possess only the status of being a subject (viṣayatā), but they have no utility in the actual act of seeing and so on. Here, however, through the act of approaching, there is an identity with the objects, and in the context at hand, this serves a purpose in the hero's estimation and so forth. For this very reason, it is [distinguished from] metaphor (rūpaka).

In that case, the superimposed [object] is connected merely by way of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*). But here, in examples such as "the servant who has committed an offense" (*dāse kṛtāgasi*), the connection is by way of identity (*tādātmya*). This is indeed *rūpaka* (metaphor) and not *pariṇāma* (transformation), because the effect produced by the superimposed thorn through the piercing of the foot is not the subject under discussion (*aprastuta*). Indeed, that [effect] belongs to no one [else].

Furthermore, this [metaphor] is employed for the purpose of establishing the matter at hand; like a *rūpaka* (poetic metaphor), it is seen to possess an elevated distinctiveness (*vaiśiṣṭya*), as for example:
"Of those forest-dwellers accompanied by their wives..."
The forest herbs, their luster resting upon the laps of the moonbeams, become oil-fed lamps for lovemaking during the night.

In this context, because the lamps possess the nature of medicinal herbs, their application in dispelling the darkness that obstructs sexual pleasure possesses a specific excellence established by the addition of the filling of oil.
In the *Vāhalidarpaya*:
"A message regarding another matter at hand, a doubt arising from intuition, is of three kinds:
pure (*śuddha*), that which contains a certainty within (*nicayagarbha*), and that which ends in certainty (*niścayānta*)."
In this matter, Sañjaya alone is the final authority; he is the one who knows. For example: "Is this a fresh sprout from the tree of youth, overflowing with the essence of sap?
Or is it a digit of the moon, the lord of the stars, emerging from the midst of its own limbs?"

"Is he the staff of direct instruction for those who possess the rising longing of love, appearing as if through the confidence of a formal exposition; or is he the very personification of the god of love himself?"
That which is true at the beginning and at the end, but false in the middle, is called *nicūḍhamadhyam*.
For example: "Is this the sun, or is it the Vasu accompanied by seven horses?"

Fire: "Does he surely spread through all directions? Is this Death himself manifest before us? Is this the buffalo-demon Mahiṣa? Thus, O Life, as they gaze upon you again and again, your adversaries harbor such doubts.

In this context, the "accumulation" (*nicaya*) of Mārttaṇḍa and others occurs in the middle; for in a collection of kings, it is impossible for a second doubt to arise. That in which there is doubt at the beginning and accumulation at the end is called *miśrānta* (ending with a mixture). For example:
“Is this a lotus in the lake nearby, or is it the face of a young woman that shines here?
Having reflected for a moment, someone reached a certain conclusion.
[This figure occurs] through the tremblings [of doubt] regarding those who dwell with one's enemies while they are out of sight;
however, when it is presented as a lack of conviction, such as in the doubt "Is this a post or a man?
and so forth, this is not an ornament (alaṅkāra).
The Tenth Chapter: “O lotus-eyed one, as for your waist, which is constricted by the weight of your breasts—
whether it exists or does not exist, this doubt does not occur to anyone’s mind.”

In this case, it is indeed *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the doubt regarding the identity of the object of comparison with the standard of comparison is itself the subject matter of this [figure]. (681) *Bhrāntimān* (the figure of error) consists in the cognition of something as being that which it is not, due to similarity, arising from a flash of genius (*pratibhā*).
For example: "Foolish women, thinking it to be milk, place pots beneath the cows;
even lovely women put blue water-lilies in their ears, suspecting them to be ear-ornaments."
The Śavarī woman gathers jujube fruits, mistaking them for pearls;
whose heart does this dense moonlight not delude?

This ornament is an error produced by its own inherent nature (*svarasotthāpitā bhrāntiḥ*), as for example: "silver in what is actually a spear-shaft. Nor is it based on dissimilarity (*asādṛśyamūlā*), as for example:
"In the choice between union and separation, separation from her here is better than union."
In union she alone exists as one, and even the three worlds are composed of her; yet in separation, she is likewise [the same].
When a single object is described as having various aspects through its different qualities or its relation to various objects,
that is considered *ullekha* (pictorial description).
The examples in their respective order are as follows:
“The Lord was perceived as ‘the Beloved’ by the cowherd women, as ‘the Child’ by the elders, as ‘the Sovereign’ by the gods,
as ‘Nārāyaṇa’ by the devotees, and as ‘Brahman’ by the yogis.”

In this case, although the Blessed One is one, he is depicted in many ways due to his connection with various objects; thus, for the cowherd women and others, their respective inclinations (*ruci*) and so forth act as the determining factors (*prayojaka*), as it is said: "In the *Bāhyārthasiddhi*..."
“Just as the meaning is differentiated according to the arrangement and according to the lack of proficiency, so too,
even in a single [text], the meaning is sublated by the lack of synthesis.”
In this case, because the Blessed One’s pleasant speech and his speaking of reality are distinct,

there is neither a *mālārūpaka* (garland metaphor), nor *bhrāntimān* (illusion), nor is this the figure of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) consisting of "difference in non-difference. For in that [latter case], as in the verse beginning "Another indeed is the beauty of her limbs," there is the state of...

The determination (*adhyavasāna*) of an object as something distinct [from its actual nature] does not occur here with respect to the Blessed One through the mediation of cowherd women and the like, because at that time, qualities such as "dearness" and so forth are indeed present in the Blessed One. Some say: "This [superimposition] is necessarily (*niyamena*) by way of its inevitable presence..."

"It has its root in the distinction between different ornaments; and in the example cited, because of the intention to restrict [the application] to childhood and so forth, there is a determination of difference from 'dearness' and the like"—this is exceedingly luminous.
Furthermore, even when that [ornament] exists, there is a perception of multiplicity due to the difference among the perceivers.

A particular state of mind (chittiviśeṣa) characterized by a distinct mental representation (ullekha) is the determinant of the poetic figure Ullekha. In the description of the land of Śrīkaṇṭha, there is a distinct domain for this figure, as seen in such hyperboles (atiśayokti) as:
"by the enemies [it is seen as] a cage of arrows," "by those seeking refuge [as] a gap in the sky," and "by the wayfarers [as] a tavern," and so forth. And here...

This is the application of the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor). In reality, however, they maintain that in instances such as "the opening of the sky," there is only *bhrāntimān* (the figure of mistaken cognition) and not *rūpaka*, because superimposition (*āropa*)—which must be preceded by the perception of a distinction between the two objects—is the very basis for the employment of *gauṇī* (secondary) and other types of *rūpaka*. As they say in the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā*: [text follows]

In his *Sābhāṣyavyākhyāna*, the venerable Ācārya Miśra Vācaspati states: "Furthermore, the word 'other' (para) functions by applying its primary meaning to something else; where there is a mutual agreement between the speaker and the listener, that is a secondary (gauṇa) usage, and it is preceded by a cognition of difference."

In this case, however, for the followers of Vātika, the attribution of the status of being the "abode of the sun" (ambaramaṇḍala) to the region of Śrīkaṇṭha is merely a product of delusion. And it is precisely because of this that sages refer to it as "the grove of asceticism" (tapovana),
while others call it "the abode of desire" (kāmāyatana).
Yoga.
The Tenth Chapter. And in the verse beginning with "by courtesans," there is the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).

“In depth you are the ocean; in majesty you are the mountain”—in such various descriptions, the distinction between the objects of depth and so forth is the determining factor. And here, there is the application of metaphor (*rūpaka*). “Venerable in speech, broad-chested, Arjuna in fame—”
"...and so forth. Thus, its object is distinct from that of *rūpaka* (metaphor), for here there is a connection with the expression of excellence (*atiśayokti*) through the remainder (*śeṣa*).
(683) Apahnuti (concealment) occurs when, having denied the subject at hand, something else is established.

This [superimposition] is of two kinds: in some cases it is a superimposition preceded by a negation (apahnava), and in others it is a negation preceded by a superimposition. The examples follow in order:
"The sky-dome is a mass of water..."
"These are not stars with the appearance of fresh foam;
this is not a coiled lord of serpents, O timid one;
and that is not a dark spot, but the reclining Murāri."
“This cool-rayed moon, possessing the luster of a mass of foam kissing the crest of the western mountain,
shines forth like the ignited lamp of Love for the night.”
"Bearing smoke under the guise of its manifest mark."
This verse is mine:
"Thus the body of the sky shines forth, containing the ocean and the stars; and therein are the ripples of foam."
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*,
it should be understood that in such cases there is a negation of the subject matter (*prakṛta-niṣedha*).
(684) Having somehow indicated some meaning that ought to be concealed...
If she should change [her mind] through a pun or otherwise, that too is Apahnuti (concealment).
She served her as follows:
"It is not possible to bathe at all if the clouds do not fall in due season;
you are longing for it, O timid one, but no, no, my friend, the path is slippery."

Regarding the phrase "without having fallen," it was stated there that this means "without [losing] her husband"; however, it has been interpreted otherwise as meaning "by way of the absence of a fall. For example, through the absence of hatred:
"With her body trembling before him..."
"What creeper is there that does not bloom with the arrival of the lord of the forest? Do you not remember, my friend, the festival of dalliance with your lover?
For the manner of the coming of the clouds has not been described [as something new]."
The distinction here is that in the former case there is a transformation of form (*paropheranyathākāra*), whereas in this case it is restricted to the *khora* (the vessel) alone;
furthermore, because that which is not to be concealed has been mentioned first by the concealer, there is no deception (*vyāja*).
(85) "Certainty" (*niścaya*), moreover, is the re-establishment of the subject matter after having negated something else.
This is the ornament known as *nicaya* (accumulation). "The other" (*anyat*) refers to that which is being superimposed. For example, from my own work:
"This is a face, not a lotus; these are eyes, not two blue water-lilies. O bee, do not wander in vain near the presence of this lovely-eyed one."
Or for example:
“The necklace upon her heart is a vine of poison, not the lord of serpents; the row of blue lotus petals around her neck is not the luster of a snake.”
Tenth Chapter: "This is sandalwood paste, not ashes; do not strike me, who am bereft of my beloved. O Anaṅga, why do you run about in anger, deluded by the thought that I am Hara?"

This is not a case of "confusion" (*miśra*), because doubt and certainty reside in a single locus; here, however, there is doubt on the part of the bee and certainty on the part of the hero. Furthermore, even for the bee, it is not a doubt, since such [doubt] occurs only when there is a cognition exceeding a single object.
Because it is impossible for her to have come here [to the hero]. Well then, let it be mere illusion. Granted that there may be an illusion regarding a bee and the like;

however, in this case, it is not that illusion which produces the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), but rather the union with such a heroine—this is what is perceived by those of sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*). Furthermore, even if [the literal meaning] were not intended...

Such a statement is indeed possible through the form of a heroine’s speech regarding the falling and so forth of bees and the like, even when they are [actually] errors. Nor is this a case of *rūpakadhvani* (suggestion of metaphor), because there is no apprehension of the face as a lotus.
Nor is it *apahnuti* (concealment), because there is no negation of the subject at hand. Thus, it is distinct [from these].
This is not a case of ornamentation (alaṅkāra), as it lacks the quality of poetic charm (vaicitrya).
For instance, when a person falls upon a conch shell perceiving it to be silver, the statement "this is not silver" made by someone else is merely a negation;
it is not an ornament because there is no strikingness of expression.
(686) There may be *sambhāvanotprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on possibility), wherein the subject at hand is [conceived] as having the nature of another;
it is considered to be first of two kinds: the expressed (*vācyā*) and the implied (*pratīyamānā*).
In verbal expression, it occurs when the word is employed; in non-verbal expression, however, it is the opposite.
Whether it be a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a substance (*dravya*), that which is to be imagined may belong to either of the two [the subject or the object].
Then each of those eightfold [powers] is further divided by the conceit of existence and non-existence,
and again by the nature of quality, action, and essence.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, they are said to become thirty-two types.
Among these, an example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the expressed meaning is given merely as a direction:
"The golden mountain shines like the victorious banner of another, its cloth-edge flickering like the eyes of a deer."

Here, there is a suggestion of a poetic figure (*vyatireka*) based on the multiplicity of the pillar of victory (*vijayastambha*). "In wisdom, silence; in forgiveness, patience; in renunciation, the reversal of greed—his virtues, because they are followed by further virtues, are as if they were siblings."
The quality of being accompanied by a productive result (*saprasavalam guṇaḥ*):
"O Gaṅgā, daughter of the Sun, your command is like a wind that is a sinner for causing the miscarriage of the fetus of the wives of your enemies."
"Movement" refers to action (*kriyā*).
For example: "The face shines like another full moon.
Here, the term *patracandra* ("leaf-moon") is a word denoting a single individual (*ekavyaktivācaka*). These are [examples of] states (*bhāva*).
And [it occurs] in conceit (*māna*). As in the case of conceit regarding non-existence (*abhāvābhimāna*):
"Alas, her two cheek-plates, having become such as they were, have reached a state of emaciation as if not seeing one another."

In the phrase *cāpasau* ("he went with his bow"), there is an absence of action (*kriyā*). The same applies to other cases. When the cause (*nimitta*) takes the form of a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*), as for example in "the waters of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāmbhasi*), the cause of the [implication of holiness] is the quality of being a sinner (*pātakitva*) in the case of the word *khātīvā*. And in "as if not seeing" (*apaśyantāvivā*), it is the action (*cāma-*).
The cause (*nimitta*) consisting of their arrival is the action (*kriyā*). Other cases are similar. An example of suggested metaphor (*pratīyamānōtprekṣā*) is as follows:
"By the slender-limbed maiden, her face was not revealed by her pair of breasts."
"Out of a sense of propriety, no place was given to this virtuous necklace."

The Tenth Chapter. Here, because there is an absence of a substance (dravya) [to serve as the basis for comparison], it is a suggested (*pratīyamāna*) poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), as in the phrase "as if she were ready. The same applies to other cases. Now, in the context of defining *dhvani*, [it was stated that] among all the poetic figures (*alaṅkāras*)...

It has been stated that [the suggested meaning] becomes manifest; now, however, how is it specifically said that the suggested sense (*pratīyamānatva*) belongs to the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)? It is replied: in the case of a suggested fancy, as in:
"O you whose heart is filled with thousands of women, do not, do not press me so hard."
Day by day, this misfortune makes my body, though already thin, even thinner.

In such cases, the sentence reaches its conclusion even without an explicit *utprekṣaṇa* (imaginative attribution); however, since shame is impossible for a "thief" in the form of a breast, the phrase "as if out of shame" (*lajjayeva*) functions solely through *utprekṣā*. Thus, there is a distinction between the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the perceived (*pratīyamāna*) *utprekṣā*. Here, regarding the *utprekṣā* of the wind, among its sixteen varieties:
He states the distinction: "In that regard, the further divisions of the denotable [meaning] are all threefold, excluding substance, consisting of the essential nature, the fruit, and the cause."

Among the varieties of expressed (*vācya*) and suggested (*pratīyamāna*) metaphors (*utprekṣā*) mentioned therein, regarding the sixteen varieties of the expressed metaphor, twelve of those belong to the three categories beginning with genus (*jāti*).

Each of these twelve is further divided into twelve types according to whether they reside in the nature (*svarūpa*), the result (*phala*), or the cause (*hetu*); thus, there are thirty-six varieties.
Since only the *svarūpotprekṣā* (conception of the essential nature) of a substance is possible, there are four [types];

thus, when combined, there are forty varieties. Here, an example of *svarūpotprekṣā* is as follows: in the previous examples, such as "the victory-pillar of the hero" (*vīrasya vijayastambha*) and "with offspring" (*sapravasā*) and so forth, these are [examples of] genus-based (*jāti-guṇa*)...
Metaphors (*parūpā*): An example of a metaphor regarding the fruit (*phalotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"O fortunate one, these breasts of yours, filled with the weight of women, grow day by day, though not joined with another, as if they were longing for the lap of a son. (Saṃgītaratnākara, Ṭīkā).
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"The longing for Rāma entered the heart of Rāvaṇa as well;
he descended to the earth to tell his beloved, as if [to inform] the serpents."
Here, the result of entering the earth, which is of the nature of an action, is poetically imagined as being "in order to tell [this].
An example of poetic fancy based on cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:
"While searching for you among the leaves of the horse-tail tree, I have indeed lost one anklet."
He was seen with his hands bound, as if out of the sorrow of separation from the lotus-feet of Lakṣmī.
In this case, suffering, which is by nature a defect, is poetically imagined as the cause. The same applies to other instances.
(688) Regarding the presence or absence of the stated cause, there are two ways [of classification].
Among those forty varieties, sixteen belong to the category of those residing in the essential nature (*svarūpagā*).
Those varieties [of the expressed *utprekṣā*] become thirty-two through the inclusion or non-inclusion of the cause (*nimitta*) of the *utprekṣā*;

thus, taken together, there are fifty-six varieties of the expressed *utprekṣā*. Among these, an example of the inclusion of the cause is found in the previously cited *utprekṣā*: "as if it were laughing" (*khādatīvety utprekṣāyām*).

The cause (*nimitta*) is sometimes not explicitly mentioned (*anupātta*). For example, in the expression "like another moon," such qualities as roundness and so forth are not mentioned. However, in the case of cause and effect, the cause must necessarily be mentioned. Thus, for instance, [in the verse]: "As if from a particular suffering..."

In this context, if the cause for being bound were not mentioned, and if the entry into the earth were not mentioned in the phrase "as if to manifest," the sentence would be incoherent. He now states the distinction among the sixteen varieties of that which is implied.
(88) And those [cases of] implied non-difference (*pratīyamānābheda*) reside individually in both the result and the cause.

For example, in the verse cited, "By the bud-like breast of the slender-limbed one," the cause—"as if by bashfulness"—is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*). In this case as well, the non-mention of the cause (*nimitta*) is not possible. [This is so] because of the word *iva*—
The Tenth Chapter.

Since the cause (*nimitta*) is not mentioned and the basis (*upādāna*) is not specified, it is impossible for the cognizer to determine the act of imagining; therefore, even "essential metaphorical fancy" (*svarūpotprekṣā*) does not occur here, because there is no identification with another attribute (*dharmyantara-tādātmya*).

In this *bandhanāyamaka*, when there is a connection with qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the initial application, an excellence (*atiśaya*) is admitted; for example: "This king is another Indra. And in the absence of qualifiers, it is a metaphor (*rūpaka*), as in: "The king is Indra. Thus it is.
The thirty-two types are *pratīyamāna-utprekṣā* (suggested poetic fancy).
(680) Depending on whether the subject at hand (*prastuta*) is explicitly stated or not, each of these is further divided into two kinds.
These are the *utprekṣās*. An example of the explicit statement (*ukti*) is: "The thigh of the gazelle-eyed woman... (*ūruḥ kuruṅgakadṛśaḥ*).
As was not stated by me in the *Prabhāvatī* regarding Prayūva: for here— “Now,
as the veil of darkness spreads across every quarter of the sky,
it is as if fashioned from heaps of collyrium, or filled with masses of musk.”
The world was as if spread over with *tāla* trees, or as if covered with dark blue garments.
Here, the pervasion of the object by the suggested element—namely, being fashioned by collyrium—is not present. Or, for example:
"Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium."
In this instance, the object of the metaphorical attribution (*vyāpana*)—namely, the act of smearing—is not explicitly mentioned.

The falling of collyrium and the descent of darkness are the two [objects] for which the cause of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is, respectively, the extreme blackness of the darkness and its contact with the surface below in the form of a stream. Some, however, [read] "alepana-... [and so forth].

"Even though darkness is the agent [of the action], it is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as the agent of the act of smearing; and the sky is likewise [imagined] as the agent of the act of raining," and so forth.
(681) Through this, its distinction from other figures of speech would be stated even more clearly.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, there is the figure of speech called *sāpaḍava-utprekṣā*. For example, from my own work:
"Under the guise of tears, the eyes of the fair-eyed woman were clouded by the smoke of a rising fire."
Without attaining honor, it dissolves within one's body like a flood of water of loveliness.
An example of a verse concerning the cause of destruction (*kṣeṣahetugā*) is as follows:
"The multitude of sages has emerged from the midst of the narrow escape [of danger] for that woman with lotus-like eyes."
"One should know that her quality of possessing a beautiful conch-like neck has attained excellence through its dwelling [upon it].
Here, in the phrase "through its dwelling upon the conch-like neck," there is a poetic conceit (*hetūtprekṣā*) based on the remainder (*śeṣa*).

This is the cause [of the doubt]. Here, the word "jāmīmahe" is expressive of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). Likewise, [words such as] "manye," "śaṅke," "dhruvam," "prāyaḥ," "nūnam," and so forth [function similarly].
Sometimes, there is poetic fancy arising from the introduction of a comparison (*upamā*), as for example:
On the far shore of the ocean,
Murāri [Viṣṇu] suddenly beheld rows of forests with dark foliage, appearing like a swarm of bees.
At every moment, they possess the attainment of the supreme white [purity].

Thus, because the word *ābhā* (appearance) expresses a comparison (*upamā*), there is a simile (*upamā*) at the outset; however, since in the conclusion it is impossible for moss to actually exist on the banks of the Jāhnavī, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) arises through the suggestion of possibility. The same applies to the verse concerning the pain of separation: "The bracelets were assumed by the limbs... and so forth.

And it should be understood from such examples as: “The curved side-glance of the deer-eyed one is like a blooming blue lotus. This is also to be known in the case of the *bhrāntimān* (error) ornament, as in: “The innocent girl [mistook] the milk...
Chapter Ten.

In [the verse beginning with] "dhiyā" and so forth, for those who are mistaken, such as Bāṇa and others, there is no cognition of the object—such as moonlight—because that [cognition] was produced solely by the poet; however, in this case [of *sambhāvanā*], there is the possibility of the agent's cognition of the object as well. This is the difference between the two. As for doubt (*sandeha*), however, it consists of equal [alternatives].
Likewise, there is the cognition of two alternatives (*koṭi*). However, here only one alternative is prominent and considered impossible.

In Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), the unreality of the object of cognition is perceived because its conclusion is reached [only] after it has been cognized; whereas here, it is perceived at the very moment of cognition—this is the distinction.
In the verse, "Has the earth been woven with various trees? Has the sky been bent down? Has it been covered?

Has the uneven ground been filled? Or have the quarters of the horizon been compressed by the darkness?"—here, the speaker suggests that the state of being overwhelmed by darkness is expressed through the form of a poetic arrangement (*racanā*) and so forth.

Some say that *cata* is "the ornament of doubt" (*sandehālaṅkāra*). That is not correct; for doubt consists precisely in the flashing forth of multiple alternatives (*anekakoṭi*) with equal force regarding a single object.
Here, however, there is a difference in the correlates (*pratisambandhin*) due to the pervasion (*vyāpti*), because [the action] such as pervading is concealed (*nigaraṇa*)—and so forth.

And there is the throbbing of the beginning [of the sentence]. Others, however, said: "This variety of doubt is distinct, even though it possesses a single dominant aspect through the persistence of the form of the non-concealed.
This is incorrect; for the perception of identity with another is indeed possible only for that whose own nature has been swallowed up.
The word *vanā* (forest); because of its clear manifestation through the suffix *-tathā* expressing actual existence (*sadbhāva*), and because it suggests that [existence] like the word *deva*,
this ought to be considered a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), according to the method of the type of doubt not previously observed.
When the world perceives this [mark] as a rabbit, sporting in the assembly of moonbeams, that is not how it appears to me; rather,
I consider it a great drop [of tear] from the ocean of the sky, overcome by the separation from its beloved.

In the verse from the *Sahityadarpaṇa*, "kaṭākṣaikapaṅktipātitacakrikṛṣṇakaṣāyitatanum," although the word *manye* (I think) is employed, the *sambhāvanā* (poetic fancy) of the *utprekṣā* (poetic conceit) is not perceived.
This is not mere conjecture (utprekṣā), which consists of mere deliberation (vitarka). When there is a firm conviction regarding something established as a fact, it is called hyperbole (atiśayokti).

Adhyavasāya is the identification of the subject with the object through the swallowing up (nigaraṇa) of the latter; it is the cognition of the subject as being non-different from the object. Of that...

In poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), the object of comparison (*viṣayin*) is indicated as being uncertain, and thus it possesses the status of a probandum (*sādhyatva*). Here, however, it is perceived precisely as something certain, and thus it possesses the status of a proven fact (*siddhatva*). Furthermore, while in poetic fancy there is a swallowing up of the object (*viṣaya-nigaraṇa*) by the mere subordination of the object, here too—as in "the face is a second moon"—this occurs.
As it is said: "Whether the object is not grasped or is grasped,
its state of being swallowed proceeds merely by the act of subduing."
Even where there is difference, there is non-difference; where there is connection, there is non-connection, and their reversals;
and the reversal of the sequence between cause and effect—therefore, that [incompatibility] is fivefold.

The opposite of that [is]: difference where there is non-difference; connection where there is no connection; and excellence where there is none. Here, an example of non-difference where there is difference is from my own work:
"How is it that above the peacock..."
Upon her forehead shines a crescent moon like that of the eighth day;
from that [forehead] a pair of blue lotuses, below them a tilaka flower, and beneath that a sprout.
In this case, there is an identification (*adhyavasāya*) of the beloved’s tresses and the like with a slow-moving mass of hair and so forth through non-difference (*abheda*).

Or, for example: "As if bound by the pain of separation... Here, although there is a difference between the silence belonging to a sentient being and that belonging to a non-sentient object, they are treated as non-different. Thus...
The Tenth Chapter:
"The beloved, possessing passion for the neck, [sees] the illusion of the lower lip."
In the case of one who lacks a substratum, *rāga* means redness; however, there is no difference between *rāga* (passion) and *prema* (love).
An example of non-difference as difference is as follows:
"The beauty of her limbs is one thing, and the abundance of her fragrance is another."
The extraordinary freshness of that lotus-petal-eyed woman [is such that] there is a non-connection in the context of a connection, as in:
"Was the Creator of her creation the Moon, the bestower of luster?"
Is he perhaps Madana himself, whose sole essence is the lover; or is he the month that brings forth flowers?
How else could the ancient Sage, who was a person devoted to the study of the Vedas, have been capable of creating this enchanting form, devoid of any longing for the objects of the senses?
In the case of a relationship with the terrifying ancient Prajāpatis, there is a non-relationship. As for a relationship within a relationship, it is as follows:
"In the circle of the sky, the pair of lotus-eyes of the Moon..."
then her beautiful-eyed face is compared to it."

In this context, if there is a connection with what is implied by the force of the meaning (*arthabala*), and if there is a reversal of the sequence between cause and effect, it occurs in two ways: when the effect exists prior to the cause, and when both exist simultaneously. In order, as follows:
“Much more so was the mind of the women from Harivarṣa agitated with longing,
as they beheld the beauty of the faces of the lotuses, which surpassed that of the blooming vakula and mukula flowers.”
Simultaneously, he who moved with the gait of an elephant ascended both the ancestral lion-throne and the circle of the lords of the earth.
Some say: "In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, it is stated that worldly excellence (*laukikātiśaya*) is superimposed upon the mass of hair and so forth by means of its [poetic] quality (*kalā*),
when the mass of hair and other such things are superimposed upon [objects like] a *kalāpa* (a bundle of feathers)."

In the passage, "It is not even mentioned, let alone in the case of the deer-eyed women," the beauty of the *vakula* trees and others, though perceived first, is subsequently determined as being mixed with [the beauty of] the five limbs; for this very reason, there is also a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) here due to the use of the word "fluidity" (*drava*). The same applies elsewhere.
When there is a connection with a single attribute among the objects under discussion or other objects, that is then *tulyayogitā* (parallel coordination).

The *dharma*—consisting of qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*)—of other things that are not the subject at hand [is another type of simile]. An example: “By that season, ointments, flowers, women who had become angry with their husbands, and the wicks of lamps awakened the god of love, who had long been asleep, as he was being roused.”

In this instance, since the increase of darkness is the subject at hand, there is a connection through a single act of cognition with the subjects under discussion— namely, the throwing of the curtain and so forth:
"Whose thought does not arise in one who beholds the beauty of your limbs?"

In the verse, "The hardness of the *mālatī*, the *śaśalekhā*, and the plantain trees," there is a connection through the single quality of hardness among the irrelevant subjects, such as the *mālatī* and the others. Likewise:
“Generosity [is extracted] from wealth, speech from vanity, fame from pride, and likewise longevity from [worldly] life;
one should extract the essence from the insubstantial through service to others.
Here, there is a single-pointed connection with the quality of being the essence for generosity and the other factors, which serve as the substrata.
The connection with the act of taking away [is established].
(686) But the *dīpaka* (illuminator) is said to occur when there is a relation between the irrelevant and the relevant;
furthermore, it occurs when a single grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is connected with multiple actions.
The examples follow in order. Chapter Ten:
"Out of the arrogance of his power, even now as before..."
By that seeker of victory, the world is oppressed;
for a virtuous woman and innate nature follow after a man even through successive existences.”
Here, there is a connection through the single action of following, established between the contextual subject, Nīcalā, and the non-contextual subject, Satī. [As it is said:
"O Lord of my life, when you had come from afar..."
Pierced by the arrow of the mind-born god, that poor woman— whether rising,
sleeping, coming to your bedchamber, departing, or looking about— is tormented by anxiety.

"This is mine. Here, a single heroine is connected with multiple actions arising from her. Furthermore, the threefold division [of these actions] based on their presence at the beginning, middle, and end has not been illustrated here;
for such variety occurs in a thousand ways everywhere.
For example: (687) That is *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism), where there are two statements whose similarity is to be understood,
and wherein even a single common attribute is expressed separately [in each].
“Blessed are you, O Princess of Vidarbha, by whose noble virtues even the King of Niṣadha was drawn away!
What praise indeed can there be for moonlight beyond this?”
It even makes the blind see clearly.”
In the *Bāhyārthadarpaṇa*,

the acts of attracting (*samākarṣaṇa*) and making superior (*uttaralīkaraṇa*) are each defined by distinct expressive terms in order to avoid redundancy. This [type of figure] is also seen in the *Mālatīmādhava*.
As it is said: "The sun shines forth only when stainless,
and the mirror reflects clearly only when polished."
Śivagiri, the brother of Śivahāla,
is indeed naturally beautiful, O Baccana.
In this instance, Vimalavādin and the others are in fact one and the same in meaning. By way of contrast (vaidharmyeṇa), for example:
“Only the cakorī birds are clever in the act of drinking moonlight;
no other beautiful-eyed woman is as skillful as the lady of Avanti.”

(698) An *udāharaṇa* (illustration), however, is the reflection of an object possessing common properties (*sadharmavat*). The exclusion of the *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence) is indicated by the phrase "not [an object] possessing common properties" (*avadharmavat*). This [type of simile] is also of two kinds, based on the presence of commonality (*sādharmya*) or difference (*vaidharmya*). The examples follow in order:
Even if its virtues are unknown, the speech of a true poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears;
for even when its fragrance has not yet been perceived, [the lotus-stalk]...
A garland of jasmine removes both [suffering and] impurity.”
"When you are seen, the deer-eyed woman's torment of love subsides;
when the moon rises, the exhaustion of the day-lotus fades."
"O Spring, how could our minds not be bound with affection for other beloved women?
Does a bee, greedy for the honey of blossoming flowers, ever long for another lotus?"
The Tenth Chapter. This is my section. Here, because the phrases "magaḥ kuto na" and "kāṅkṣati vaśimanyām" terminate in an identical form, there is indeed a *pratibala-upamā* (counter-comparison).
In the case of *tukarṣa* (conjunction), there is only similarity between the pouring of streams of honey and the drawing away of the eyes, not identity.

Furthermore, the distinction is that *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) occurs when there is a relationship of general and particular between the statement of the capable and the statement of the capable agent,
whereas such is not the case for *prativastūpamā* (counter-simile) and *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration).
Whether the connection between things is possible or impossible in some respect,
that which makes known the state of being an original image and its reflection is *nidarśanā*.
Here is an example of *nidarśanā* based on the connection between a possible object and a thing:
"Who here, tormenting people pointlessly for a long time in this subterranean realm, attains prosperity?"
Then, by day, the sun reached the supreme mountain, Veśyāntra, through his own power.
The sun’s connection as the agent (*kartṛ*) in the act of making known such a desired object is indeed possible,
because it possesses the quality of reaching the final mountain [the setting mountain] which is capable of making known such a desired object;
and that [quality] consists in the sun’s arrival at the western mountain being a calamity that scorches others, [establishing] a relationship between the original and its reflection.

It brings about understanding. *Nidarśanā* (illustrative simile), which consists in the representation of a relationship between two things that cannot possibly exist, is of two kinds: occurring within a single sentence or occurring across multiple sentences. Among these, an example of that occurring in a single sentence is as follows:
"The curved casting of her sidelong glances, adorned with a garland of blue lotuses, imparts a dark hue."
Her lower lip possesses the grace of a young sprout, and her face is the splendor of the moon, the treasury of arts.

Furthermore, how could one thing belong to another? Thus, the attribution of glances, cosmetics, and so forth to blue lotuses and the like, or of trembling and so forth to faces and the like, is impossible;
this is explained in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* as "superimposition" (*tadrūpakatā*).

Indeed, a smile, a stumble, and so forth, like the casting of a side-glance or the *kuvalayamālā* flower, makes known the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). Or, for example:
"O Indra among kings, when you are enraged, the tears of the deer-eyed women of your enemies [are released]."
With a gait like that of a royal swan, he was resplendent with a face possessing the luster of the moon.

In this instance, since the movement of a royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*) is impossible for two feet that are not connected [to such a bird], their connection to it is asserted; and that [assertion] conveys a movement that is impossible, like the movement of a royal swan. An example occurring across multiple sentences is as follows:
“Whoever indeed desires to accomplish with this naturally beautiful body, which is capable of enduring ascetic toil, [the goal of liberation],
surely he would seek to pierce a mountain peak with the edge of a blue lotus petal.”
The Sage intends to cut through the bondage of birth.”

In this case, since the syntactic connection between the two sentence-meanings indicated by the words *yat* and *sat* cannot be established through identity, the desire to accomplish the austerity of such a form— being like the desire to cut a lotus stalk with the blade of a blue lotus petal— results in a relationship of reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*). Or, for example:
“This birth has been brought to bondage by the addiction to worldly enjoyments;
alas, for what price have I sold the wish-fulfilling gem!”

In this case, the ultimate conclusion is that by greed for a mere portion of existence, one brings one's entire birth to futility, like selling a wish-fulfilling gem for the price of a single cowrie. Likewise:
"Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?"
"Out of delusion, I desire to cross the difficult-to-traverse ocean by means of a mere raft."

The conclusion is that, by my own estimation, crossing the ocean with a small boat is like [crossing it] during the reign of the Solar dynasty. This twofold [type of comparison] occurs in some cases even when what pertains to the object of comparison (the *upameya*) is impossible in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
For example:
The Tenth Chapter:
“The sweetness experienced by that connoisseur of flavors upon the lower lip of this fawn-eyed woman was tasted [by him] in the juice of the grape.”

Here, since the quality of sweetness belonging to the subject under discussion—the lower lip—is impossible in a grape, as in the previous example, the figure culminates in a comparison (*sāmya*). An example of the *mālā* (garland) form is as follows, by me:
"You cast the parrot into the jaws of the cat..."
You offer a deer to the mouth of a predator;
you bestow a horse while fixing your mind upon the expanse of a buffalo's horn.
The completion of the sentence-meaning occurs without the implication of the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*);
however, once the sentence-meaning has been completed, the cognition of that *bimba-pratibimba* relationship arises through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*).
This is not [an instance of] presumption (*arthāpatti*), for in that case—[as in the verse]: "This necklace of the deer-eyed women..."—the sentence-meaning is already fully established.
Because there is no absence of a conclusion [in such cases], there is no fault.

"The excellence of the object of comparison (upameya) over the standard of comparison (upamāna), or its inferiority, is called Vyatireka (Distinction). It is said to be threefold: when the cause is stated, or when it is not stated."

Since each of the four types [of *śleṣa*]—verbal, objective, both, and *sāmya*-based—is twelvefold, there are thirty-six varieties; when combined with *sāmya*, they become forty-eightfold. Furthermore, when these are taken together, they constitute forty-eight divisions.

The cause for the superiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) consists of the cause of excellence residing in the *upameya* and the cause of inferiority residing in the *upamāna*. When both of these are expressed, there are three varieties—either individually or by their combination; thus, in all four types of this [figure], the superiority of the *upameya* over the *upamāna* [is established].

The presentation of the exclusion of the denotatum (*vācyārtha*) is twelvefold—namely, by means of the word (*śabda*), by means of the meaning (*artha*), and in its entirety (*aśeṣa*). Even when there is a discrepancy (*bheda*) regarding the word or the meaning, it becomes twenty-fourfold. This also applies to cases where the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is deficient.
And by way of [the distinction between] the *bhaṅgī* (the broken form), there are twenty-four types; thus, taken together, the *ghaṭitaka* (the connected form) consists of forty types. An example:
"The face is not like the moon, nor is the moon like the face."

The two reasons—the absence of blemish (*akalaṅkatva*) residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the possession of a spot (*sakalaṅkatva*) residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—have also been stated. For example, as in the case of verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*), which is produced by words. In this very context, regarding the reading "not at all like the moon" (*na kalayāpi vidhūpamam*), the meaning is "it conquers the moon [despite its] having a spot" (*jayatīnduṃ sakalanimiti*).

In the recension [of the verse], because of the absence of words such as *vivādita* and so forth, it is implied. Here, by the omission of the word *akalaṅka*, there is the non-perception of the cause of the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*). By the omission of the word *kañcid dhi*, there is the non-perception of the cause of the inferiority residing in the object of comparison (*upamāna*). When both are omitted, there is the non-perception of both. In the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia)...

"And those whose faces are not agitated by the force of passion due to their exceedingly deep devotion to virtue"—here, because the suffix *vati* is used in this sense, there is a verbal comparison (*śābdamaupamyam*). There is a statement of both causes for excellence and deficiency;
the word *guṇa* is used in its primary sense (*mukhya*). The other varieties are to be understood as before. These...

Examples of the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*apamāna*); a mere illustration of its inferiority follows: for instance, "Though thin, he is like a mass of collyrium..."
"He increases ever more and more constantly;
cease, be gracious, O beautiful one,
for the journey that has begun is irreversible."
The statement that there is no possible object for comparison (*anopameyabhūta*) is due to the superiority of generosity; therefore, it is said here:

"When the object of comparison (*upameya*) is superior to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or in the reverse case, it is *vyatireka* (distinction)," according to the definition of some. In the [verse] beginning with "viparyaye... [it is stated]: "In the reverse case... [and so on].
As for the claim made by some that the word *yathā* is redundant, that is not tenable under scrutiny.
For in this context, it is precisely the non-existence (*asattva*) of the moon relative to the face that is intended to be expressed.
And the non-existence of the youthfulness relative to the moon is indeed quite evident. Or rather, let it be as stated in the *Udāharaṇa*:
The *Kabacchiti* [verse]:
"O slayer of Madhu, by me, through the power of my penance, the path of the messengers has again been measured out with arrows."

"What is the resolution for such cases? [The author replies: "It is either a deficiency or a 'suggestion' (*dhvani*). (701) When, by the force of the meaning, a single word should be expressive of two things, that expression is called *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) when it serves as its foundational basis.

In this [figure], *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based on the relation between effect and cause consists of two types: that rooted in the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) [of two things] and that consisting of the reversal of the object (*arthaviparyaya*). Even that which is rooted in identification is further divided into two: that based on *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and otherwise.
And: the examples in order are as follows:
"In her youth, her great lower lip possesses a royal redness.
Here, there is a *śeṣa* (elliptical) [use] of the word *rāga* (redness/passion).
“Together with the clusters of night-lotuses, they cause desire to dwell;
together with the masses of thick darkness, they drive away weariness;
and together with the rows of day-lotuses, they fill their hearts with longing.”
"The rays of the moon, the son of Aṃśumat, move toward every direction.
This is my [verse]. The distinction between the *ojas* and other [guṇas] arises solely from the difference in their respective relations, and not from their inherent nature.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"Just as the flame of a slender lamp perishes along with a drop of oil, so did she, her consciousness stolen by the intense shock of grief, vanish from the king's sight."
The compound *bañca* (the *śākapārthivādi* class) is also possible; for example, as illustrated in “*saha kumudana-damair-*” and so forth,
and in “*sa caṇena samaṃ rāmaḥ kānanaṃ gahanaṃ yayau*” and so forth.
This is not an ornament [of poetry], because it lacks the foundation of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
(702) *Vinokti* [is defined as]: "If, without another thing, one thing is neither good nor bad"—where "not bad" means it does not become unattractive. And thus, although it is beautiful...

Although this is the ultimate conclusion, the intention behind the statement regarding "beauty" by way of the absence of "ugliness" is as follows: the ugliness of something that is inherently beautiful is a defect caused solely by its proximity to another object;
its own nature, however, remains beautiful. For example:
"Alas! Without the rainy season, the moon has become despicable;
without the sun, the forest grove has become beautiful."
This is inauspicious. For example:
"O lady, you have done well by leading away my beloved;
for what day is there without the sun, and what night without the moon?"
“My birth has passed in vain,
for I have not seen the orb of the cool-rayed moon; even the very arising of the moon is as if fruitless.”
"By whom has the lotus pond not been seen while it is awake?
Here, there is an extraordinary degree of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) through the device of mutual *vinokti* (the figure of "without"). This concludes the tenth chapter on the word *vinā*.

Even in the absence of the actual use of the word *saha*, this [expression] occurs through the intention (*vivakṣā*) to convey the sense of "together. In the same way, it should be understood that even in the absence of the use of the word *saha*, the term *mahā-* also occurs through the intention to convey the sense of "together.
(703) *Samāsokti* (Concise Expression) occurs where, by means of similar effects, marks, or adjectives, [the intended object is suggested].
The superimposition of another object upon the subject at hand is *vyavacārasamāropa*.
Here, there is the superimposition of the behavior of the unmentioned upon the mentioned through a common action. For example:
"Upon the face of her whose eyes are like lotuses, and upon her two breasts which possess the grace of golden jars, [the mark of the hunter’s arrow has appeared]."
O Malaya breeze, you alone are blessed, for you forcibly embrace every limb of hers.
In this instance, there is the superimposition of the behavior of a forceful lover upon the wind (*gandhavāha*). An example based on similarity of gender (*liṅgasāmya*) is as follows:
"What anxiety for women can there be for a high-minded man who has not yet completed his desire for conquest?"
Having traversed the world-circle, the sun now resorts to the twilight.

In this instance, the treatment of the sun and the twilight as a hero and a heroine is based solely on their masculine and feminine genders. As for the similarity of attributes (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*), it is of three kinds: through wordplay (*śliṣṭatayā*), through commonality (*sādhāraṇyena*), and as containing a simile (*aupamyagarbhatvena*).
Among these, an example of wordplay is as follows, by me:
O Lord of the Eastern Mountain, with face blossomed by attachment to passion, you see before you the eastern quarter— its veil of darkness falling away as it is touched by the rays of the sun—
while you yourself possess a complexion pale as the *varaṭha* fruit of the *lavalī* tree, your inner being turbid.
Alas! The melting of the frost now resorts to the green southern quarter.

In this [verse], there is the punning (*śliṣṭatā*) of words such as *mukhara*, *gādi*, and so forth. For here, in the reading "timirāvāhila-darpaṇe iti," and in the reading "timirāṃḍuka iti," there is a partial similarity of form (*ekadeśasārūpya*).

This is indeed a *samāloki* (unified identification), and not a *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (partial metaphorical identification). For in that case, the relationship between the object of comparison (*rūpya*) and the subject of comparison (*rūpaka*)—namely, darkness and a garment—is clearly established by their common quality as concealers; thus, even without depending on mutual proximity, it rests upon its own inherent nature and does not give rise to the cognition of *samāloki*.

[This is] for the purpose of removing [that objection]. However, where the similarity between the *rūpaka* (the object of superimposition) and the *rūpya* (the subject of superimposition) is indistinct, there that [superimposition] would be inconsistent without the description of another part; thus, even in a verbal *sāhitya* (unification), it necessarily requires the description of another part as an implied (*ārtha*) element. In that case, it is precisely "metaphor existing in one part" (*ekadeśavivartirūpaka*), as follows:
"Where the king’s harem acts as the moon’s orb, even the army of enemies turns its back, though it be an ocean of passion.
Here, the similarity between the harem (*antaḥpura*) and the orb (*maṇḍala*) is indeed indistinct. And in some cases where it is distinct—

Even when there is a verbal representation (*rūpaṇa*) of many similar things, if it pertains to only one part [of the object], that is precisely *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (metaphor residing in a single part). This is because the cognition of *samāsokti* (speech of brevity) would be obstructed by the cognition of *rūpaka*. Now, [one might argue] that there is indeed a similarity between the battlefield and the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*) in terms of being places where one can move about with ease.

If it is argued that the similarity is manifest (*sphuṭa*), that is true; however, it exists only insofar as it depends upon a full consideration of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), and certainly not independently. This is because, for instance, in the case of "the face-moon" (*mukha-candra*) and so forth, there is no inherent quality of being a pleasant place for wandering within the harem [of the face] or the like. An example of [similarity] through commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) is as follows:
"The lotus-born [Sarasvatī] was born from Mount Meru when the Lord of the Day had risen—she who is graced by the song of the swans at the end of their enjoyment of natural fragrance.
Regarding the word *jassa*: "In whose inner palace, the state of being the abode of the circle of kings was in his hand..."
"Even when facing him with passion, the army of enemies suddenly turns its back," according to the Saṃskṛta-ṭīkā.

[The sword-blade] is like a creeper belonging to the circle of the earth; "facing with passion" means being turned toward him by means of *rasa*—that is, by the flow of one's own essence and by the desire for sexual union (*surata*).

The Tenth Chapter. Here, due to the similarity of the qualifiers beginning with "by nature" (*nisarga*), the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the quality of being fond of pleasure (*soratva*), which pertains to women in general, upon the lotus-pond— which is perceived as a female boatman— is the cause.

For it is impossible for the designation "heroine" to be understood through the mere similarity of attributes alone without that [qualification]. Furthermore, the state of containing a comparison (*aupamyagarbhatva*) occurs in three ways: by virtue of containing a simile (*upamā*), a metaphor (*rūpaka*), or a combination (*saṃkara*). Among these, an example of its containing a simile is as follows:

"In the verse: *'dantaprabhā puṣpacitā pāṇipaṇavaśobhinī | keśapāśālivṛndena suveśā hariṣecanā* ||', because of the [intended] quality of being well-attired (*suveśatva*), there is first the suggestion of a simile (*upamā*) within the phrase 'the radiance of her teeth is like flowers'."

The compound [is formed] by means of *tva*. Immediately thereafter, by resorting to other compounds such as "with flowers shining like the luster of teeth" (*dantaprabhāsadbhaiḥ puṣpaiḥ*), there arises from the sentence containing these common qualifiers the cognition of the treatment of the fawn-eyed woman as a creeper (*latā*). An example of that which contains a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is as follows:

“Full of salt and honey,” and so forth. An example of *sahokti* (conjoint expression) is found in “The radiance of her teeth is the flower,” and so on. In the reading “well-dressed” (*suveśa*) and “surrounded” (*parīta*), because there is an absence of any means to establish either a simile (*upamā*) or a metaphor (*rūpaka*), recourse is taken to *sahokti*. This is another type of compound.

As before, there is the cognition of a creeper through another type of compound. Among these, according to the view of those for whom there is no "partial metaphorical representation" (*ekadeśavivartin*) in either the simile (*upamā*) or the compound, the two types—*āropitā* (superimposed) and *samāsokti* (compound-utterance)—are [the categories]. However, the second variety pertains exclusively to the domain of partial metaphorical representation (*ekadeśavivarttirūpaka*).

Upon close examination, however, in the first type [of this figure], it is more appropriate to accept it as merely a *vyatireka* (dissimile) based on a partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*). Otherwise, [one would have to interpret] the verse:
"Autumn, bearing upon her breast a pale rainbow that shimmers with the luster of a pearl necklace... [as a simile].
"Delighting the entire half-moon [of her face], she made the heat of the sun even more intense.
In this verse, how is there the perception of the conduct of a heroine (*nāyikā*) in autumn? [This is explained] in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* as "the heroine's... [and so forth].

This is because it is impossible for Indra to possess a bow with the luster of a fresh nail-mark. Furthermore, in the phrase "having the luster of a fresh nail-mark," although the status of being the object of comparison (*upamānatva*) resides in the *citam* (the mark), through an examination of the actual state of things, it must be transferred to the rainbow of Indra. This is just as in the case of "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where the [instrumental] status of the *dadhi* is [transferred].

If it is argued that the rule [of the suffix] is transferred by way of being established otherwise (anyathāsiddha), such that there will be the cognition "bearing a face resembling Indra’s bow," [we reply:
even if such a resolution were possible, the assumption of a forced construction is more cumbersome than simply accepting a partial metaphor (ekadeśavivartinī upamā). Let it be so.

Or rather, in such cases as "eyes like blue lotuses" or "lotuses [like] eyes," there may be some kind of *samāsokti* (synecdoche/metaphorical identification) because no other alternative is possible. Furthermore, since there is no cognition of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) in a mere simile (*upamā*), how could *samāsokti*, which depends upon that [simile], find a place here? As it has been said:
"If, in a comparison, neither conventional usage nor reality is perceived,
then that comparison is clearly a *samāsokti* (synecdoche) or a *ekadeśopamā* (partial simile).
Thus, when it is accepted that both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) are instances of partial manifestation (*ekadeśavivartin*), there arises a blending (*saṅkara*) based on that foundation.

Even so, the inclusion [of this] within *samāsokti* is indeed established by logic; therefore, its scope does not extend to that which is brought forth by an adjective containing a simile (*upamā*). When there is equality of adjectives, it is of two kinds: that which is brought forth by a specific [adjective] and that which is brought forth by a common [adjective]. Regarding the effect (*kārya*)— [The text continues: ...the effect is of three kinds: that which is brought forth by the cause (*kāraṇa*), that which is brought forth by the object of comparison (*upameya*), and that which is brought forth by the subject of comparison (*upamāna*). Among these, that which is brought forth by the cause is of two kinds: that which is brought forth by a specific cause and that which is brought forth by a common cause. An example of the first: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king [Himālaya], has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses. Here, the blossoming of the night-lotuses is the effect, and the moon’s becoming the crest-jewel of the mountain-king is the specific cause. An example of the second: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses. Here, the blossoming of the day-lotuses is the effect, and the moon’s becoming the crest-jewel of the mountain-king is the common cause. An example of that which is brought forth by the object of comparison: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses. Here, the blossoming of the night-lotuses is the effect, and the moon’s becoming the crest-jewel of the mountain-king is the object of comparison. An example of that which is brought forth by the subject of comparison: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses. Here, the blossoming of the day-lotuses is the effect, and the moon’s becoming the crest-jewel of the mountain-king is the subject of comparison. Thus, *samāsokti* is of six kinds. It is said: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses. This is the sixfold *samāsokti*. Furthermore, the following is said: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses. This is the sixfold *samāsokti*. Moreover, the following is said: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses. This is the sixfold *samāsokti*. Furthermore, the following is said: "The moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the night-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the mountain-king, has become the sole cause for the blossoming of the day-lotuses; the moon, having become the crest-jewel of the
Furthermore, when there is a state of satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*), there is a fourfold *samāsokti* (metaphorical identification) of two kinds.

In all these cases here, the cause is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of worldly usage. And that [superimposition] is, in some instances, the superimposition of worldly usage upon a worldly object, and [in others], the superimposition of technical (*śāstrīya*) usage upon a technical object.

The superimposition of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-samāropa*) is fourfold: either the superimposition of the linguistic usage of scriptural objects upon worldly objects, or the superimposition of the linguistic usage of worldly objects upon scriptural objects.
Among these, even worldly objects are of many kinds due to the distinctions of *rasa* (flavor) and so forth; and scriptural objects likewise [are manifold].
The tenth chapter: A summary of the various types [of *arthāpatti*] as they are well-known in logic (*tarka*), Ayurveda, the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), and so forth.
A mere illustration is as follows: "By those who, having shaken off... and so on. *Khai ki ke*.
There is the superimposition upon the object of worldly, forceful desire, and conventional practice, such as:
"By those who perceive you as uniform in all states of being, as immutable, and as proceeding through non-existence..."
"It is said that elision was performed because of its position as a subsequent element;
I certainly believe that the definition of a *bha*-stem was applied to you."

In this case, there is a superimposition of the linguistic usage of a thing well-known from grammar upon a thing well-known from the scriptures and treatises. It is the same elsewhere. In a metaphor (*rūpaka*), the form of the subject is concealed by the imposition of the essential nature and configuration of the non-subject. But here, by the superimposition of its own state, [the non-subject] does not [conceal it].
It distinguishes that [object] from its state as the sun (pūṣan) precisely by its concealed true nature. For this very reason, they say here:

"This is a superimposition for the sake of conventional usage, but not a superimposition of the true nature. In the case of the suggested simile (upamā-dhvani) and the rest, there is similarity even of the substantive (viśeṣya), but here it is only of the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).

In *prastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), the subject at hand is what is to be understood; here, however, it is the non-subject—this is the distinction. (704) *Parikara* (the circumstantial elaboration) is considered to consist of significant epithets used in a specific statement. For example: "O King of Aṅga, O General, O Droṇa, O Karṇa, protect this Bhīma!"... [text fragment] ...protect him! Do not let him be slain by Arjuna. Here, the epithets such as "King of Aṅga" and so forth are significant because they serve to suggest that the speaker is himself a king, a general, and so on. Thus, the meaning is completed through the power of suggestion (*dhvani*). This is *parikara*. Furthermore, when the suggested sense is not intended to be prominent, it is merely a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), whereas when it is intended to be prominent, it is *dhvani*. This is the difference between the two. Now, regarding *samāsokti* (speech of brevity): (705) *Samāsokti* occurs when the description of one thing suggests another, through the commonality of attributes. For example: "The sun has set, the day has departed, and the lotus has closed its eyes; alas, even the bee is departing from the lotus, having abandoned its beloved. Here, the description of the sun and other objects suggests the departure of a lover who has been rejected by his beloved. This is *samāsokti*. Furthermore, when the suggested sense is not intended to be prominent, it is merely a figure of speech, whereas when it is intended to be prominent, it is *dhvani*. This is the difference between the two. Now, regarding *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description): (706) *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* occurs when the non-subject is described for the sake of the subject. For example: "The moon rises, the night has arrived, and the lotuses have opened their eyes; alas, the bee is entering the lotus, having abandoned the lily. Here, the description of the moon and other objects suggests the arrival of a lover who has come to meet his beloved. This is *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.
