Furthermore, when the suggested sense is not intended to be prominent, it is merely a figure of speech, whereas when it is intended to be prominent, it is *dhvani*. This is the difference between the two. Now, regarding *ākṣepa* (paralipsis): (707) *Ākṣepa* occurs when a statement is made with a view toward its own negation. For example: "O friend, do not speak thus; this is not the time for you to speak. Here, the statement "do not speak" is made with a view toward its own negation, namely, "speak. This is *ākṣepa*. Furthermore, when the suggested sense is not intended to be prominent, it is merely a figure of speech, whereas when it is intended to be prominent, it is *dhvani*. This is the difference between the two. Now, regarding *vyājastuti* (disguised praise): (708) *Vyājastuti* occurs when there is praise through a pretext of censure, or censure through a pretext of praise. For example: "O King, your fame has reached the heavens; alas, it has caused the moon to fall from the sky. Here, the praise of the king's fame is expressed through the pretext of censuring the moon. This is *vyājastuti*. Furthermore, when the suggested sense is not intended to be prominent, it is merely a figure of speech, whereas when it is intended to be prominent, it is *dhvani*. This is the difference between the two. Now, regarding *vyatireka* (distinction): (709) *Vyatireka* occurs when the excellence of the subject is shown through its contrast with the non-subject. For example: "The face is like the moon; yet the moon is eclipsed by the darkness of Rāhu, while the face is not. Here, the excellence of the face is shown through its contrast with the moon. This is *vyatireka*. Furthermore, when the suggested sense is not intended to be prominent, it is merely a figure of speech, whereas when it is intended to be prominent, it is *dhvani*. This is the difference between the two. Now, regarding *
“Do not [speak] difficult-to-govern words.
(705) A word is single-meaning by its own nature; the remainder are those expressing multiple meanings.
The phrase “by its own nature as single-meaning” serves to exclude *śabdaśleṣa* (phonetic punning). “[Expressing] multiple meanings.”
And [this applies] to sound (*dhvani*). An example:
"The combination of words with suffixes and compounds are the modes (*vṛtti*); such is their definition. The meaning of the commentary (*ṭīkā*) is: "In the connections between word-meanings."
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"Setting in motion auspicious activities, stealing the greenness of the quarters,
and swiftly consuming the surface of the earth, the radiant sun shines forth."
In this case, because there is no restriction by context or other such factors, both are intended as *rājasūya* sacrifices.
(70h) Sometimes a particular [is inferred] from a general, or a general from a particular;
a cause from an effect, or an effect from a cause; and likewise, the equal from the equal.

If the subject at hand is understood from that which is not the subject at hand, then there is *prastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Subject), which is fivefold; here follow the examples in their respective order.

"When a man, having been struck down, nevertheless climbs to the very top, it is better even for him to be silent than to speak, for even in the face of humiliation, a living being must endure ten-fold [retribution].
Here, by means of the general statement (*sāmānya*), the specific point (*viśeṣa*)— that even for one who has fallen, silence is better than speech— is suggested.
He spoke thus:
"O gentle one, if you have been placed within my heart, why do you not take away my life?"
"By the will of the Lord, poison may sometimes become nectar, or nectar may become like poison.
Here, by the will of the Lord, even that which causes harm may become beneficial.
Although "acting as a benefactor" was the general topic under discussion, the specific quality of "acting for one's own detriment" has been stated;

thus, this is a *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter) based on *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). In the case of a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), it is the actual departure itself that is taken up as the reflection of the subject matter; here, however, it is through its state of being overwhelmed by sorrow...
Since the substitution of *ś* is not established [in that context], its existence there is not possible.
The Tenth Chapter:
"The moon is as if smeared with lampblack; the gaze of the deer-eyed women is as if dulled; the coral leaf has lost its redness as if by darkness; and the luster of gold is as if turned to black."
"In this [verse], from the eyes of the female cuckoos, which are like the petals of a *kārka* flower, and from the peacocks, which are as it were fit for the presence of Sītā—
" here, from the eyes and so forth belonging to the cuckoos and others, which are being imagined... [the rest of the sentence appears to be truncated].
From these [words], the intended cause— the specific beauty residing in her face and so forth— is perceived.
"When I said, 'I am going,' Mṛgajā let out a sigh..."
"Who is this that, having scrutinized my face with a single eye, has cleared away the impurity of doubt?
Now, let the love offered by me be likewise bound to the circle of dear friends"— thus was she addressed with a smile by her friend, whose joy was increasing.

In this instance, a cause has been stated for an effect consisting of the non-occurrence of something. When that which is not the subject at hand (aprastuta) is expressed through similarity (tulyābhidhāna), it is of two kinds: based on the state of being a remainder (śeṣabhūlā) and based on mere invisibility (adṛśyamātramūlā).

That which is based on the state of being a remainder is also twofold: as a simile (upamā) and as a metaphor (rūpaka); and in the case of the metaphor, there is also the metaphorical identification of the remainder with the object to be compared (śeṣavadviśeṣya).
It becomes twofold; according to the sequence, as follows:
"The mango tree, possessing a pervasive fragrance, adorned with the beauty of spring,
radiant in luster, glorious, and thick with flower buds"—
here, by virtue of the [intended] specific quality, [the meaning refers to] a certain person from whom the irrelevant mango tree [is distinguished].
And the cognition of the suggested meaning is indeed what is under discussion:
"Even if he were to melt away like a drop of collyrium, even if he were to go to the depths of the underworld,
even if he were to become as small as a mustard seed through the power of destiny..."
"Even this entire universe is awakened"—
such is the direction revealed by a certain Puruṣottama in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.

In this case, because of the extensive renown of the term *puruṣottama* as a qualifier, Viṣṇu alone is first understood; by that, a certain person who is the subject of description is perceived. An example based on similarity is as follows:
"A single young pigeon, while armies by the hundreds rush toward him with cries of 'Sudhā'!
The sky is devoid of cover—Hari Hari! Only the compassion of the Creator is our refuge!"
Here, from the irrelevant pigeon (*kapota*), some relevant subject is understood. In some cases, this occurs even through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). For example:
"Blessed indeed are the winds in the forest, as cool as they are in rivalry with the *kahlāra* lilies."
"Those who touch Rāma, who is dark as a blue lotus, are obstructed by their sins."

In this regard, the incongruity (*vaidharmya*) consisting of "the wind is fortunate, I am unfortunate" has been introduced; it is countered [by the following]. This [incongruity] is of three kinds, according to whether the expressed subject is possible, impossible, or both. Among these, the examples for the possible have already been given. As for the impossible, for example:
“I am a cuckoo and you are a crow; we are equal as crows.
However, those who are experts in the art of sweet warbling will speak of the difference between us.”

In this case, the dialogue between the crow and the cuckoo is impossible without the superimposition of the subject at hand (*prastutārthāropaṇa*). An example of both forms [of *asambhava*] is as follows:
"You adorn the internal cavities with thorns, while the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*) blazes outside."
"How might my virtues not become as fragile as the fibers of a lotus stalk?"

Here, without the superimposition (adhyāropaṇa) of anything irrelevant, the fact that the holes in the tips of the lotus stalks are impossible causes for the breaking of the string, whereas for others it is possible,
constitutes its dual nature. And because of this, the designation "samāsokti" (synecdoche/metaphorical expression) applies due to the predominance of superimposition.

Tenth Chapter: The distinction from *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) lies in the fact that in *upamādhvani* (suggestion of simile), the unstated subject (*aprastuta*) is the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
Likewise, in *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia), both [the stated and the unstated] are expressed as the literal meaning (*vācya*).

The figure of speech *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) has been described. When praise and censure are understood through the words of censure and praise respectively, and when praise is understood through censure, it is called *vyājastuti* based on the etymological derivation: "praise by means of a pretext (*vyāja*)."
Praise that is intended as censure is praise in the form of a pretext when it is understood as such. Examples in order, beginning with my own: This is mine.
"O King, even though you are enraged, the wives of your enemies have become as trusting as before, wearing ornaments of worn-out pearls and carrying staffs bristling with thorns."
"O cloud, this 'praise by artifice' (vyājastuti) has been uttered by me regarding you: that your waters serve as the very life for the life of the world.
But let this great [irony] of yours be noted, O King of Clouds!"
"You provide assistance to travelers by destroying [their] paths."
(78) *Paryāyokta* (Indirect Expression) occurs when that which is already implied is stated by means of a particular artifice. An example:
"Those [trees] in the Nandana grove were touched by Śacī, marked by the enjoyment of her hair."
"By whose soldiers the couch of the *pārijāta* tree was seized"—

here, although it is already suggested that Hayagrīva has conquered heaven, this is stated as the cause (*kāraṇa*) in the form of a specific distinction in order to convey a particular strikingness (*vaicitrya*), namely, the contempt shown by the army toward the *pārijāta* couch.

This has been stated by way of the meaning of "the figure of speech based on rivalry" (*spardhanarūpaka*). Nor is this [an instance of] "Suggestion of the Unrelated" (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*)— as defined in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*— because in that case the effect (*kārya*) is what is irrelevant (*aprastuta*), whereas here it is the process (*vartanīya*) that is relevant.
The effect is also introduced here, just like the cause, because it makes known the excellence of [her] power. And so:
"By him, as he wiped away the teardrops from her breasts, which were as large as pearls..."
The sword of the science of enemies was delivered back [to him] by a mere mention of its name,
even without arrows.

[The figure] *Dīpaka* (Illuminator) consists in the fact that the qualifier alone is introduced everywhere as being beautiful.
And here, all the causes descend together, like pigeons on a threshing floor.

“[The opponent argues: ‘The status of being an ornament (*alaṅkāratva*) belongs [to Rasa] merely by virtue of its assistance; in the case of metaphors (*rūpaka*) and the like, there is a primary [status], whereas in the case of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and so forth, it is a subordinate addition according to the maxim of the goat’s nipple. [To this we reply: ‘But the learned [hold that] through the assistance of the expressed meanings and the expressive words—which serve as the subordinate parts (*aṅga*)—and through the primary elements such as the *rasas* and so forth, which act as the principal body (*aṅgin*), [the ornamentation occurs] by way of the embellishment of the expressed meanings and the expressive words.’”

Those who provide assistance [to the primary meaning] receive the designation of "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*). However, in the case of *samāsokti* (synecdoche), they maintain that only the conventional usage of terms such as "lord" (*nātha*) and so forth constitutes the ornament, not the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), because the latter lacks the aforementioned mode of operation. For this very reason, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* stated:
The Tenth Chapter:
"In that poem where the rasa and other elements are subordinate to another primary sentence-meaning, my view is that rasa and so forth constitute the ornament (alaṅkāra)."

If, moreover, the status of being an ornament were based merely on the assistance rendered to rasa and so forth, then the same would necessarily apply to the expressive words and other elements as well. And thus, that which has been stated by some—namely, "when rasa and the like are the predominant factor (aṅgin), there is the ornament *rasavat* and so forth; but when they are subordinate (aṅga), there is the second ornament, *udātta*"—is also [refuted].
Refuted:
(755) If these very same figures of speech are mutually mixed together, then there are two distinct figures of speech: *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) and likewise *saṅkara* (blending).

Just as even among worldly ornaments, when they are mixed with one another, each retains its distinct beauty and thus constitutes a separate ornament, so too among the poetic ornaments described above,
when they are mutually combined, there are two distinct ornaments known as *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) and *saṅkara* (commixture). Regarding these:
(756) The coexistence of these [figures] without mutual dependence is called *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling).
This refers to these figures of word, meaning, and ornament. For example:
"May the Lord, whose eyes are like smiling blue lotuses, protect us from the states of woe."
The swan that destroys the darkness of saṃsāra, the subduer of Kaṃsa.

Here, in the phrase "pāyādapāyāditi," there is a *yamaka* (rhyme), and in the word "saṃsāra," there is an *anuprāsa* (alliteration); thus, there is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) of two verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*). In the second quarter, there is a simile (*upamā*) and a metaphor (*rūpaka*); thus, there is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* of two semantic ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*). [This applies] to both.

(757) Because it persists, there is a commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of verbal and semantic figures; when figures stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgitva*), they constitute a single unified figure;
and when there is doubt, there is a blending (*saṅkara*). Furthermore, this [blending] is of three kinds.
In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*,
subordination (*aṅgibhāva*) is as follows:
"He describes the coils of the lord of serpents, which are pure with speed..."
Where the Mandākinī river wound for a long time around the base of the mountain, as if to soothe the pain of its pride, like a mass of wind enveloped by a whetstone.
Here, there is an *apahnuti* (concealment) consisting of the superimposition of the Mandākinī upon the emerald slab by means of its concealment.

And that [superimposition] is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the *śleṣa* (paronomasia), because the winding around the base of the foot—which is the actual object of the Mandākinī—is made to appear as the winding around the foot of the god [Śiva]. Furthermore, the winding around the base of the foot is itself the *śleṣa*.

The "wrapping around the base of the feet" is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*); and the "excessive whiteness," expressed as "as if for the sake of allaying the pain of grief," is a subordinate element of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). And since this poetic fancy leads one to perceive the behavior of the ocean, the Mandākinī, and the heroine as a bridegroom, a river, and a woman respectively, it is a subordinate element of the metaphorical identification (*samāsokti*). Or, for example:
"The twilight is full of passion, and the day stands before it;
oh, how strange is the course of fate, for even so, there is no union."

In this instance, *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression) is the distinguishing factor. An example of *sandehasamāsa* (compound doubt) is as follows: "This lunar orb shines in the sky, piercing the dense darkness and bestowing intense joy upon the night-lilies."

In this case, is it *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) because of the identification of the face with the moon; or is it *rūpaka* (metaphor) because, having determined "this" to be the face, the quality of being the moon is superposed upon it; or rather, is it [the third type of *rūpaka*] where both the face and the lunar orb—the two subjects—are identified through a single common attribute?

Is it *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), or is the moon the suggester (*dīpaka*) of the subject at hand? Or is it *samāsokti* (speech of brevity) due to the similarity of attributes, whereby the face—the subject at hand—is understood through the mention of the moon, which is not the subject at hand?
Or is it *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), wherein the subject at hand, the face, is understood by means of the description of the moon, which is not the subject at hand?

The Tenth Chapter: Since the time that inflames the god of love has been described by means of the description of the moon, which is its own effect, this is *paryāyokti* (periphrasis); and because there is doubt among many ornaments [regarding the specific one], it is *sandeha* (doubt).

Confusion (*saṅkara*) occurs, for example, in the phrase "I kiss the moon of the face," where there is doubt as to whether it is a simile (*upamā*)—meaning "the face is like the moon"—or a metaphor (*rūpaka*)—meaning "it is the moon itself. However, this doubt does not persist when either a supporting or a subverting factor is present. For instance, in "I kiss the moon of the face... [the presence of the word "kiss" acts as a subverting factor that confirms the metaphor].

In this context, the fact that kissing is favorable to the face serves as a proof for the simile (*upamā*), whereas its being unfavorable to the moon serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*) of the metaphor (*rūpaka*). In the expression "the moon-face shines," the attribute called "shining" proves the metaphor because it is applied figuratively to the face.
The phrase "it is possible" does not invalidate the simile:
"Queen Lakṣmī embraces Nārāyaṇa intensely.
Here, the embrace of a woman by the hero is indicated as being appropriate for one who is his equal.
Because a *liṅga* (mark/sign) is possible in a king, it subverts the *upamā* (simile); because it is possible in Nārāyaṇa, it constitutes a *rūpaka* (metaphor).

In the example, "Thus the lotus-face of the deer-eyed one shines with its flickering eyes," there is a subversion of the *upamā* because the presence of eyes is possible in the face, [whereas it is not possible] in the lotus.

Furthermore, because it is impossible [for both to coexist], the metaphor (rūpaka) acts as a sublater (bādhaka). Likewise, in instances such as "the beautiful lotus-face," since the common attribute is explicitly stated, a compound based on simile (upamitasamāsa)—which according to the rule "that which is compared with tigers and the like [forms a compound] when the common attribute is not stated"—is not possible; thus, the metaphor is the sublater of the simile.

And thus, in this case, it is simply a *rūpaka* compound according to the rule for the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*. An example of simultaneous entry (*ekāśrayānupraveśa*) is as follows in my own work: "If she were to look at me even for a moment, even from the corner of her eye..."

In the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*:
"Who indeed could be an embrace that is not a treasury?"

In the phrase “kaṭācecāpīvatvaramapi,” there is alliteration (*dekānuprāsa*) based on the letter *da*; and in the word “birīceta,” by taking the letter *ca*, there is rhyme (*vṛttyanuprāsa*). Thus, these two reside in a single locus. In this way, here too, there is the coexistence of alliteration and the figure of speech known as *arthāpatti*. Or, for example: “saṃsāradhyā-” [and so forth].

And in the phrase “nāvidhvaṃsa,” there is both a metaphor (*rūpaka*) and alliteration (*anuprāsa*). Or, for example: “*kuravakā ravakāracatāṃ yayuḥ*. Here, *ravakāravakāḥ* is one [instance of alliteration] and *vakāravakāraḥ* is another; thus, there is a charm (*camatkāra*) arising from two distinct [sounds]. Or, for example:
“On these auspicious days of the bright fortnight,
during the sacred months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada, [there is] the splendor of the songs of the peacocks and the pure lotuses.
Here, in the phrase “during the sacred months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada,” there is one [instance of] the word *śrāvaṇa*.
Thus, there is a simile (*upamā*); in the phrase "among the rows of lotus petals," a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is employed.

Having examined this *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, a treatise composed by the illustrious King of Poets, Viśvanātha Kavirāja, who is a moon among great poets under the auspicious Candraśekhara, may the wise take pleasure in it.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra, rejoice indeed in happiness!
As long as the beauty of Nārāyaṇa’s body, resembling the moon at its fullness, continues to adorn his limbs,
so long may this celebrated composition of the poets remain renowned in the world.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
And thus ends this Sāhityadarpaṇa.
Oṃ tat sat.

O traveler, on these days that have turned dark with the coolness of fresh rain-clouds, it is beautiful to see the flocks of peacocks performing their dance with necks outstretched. [Sanskrit Text] [Commentary].
